articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Ukrainian troops infiltrate Russian rear near Kupiansk through 15 kilometers of gas pipelines
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Ukrainian troops infiltrate Russian rear near Kupiansk through 15 kilometers of gas pipelines
Key developments on Oct. 22:
- Ukrainian troops infiltrate Russian rear near Kupiansk through 15 kilometers of gas pipelines, Khartiia says
- Ukraine to gain access to NATO procurement system for weapons, ammunition, Financial Times says
- Ukrainian military intelligence reveals new Russian cruise missile 'Filin'
- Ukrainian partisans claim sabotage of military communications near major Moscow data center
- Deadly Russian missile strike on Kyiv used cluster warheads, hours after Putin-Witkoff meeting
Ukrainian troops infiltrated the rear of Russian forces near Kupiansk in Kharkiv Oblast after moving about 15 kilometers (9 miles) through underground gas pipelines, Ukraine's National Guard’s 2nd Khartiia Corps said on Oct. 22.
The operation, code-named "Veles," was carried out by the 2nd Khartiia Corps together with other Ukrainian units, according to the corps.
Khartiia commander Brig. Gen. Ihor Obolienskyi said Ukrainian forces had studied how Russian troops were using underground routes and anticipated that they would try to exploit major gas pipelines running through Kharkiv Oblast.
"The Russians intended to use the gas routes to penetrate the rear of our forces. So we went underground ourselves," Obolienskyi said.
According to Khartiia, Ukrainian troops moved through the pipelines before combining the underground advance with operations above ground, including drone strikes.
The corps said more than 30 Russian soldiers were captured during the operation and that Russian forces suffered more than 100 casualties. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify those figures.
Obolienskyi said the aim was both to stop Russian troops underground and to undermine tactics they had been using on the ground and from the air.
"We anticipated the enemy's actions and mastered the tactics of conducting combat operations underground," he said.
Russian forces have used gas pipelines on several occasions to move troops covertly around the Kupiansk sector. In January, Ukrainian troops said they had stopped a Russian assault involving about 50 soldiers attempting to advance through the Soyuz gas pipeline.
More recently, Khartiia said, Russian troops retreating near Kupiansk used civilians as human shields, leading a group that included children and elderly people to the Shebelinka–Ostrogozhsk pipeline and forcing them inside the pipe toward Russian-held territory. Ukrainian troops said they did not open fire, because civilians were present
"When the battlefield became transparent, the war went underground," the corps said when it first announced the operation on Oct. 21.

Ukraine to gain access to NATO procurement system for weapons, ammunition, Financial Times says
Ukraine will be able to purchase weapons, ammunition, and other military equipment through NATO's centralized procurement agency, potentially giving Kyiv faster and cheaper access to defense supplies, the Financial Times reported on Oct. 22.
Ukraine is entering a partnership with the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA), which handles procurement and logistical support for alliance members and partners, according to the Financial Times.
"It provides Ukraine with the ability to have a more structured framework to leverage a broad range of capabilities that we offer: procurement expertise, support services, and access to established industrial base," Jacqueline Borsboom, NSPA's director of support to operations, told the Financial Times.
The arrangement might allow Ukraine to use NATO's existing procurement system and supplier network rather than negotiating each purchase independently.
The NSPA also held an event in Kyiv last week attended by about 150 Ukrainian companies, explaining how manufacturers could register as eligible suppliers and compete for contracts, according to the Financial Times.
The new mechanism is separate from the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), under which NATO allies and partners fund purchases of U.S.-made weapons and ammunition for Ukraine. More than $6 billion in military equipment has been funded through PURL since the initiative was launched in July 2025, according to NATO.
The agreement comes as Kyiv seeks to diversify and stabilize its access to military supplies amid growing uncertainty over U.S. support.
In recent weeks, Ukraine has reported disruptions to some U.S.-provided capabilities, including intelligence sharing and the Starshield satellite system used by Ukrainian forces. President Volodymyr Zelensky said after talks in Oslo this week that efforts were underway to resolve those issues.

Ukrainian military intelligence reveals new Russian cruise missile 'Filin'
Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) announced details of a new Russian cruise missile called "Filin" and released a 3-D model of the missile alongside a list of components and electronics on its website on Oct. 22.
Russia began using the missile at the end of summer, HUR said, calling it a continuation of a Russian trend to build "inexpensive air attack means with jet propulsion and ground-based launch."
The missile is 3.5 meters long with a wingspan of 3 meters, ablte to carry either 50 kilogram or 100 kilogram warheads, HUR said. It can fly both at ultra-low altitudes and up to 6 kilometers (about 3.7 miles) high, at a top speed of 800 kilometers per hour (about 497 miles per hour), across a distance of 1,200 kilometers (about 745 miles), according to the agency.
Some parts of the missile are apparently 3-D printed, HUR said, while the electronic component base of the onboard equipment is similar to other Russian missiles, but stands out for the increased share of Chinese components. Besides Chinese components, the agency also said the "Filin" included 35 U.S.-made components.
The onboard equipment is manufactured by PLAZ LLC, which is also involved in producing the Harpiya drone, HUR said, while the engine is the Russian-made R500, produced by Reynolds LLC.
Russia uses cruise and ballistic missiles to strike at Ukraine, and increasingly at the country's energy infrastructure. On Oct. 22, Russian ballistic missiles and cluster munitions struck transport and medical infrastructure in Kyiv in several waves overnight, killing at least one person and injuring 24 others.
"Three waves of ballistic strikes were launched by Russian 'humanists' on Kyiv since the evening," President Volodymyr Zelensky commented on the attack.
Russian forces launched a mass combined attack overnight with Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles, as well as 210 drones of various types, including 110 jet-powered drones, the Air Force reported. Zelensky said Russia fired 21 missiles.

Ukrainian partisans claim sabotage of military communications near major Moscow data center
Agents of the Ukrainian partisan group Atesh said they disrupted Russian military communication lines around IXcellerate, one of Moscow's largest commercial data center operators, to interfere with Russian air-defense coordination and help Ukrainian drones reach their targets, the group said on Oct. 21.
"We are disabling the enemy's channels, disrupting command and control, and helping UAVs reach their targets," Atesh said.
The group claimed Russia's Defense Ministry uses infrastructure linked to IXcellerate for military communications and air-defense command systems, while concealing that traffic within civilian server networks.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claim, and Atesh did not provide details on the extent or duration of the disruption. There has been no public confirmation from Russian authorities or IXcellerate that military communications were affected.
IXcellerate operates several data centers across Moscow and describes itself as a leading commercial data center operator in Russia. Its facilities host telecommunications and other digital infrastructure used by banks, retailers, and business customers.
The partisan group has previously claimed sabotage operations against Russian military and defense-linked infrastructure inside Russia, including attacks on railway and energy facilities.

Deadly Russian missile strike on Kyiv used cluster warheads, hours after Putin-Witkoff meeting
Russian ballistic missiles and cluster munitions struck transport and medical infrastructure in Kyiv in several waves overnight on Oct. 22, killing at least one person and injuring 24 others, according to Ukrainian officials, only hours after U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff visited Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg.
The Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office reported these numbers in the morning, saying Russia had struck across Holosiivskyi, Obolonskyi, Pecherskyi, Svyatoshynskyi and Dnipro dsitricts in Ukraine's capital.
Among the injured are four children, one of whom has been hospitalized, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said.
"Last night, the Russians used, among others, three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads against Kyiv. The peculiarity of these missiles is that they explode in the air, hitting the target, and hit everything around within a diameter of 400 meters," President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
"Three waves of ballistic strikes were launched by Russian 'humanists' on Kyiv since the evening," Zelensky commented on the attack earlier.
During a meeting with Putin in St. Petersburg, Witkoff lauded Putin — wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes in Ukraine — as a "humanitarian."
Russian forces launched a mass combined attack overnight with Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles, as well as 210 drones of various types, including 110 jet-powered drones, the Air Force reported. Zelensky said Russia fired 21 missiles. Ukrainian air defenses shot down 181 drones, including 87 jet-powered ones, according to the Air Force. Strikes were recorded at 32 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at eight others.
Presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said that the Iskander missiles carried a K5 cluster munitions warhead.
"This warhead explodes above the ground and is specifically designed to cause maximum damage to people and equipment in an area of 400 by 400 meters," Beskrestnov said.
"This strike was not carried out with a military purpose. The goal was to destroy part of the old city and injure as many people as possible," he added.
Zelensky said one of the missiles struck Pechersk, in Kyiv's historic center, in an area between the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra and the Sviato-Vvedensky Monastery. Buildings belonging to the monastery, residential buildings, shops, cafes and other civilian infrastructure were damaged, he said.
"There was not even theoretically any military facility nearby," Zelensky said. "It was a deliberate choice of weapon, a deliberate choice of the area of use, a deliberate attempt to inflict as many casualties and as much damage on civilians as possible."
Zelensky reported two people were killed and 34 injured, including five children, in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast as a result of the attacks.

articles.title: Michael Wynne, Fired as SECAF Alongside CSAF Moseley, Dead at 82
articles.body:
Michael Wynne, the 21st Secretary of the Air Force died Oct. 17. He was 82 years old.
Wynne was Secretary from 2005 to 2008, a stretch of time when the U.S. military was struggling to quell insurgencies in Iraq and Afghanistan and the Army was struggling to simultaneously man occupation forces in two theaters. Roadside bombs and insurgent attacks were killing U.S. troops, and the Air Force was under intense pressure to support its sister service with increased intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance coverage and manpower and force cuts to ease the Army’s burden.
The Air Force was also fighting to protect its modernization efforts at the time, especially the F-22 Raptor program, which was less than halfway to its objective of 750 planes, new tankers (which would ultimately become the KC-46), and a future bomber (which would eventually yield the B-21).
In 2006, an Air Force B-52 took off from Minot Air Force Base, N.D., and flew to Barksdale Air Force Base, La., its crew unknowingly carrying nuclear weapons on board, a so-called “bent spear” incident. The discovery kicked off an investigation, recriminations, self-examination, and subsequent organizational, procedural, and cultural changes across the nuclear community.
The incident added to the tension between the Air Force and then-Secretary of Defense Robert Gates, who saw the service and particularly then-Chief of Staff Gen. T. Michael “Buzz” Moseley as recalcitrant in their pushback over budget, manning, and modernization. Seeing Wynne and Moseley as a close knit tandem, Gates fired both in June 2008, beheading the service—the first-ever simultaneous removal of a service chief and secretary.
Military Roots
Wynne hailed from a military family and followed his father’s footsteps to attend the U.S. Military Academy at West Point, graduating at the height of the Vietnam War. Among his 578 classmates, 30 died in Vietnam and about 100 others were wounded in fighting in Southeast Asia.
Instead of joining the Army, however, Wynne followed his older brother into the Air Force, reporting for Active Duty in August 1966.
“The day I reported for Active Duty, the report of my brother being shot down was announced,” Wynn recalled in a 2005 interview with the Washington Post. Maj. Patrick Wynne, a 1963 graduate of the U.S. Air Force Academy, had trained as a pilot, and was assigned to the 555th Tactical Fighter Squadron in Thailand. After only four months in country, his F-4C Phantom was shot down over Vietnam on Aug. 8, 1966. He was declared missing in action, and remained so until 1977, when his remains were identified and later returned to the United States. He is buried at the Air Force Academy.
The younger Wynne served seven years in the Air Force, his final tour as an assistant professor of astronautics at the Air Force Academy.
Wynne then went to work for General Dynamics. For the next 26 years, he worked as an executive there, save for a three-year stint with Lockheed Martin after Lockheed acquired GD’s Space Systems Division. His work during in those years spanned General Dynamics’ F-16 and M1A2 tank divisions as well as space systems, including work on the Atlas, Titan, and Centaur launch vehicles.
In 2001, Wynne joined Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld’s Pentagon leadership team. Following the election of President George W. Bush, Wynne was confirmed as Principal Deputy Undersecretary of Defense for Acquisition, Technology, and Logistics, the start of a seven-year run in public service. In 2003, he was made Acting Undersecretary and he remained in that role until June 2005. Among his tasks at the time were leading the Pentagon’s preparations for the 2005 Base Realignment and Closure plan, which sought to “rationalize” the Defense Department’s far-flung bases and increase cross-service cooperation.
The 2005 BRAC results proved disappointing. Projected to save the Pentagon more than $25 billion annually by 2011, the plans failed to deliver due to higher-than anticipated construction costs, inflation, and incorrect assumptions. Instead of savings, the changes yielded a net cost increase, even when spread out over 20 years.
As Air Force Secretary, Wynne opposed efforts to consolidate and adopt joint basing, having come to embrace the Air Force’s explanation that many of its units operate and fight from their home bases rather than deploy to forward theaters.
“The Air Force has a very different concept of operations,” he would tell Air Force Magazine in 2008, weeks after his departure. Putting Air Force bases under the control of other services would undermine combat effectiveness, he said, adding, “I’d probably get fired again over my objection to the way the joint basing is happening.”
During his Air Force tenure, Wynne came under increasing pressure to cut the service’s budget, force structure, and modernization, and increasingly found himself in opposition to Gates, who took over as Secretary about a year after Wynne had been moved to the Air Force.
While he tried to justify force cuts in a 2006 interview, citing emerging technology like cell phones and more capable aircraft as supporting the case for downsizing by a planned 40,000 troops, “trimming in advance of new systems coming on and planning for the future right now,” he acknowledged that the current way the force was being utilized was unsustainable. At the time, 5,000 Airmen were doing Army jobs in Iraq, primarily jobs like convoy duty. “At some point in the future, it doesn’t work in the math—the Army has to pick up combat service support,” he said.
Wynne also butted heads with Gates over the F-22. While Gates suggested the Air Force could give up the “exquisite” F-22 because the then-fledgling F-35 was scheduled to join the fleet in 2014, Wynne disagreed.
“The notion of the F-22 [is] … similar to the F-35—we need to get rid of that,” Wynne said in his 2008 debrief with Air Force Magazine. The F-35, rather, “complements the F-22, but the F-22 is clearly an air superiority and air dominance weapon. The F-35 is a multinational, multirole, [air-to-ground] versatile airplane.”
The Air Force’s pursuit of a new tanker aircraft, a protracted and contentious effort that preceded him and would continue to drag on for years, was another challenge during Wynne’s tenure. As Secretary, he pressed for a single tanker aircraft rather than splitting the order between Boeing and Airbus platforms, as some urged. But after departing the Pentagon, he reconsidered, seeing value in it. He also came to regret not requiring that tankers become network nodes, an extra role for which they might have been well-suited.
And while many in the Pentagon failed to appreciate the Air Force’s contributions to the war in Iraq, Wynne became a strong advocate, noting that the 2007 “surge” of forces in Iraq was not merely an Army ground operation. “We surged 400 percent in the number of sorties and 1,000 percent in the pounds of ordnance dropped,” he said in a press conference on his final day in office. “What happened? I would tell you that what happened was the realization that we could get connectivity between the ground commanders and the air component—that there was true situational awareness available.”
On June 5, 2008, Gates decided he’d had enough. Wynne and Moseley were en route to a Corona meeting of Air Force leaders at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, when Gates demanded their resignations.
The stated reason was the failures of Air Force leadership to safely steward the security of nuclear weapons. But by then it was generally well known that Gates and the Air Force were at odds on a number of issues, from the number of “orbits” flown by surveillance drones over Iraq and Afghanistan to support troops operating on the ground to what Gates termed “next-war-itis” in the Air Force’s conviction that it needed high-end stealth fighter jets to deter a rising China in the Pacific.
Moseley, in an interview, recalled his close working relationship with Wynne as “a privilege and a gift.” The two tried to meet daily and they shared a perspective both in terms of their duty and vision for the service. They also became friends.
“Mike Wynne and I had the best relationship of any that I’ve seen with 13-plus secretaries I worked with,” Moseley said. Wynne was well versed in the workings of the Pentagon hierarchy, the needs of each of the services, and how to get things done, the former chief said. “But he also understood the theater logistics, the technology to address the new world, and he understood the acquisition process better than anybody.”
Together, they worked to lay out and explain their priorities, the need for increased resources—estimated then to be $20 billion annually to modernize, in order:
- tankers
- search and rescue
- satellites that could be protected from cyber and maneuver attack
- F-35s to replace the F-16
- a new bomber
They laid out that plan shortly before the firing in a Pentagon meeting with Gates and other officials. Mosely recalled that afterward Wynne declared the presentation a success.
“I think that meeting went well,” Wynne told him, draping an arm around Moseley’s shoulder as they walked the Pentagon hallway. “But I think we’re both dead.”
Wynne may have been the only one who saw it coming.
When the decision came down to fire them, both were at Scott Air Force Base, en route to Dayton for a planned Corona meeting of Air Force leadership at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio. Moseley was ordered back to Washington, where Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Adm. Mike Mullen delivered the news. In Dayton, Wynne was told to stand by for an unscheduled visit from Deputy Secretary of Defense Gordon England, who was flying in. No reason was given. Was England coming to discuss Moseley’s successor, someone wondered. “No,” Wynne said. “He’s coming for me.”
As the Corona meeting unfolded, Moseley called Wynne from Washington to say he was being relieved. Reporters began to call before England even arrived, adding to Wynne’s convictions. CNN might have been first to report the firings. Defense News Editor Vago Muradian, a rare press gallery guest at the Corona gathering, got his story out online on Defense News and Air Force Times. At the Pentagon, frustrated reporters gathered outside the press secretary’s office looking for answers; inside, staff was still trying to piece together what happened.
Two weeks later, Wynne departed the Pentagon at an official ceremony presided over by Gates, with Moseley at his side. What had been a very public firing was glossed over for public consumption as Gates pinned a medal on Wynne’s chest. Having Gates preside was Wynne’s idea, said retired Maj. Gen. Daryl Burke, Wynne’s military aide at the time. It was a challenge: Gates would either have to refuse or honor Wynne for his public service.
At the ceremony, Wynne expressed love for the service. “But it is the people of the Air Force that make the Air Force,” he added, “so in loving the Air Force, we love the people.”
Burke recalled how Wynne advised him to stand away as they awaited England’s arrival. Burke insisted he would stand with Wynne regardless, but Wynne was trying to ensure that Burke wouldn’t be damaged by association in the future by being seen as too closely associated with a politically unpopular boss. Wynne subsequently worked behind the scenes to find Burke a next assignment that would keep his career on track. In doing so, Wynne demonstrated both caring for his Airman and a savvy hand on the tiller for navigating Pentagon politics.
Lt. Gen. David Deptula, now dean of AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, was on the Air Staff at the time, recalling that Wynne kept working on the issues he believed in up to the very end—in particular, his opposition to joint basing.
“Secretary Wynne was a leader of uncommon integrity, genuine kindness, and extraordinary loyalty,” Deptula said. “He never confused holding a position of authority with the responsibility to do what was right. I witnessed his character firsthand when, even after learning he would be removed as Secretary of the Air Force, he continued working tirelessly to strengthen the service he loved. He put principle above position, loyalty above personal ambition, and the nation’s security above all else. In a famous action, when SECDEF Gates told Secretary Wynne to fire Chief of Staff, Buzz Moseley… Wynne refused. So, Gates fired both. The Air Force and our nation are better for his service, and I am better for having known him. He will be greatly missed.”
Robbin Laird, a military analyst and prolific writer who worked for Wynne during his Pentagon tenure, wrote admiringly of the former secretary in a remembrance, citing what he called the Wynne Doctrine: “If you are ever involved in a fair fight, it is the result of poor planning.”
“It is easy to hear it as swagger. It was the opposite,” Laird wrote. “A fair fight is one whose outcome is in doubt. When the outcome is in doubt, young Americans pay for that doubt with their lives. Mike believed a leader’s first duty was to make sure it never happens. That meant technology, organization, the unglamorous work of logistics and sustainment, and the discipline to think years ahead of the adversary.”
Michael Walter Wynne was born in Clearwater, Fla. He is survived by his wife Barbara and four married daughters.

articles.title: “Write like a 38-year-old Israeli woman”: The Kremlin used fake media and fabricated “experts” to spread disinformation in Israel
articles.body:
As Israel prepares for a key legislative election on Oct. 27, Kremlin-linked disinformation operatives in the country remain active. Their tools include not only media outlets and Telegram channels, but also a newer tactic: specially created “expert centers” that do not possess any actual expertise. Leaked files from Russia’s Social Design Agency (SDA) — described in detail in a recent investigation by The Insider — show which narratives Moscow has sought to promote in Israel and which local media outlets, influencers, rabbis, and even Knesset MPs have been drawn into the effort.
The Kremlin’s agenda in Israel
The Israeli social media space has been polluted by a range of anti-Ukrainian narratives — “NATO weapons supplied to Ukraine are ending up with Hamas!” and “Ukraine is forcibly conscripting Israeli citizens!” — which appear alongside posts from fake Ukrainian personas mocking Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claiming Ukraine had “brought the Israeli prime minister to heel” during a dispute over grain. As it turns out, the Moscow-based Social Design Agency was responsible for their creation and dissemination.
The SDA has been targeting Israel since at least early 2023. The country has a large Russian-speaking immigrant population, but the campaign was clearly intended to reach audiences beyond that community alone. Internal SDA documents connected with the international Doppelgänger campaign outlined four broad lines of messaging:
- “The war is over. The world after the war”
- “Change of government in Ukraine” — #OutgoingZelensky
- “Get America out of Europe!” — #GetAmericaOutofEurope
- “Sanctions against Russia are sanctions against the whole world. The end of the dream”
For obvious reasons, only the first two were deployed in Israel.
The SDA team was given specific performance targets, including the objective that after two months of work from the Russian side, mainstream Israeli media and online platforms would begin discussing possible postwar settlements for Ukraine, along with potential alternatives to Volodymyr Zelensky as president.
In June 2023, suggested SDA-driven article topics included:
- Undermining trust in the United States as a guarantor of Israel’s security.
- Arguing that several people in Zelensky’s circle could become Ukraine’s next president, including Valerii Zaluzhnyi, Kyrylo Budanov, Oleksii Arestovych, and even Olena Zelenska (but that only Zaluzhnyi would serve U.S. interests).
- Forecasts and parallels for Israel in the event that it supplied weapons or other aid to Kyiv.
Fake websites
The campaign did not go unnoticed. By July of 2023, intelligence officials had begun warning about Russian influence operations. Around the same time, cybersecurity company Cybereason determined that Russian propaganda and disinformation in Israel had initially been spread through X (then still known as Twitter) and Telegram.
“We uncovered the Russian government’s fake infrastructure in Israel, aimed at influencing public opinion by impersonating news websites,” Cybereason researcher Ilan Sokol said at the time. “As part of the campaign, well-known Israeli media outlets were forged. For example, the layout and content of the Walla website was copied. This was done to confuse visitors and make them believe they were on the real website.”
Impersonating legitimate media websites became a hallmark of the Doppelgänger campaign in 2022 and 2023, with Cybereason finding that websites imitating N12 and mako.co.il had also been created. Judging by the documents, in June 2023 the project was once again pitched to its client — i.e. the Kremlin — in an effort to secure an extension and increased funding.
By August, campaign planners were considering spreading graffiti and leaflets in Israel, and in September 2023, a report seeking another round of funding proposed highlighting the Israel campaign as an example of the effectiveness of the SDA’s “factory of augmented reality” — its internal term for producing fabricated content.
Then came Oct. 7, and the team developed new ideas and assignments.
How the Kremlin exploited the Oct. 7 attack
As a document dated Oct. 17, 2023 began: “There are currently several emerging trends that can be proactively developed into new and effective lines of attack. The United States is losing the remnants of its influence in the Middle East. The situation around Israel is heating up. And there is no guarantee that U.S. warnings to ‘leave Israel alone’ will be heeded. It is one thing to launch a massive missile strike and impose sanctions on two or three countries. But if the entire Arab and Muslim world is drawn into the war, this will become an extremely serious existential challenge from the Global South to the collective West. At the same time, it is obvious that the United States will leave the EU to deal with the problem on its own while taking shelter on its own continent.”
At an Oct. 20 meeting with Alexander Kharichev — a senior Kremlin official who has been linked in investigations to domestic political management and influence operations — participants proposed exploiting a statement by U.S. President Joe Biden about aid to Ukraine.
“$60 billion for Ukraine, $12 billion for Israel. We have nothing to argue with here. Talk about the shells transferred to Israel! As AXIOS writes! Push it! + they are sending 4,000 troops,” read notes from the meeting reviewed by The Insider.
The propaganda plan targeting Ukraine was adjusted at the same time.
“The U.S. redirected 155 mm shells to Israel instead of Ukraine. ‘Our’ 155 mm shells from the U.S. went to ‘them,’” one set of instructions read.
“Add examples involving aerial bombs and other weapons supplied to Israel. Emphasize the theme: ‘Why them and not us?’ They will get money/we won’t. All world leaders went to Israel, not Ukraine. Israel refused Zelensky entry, while Biden and Scholz entered the country without any problem. Western leaders are already redirecting all aid from us to the Jews, sending another aircraft carrier to Israel with more than 4,000 Marines aboard.”
Prompts intended for the authors of artificial social media comments added that the “first three narratives” should be pushed more heavily in western Ukraine “using traditional antisemitism.” Operatives were also instructed to spread rumors in Ukraine that Muslim units of the Armed Forces of Ukraine would leave to defend Palestine, as well as claims that Jewish troops were being released from the Ukrainian military to defend Israel.
When Readovka founder Alexei Kostylev joined meetings focused on disinformation in Ukraine, he suggested “planting among the Nazis” the idea that they should “go after Ze[lensky] for supporting the Jews.”
Project staff continued posting fake comments on social media.
Examples of AI prompts from April 2024 included:
“Talking points: The country is exhausted by military operations. Burnout and overwork among medical personnel are only one sign that the war has dragged on for too long. If the government had acted more decisively and wisely, and if the United States had really helped us, we would have won by now.
Write a 400-character comment from the perspective of a 38-year-old Israeli woman who believes Israel is overburdened by military spending. Medical workers are now under pressure and stress, as they were during the pandemic. The war is dragging on, and the United States is criticizing the methods used to conduct it. If the government had acted more decisively and wisely, and if the United States had truly helped us, we would have won by now.
Talking points: The government understands that it cannot solve the hostage problem and that the war is gradually reaching a dead end. The minister fled a meeting with evacuated citizens because he had nothing to tell them.
Write a 400-character comment from the perspective of a 45-year-old Israeli woman who thinks the minister is simply a coward. Instead of listening to the problems of people in need and trying to support them, he ran away! The Israeli government understands that it cannot solve the hostage problem and that the war is gradually reaching a dead end. The minister fled the meeting with evacuated citizens because he had nothing to tell them, but rushed to accuse them and call them a ‘loud minority’!”
Kremlin-sponsored content in legitimate media
In late 2023, articles that were also apparently commissioned as part of the project began appearing in genuine news outlets. Starting in November of that year, journalist Nick Kolyohin began putting out interviews in Walla with Israeli politicians, political scientists, and security experts, as well as with former hostage Roni Krivoi, who was said to have been released as a gesture of Hamas’ respect for Vladimir Putin.
Kolyohin presented the series as a joint Walla-Jerusalem Post project titled “The World on Fire,” but in violation of the outlets’ rules, he failed to disclose that the articles themselves had been sponsored by a Russian organization.
As Israeli media watchdog The Seventh Eye noted in its own investigation, the pieces were edited to emphasize themes of interest to the Kremlin, often by taking interviewees’ statements out of context.
For example, an interview with Likud lawmaker Hanoch Milwidsky was headlined: “Israel should focus on domestic affairs and avoid involvement in the Ukraine conflict.” However, in the video version of the interview, Milwidsky criticized Russia’s friendly relationship with Hamas — remarks that were omitted entirely from the published article.
The pieces were edited to emphasize themes of interest to the Kremlin
An interview with Tel Aviv University lecturer Yevgeny Klauber was edited in a similar way. In the video, viewers can hear Klauber criticizing Putin’s “disgusting statements” and even his “antisemitism.” Yet in the written version, only his criticism of the Ukrainian government remained.
The Seventh Eye’s investigation found that Kolyohin was paid for the series by an anonymous organization called the Russia-EU Communication Platform. Its website is now offline, but it previously published poorly formatted articles in Russian and English featuring experts criticizing sanctions, Ukraine, and NATO while praising Russian foreign policy. The Insider found that some of those experts were also part of the Social Design Agency’s pool of commentators.
Kolyohin, also known as Nikita Kulyukhin, was an obvious choice for promoting Russian narratives in Israel. His family moved there from St. Petersburg in 1992, when he was 9, and he speaks Hebrew, Russian, and English fluently.
A decade ago, Kolyohin worked as a special correspondent for Israel’s Channel 10, but his career there later ran into trouble when he produced an investigation into the Israeli Center for Cult Victims, eventually ending up in court after failing to disclose that it had been commissioned by Gilad But, the director of the right-wing organization Ad Kan.
In 2025, Kolyohin and a colleague were ordered to pay 755,000 shekels in damages (nearly 218,000 euros).
Kolyohin is known for more than commissioned articles. Since leaving Channel 10, he has worked mainly as a freelance reporter and regularly appears as a correspondent or “expert” in pro-Kremlin media, including on RT, Channel One, and Channel Five. Channel Five is controlled by National Media Group, whose board is chaired by Alina Kabaeva, widely reported to be Putin’s romantic partner and the mother of two of his children.
Kolyohin’s funding was most likely arranged with the help of the Social Design Agency, which actively involved him in its work. In leaked SDA correspondence, The Insider found a January 2025 proposal to bring “American Gen. Paul Vallely” into the project. As a campaign employee reported to the Kremlin:
“The speech by American Gen. Paul Vallely is ready. Script and screenshot are in the chat. Topic in brief: NATO is losing, Russia is winning. Important: Vallely is close to Trump and is perceived accordingly. Preliminary agreements have been reached with major Israeli media outlets for Vallely to publish ‘his’ experts through them. We are now preparing a letter from Vallely’s organization, the Stand Up U.S. Foundation, to the media and working out the financial arrangements. Probability of success: 90%.”
At the end of February 2025, an interview with Paul Vallely was indeed published by the Israeli radio station Galey Israel. It was summarized by none other than Nick Kolyohin, and the piece was edited much like the earlier interviews with Israeli experts — with an emphasis on narratives favored by the client.
The publication of the Hebrew-language interview then gave Russia’s state news agency TASS an opportunity to republish it less than a week later, saying that “a transcript was obtained by TASS” — without explaining where it had come from. Vallely himself later reposted the TASS text on his foundation’s website.
The main talking points argued that Trump would work with Putin to end the conflict, that “Russia will retain Ukraine’s four eastern regions,” that Zelensky would be replaced by another leader as early as 2025, that NATO would undergo fundamental changes due to the unpopularity of its policies, that the United States would sharply reduce its support for the alliance if Ukraine continued to be pushed toward membership, and that Europe would undergo a “shift to the right” that would see more leaders like Viktor Orbán come to power.
In a later conversation with OCCRP, Vallely said he did not remember giving any interview to Israeli media that he had no ties to Russia. Whether Vallely knew that his remarks would be used for Kolyohin’s Galey Israel publication remains unclear.
In 1980, Vallely, then commander of the U.S. Army’s 7th Psychological Operations Group, co-authored a paper titled “From PSYOP to MindWar: The Psychology of Victory” with his subordinate Michael Aquino, a psychological operations analyst and founder of the Satanist organization Temple of Set. In a preface to a 2003 reissue, Aquino noted that the paper had become a popular subject of conspiracy theories.
In 2005, Vallely founded the conservative organization Stand Up America US. It advocates for a strong national defense, secure borders, state sovereignty, support for the armed forces, limited government, and the protection of Americans’ First and Second Amendment rights. According to the organization’s co-founder, retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Thomas McInerney, its purpose is to defend the United States and explain the dangers of radical Islam and global jihad.
In 2010, Vallely was one of three retired generals who supported U.S. Army Lt. Col. Terrence Lakin, who refused deployment to Afghanistan on the grounds that Barack Obama was not a legitimate commander in chief. Vallely said at the time that many military personnel and civilians doubted Obama had been born in the United States, describing him as “a Muslim by nature” while refusing to rule out the possibility of a “civil uprising” against a president he accused of helping spread radical Islam.
Vallely has also voiced support for the QAnon movement, describing it as a “white hat” operation linked to a group of more than 800 military intelligence specialists advising the president. He has called Q posts a credible source of intelligence.
In 2020, Vallely was among 235 senior military figures who endorsed Donald Trump’s reelection.
Vallely has also visited Russia. He traveled there for Victory Day celebrations in 2014 and was in Moscow again in February and March 2017.
Who was behind the Israeli disinformation campaign
The project was led by Ilya Gambashidze, with Andrei Perla and Alexei Ulyanov serving as ideologues. Both also work for the Tsargrad media group, a Russian ultraconservative, pro-Kremlin media organization.
In the early 2010s, Perla worked as an aide to Igor Kholmanskikh, then the Russian president’s envoy to the Urals Federal District. In 2016, he became head of the Sevastopol government’s public communications department, but he did not remain in the position for long. After dismissing Gambashidze, Sevastopol’s acting governor tasked his successor with “correcting the mistakes accumulated by the department.” Despite that episode, the political consultant still describes himself as “the smart Jew at the governor’s side.”
Perla now works on ideological messaging for fake-content campaigns around the world. In November 2023, the U.S. State Department accused him of involvement in influence operations as far away as South America. Within the Doppelgänger campaign, he produces analysis and sociological material and supervises several staff members.
Alexei Ulyanov is an “advertising and PR specialist” from Tver. He once worked at a creative studio called “The Secret of the Selling Word,” was later declared wanted over unpaid child support, and then began working with the Social Design Agency as head of its writing team. That work led to his inclusion on a British sanctions list in 2025.
Alexander Balakshin handled operational planning and studied social media in Israel and other countries. Anastasia Kazakova served as head of social media operations. And Oleg Perelman translated texts into Hebrew. (Material was also translated into Arabic, but that translator’s identity is unknown.)
For the project, the SDA compiled a list of Israeli media outlets and experts through whom its preferred narratives might be promoted. It is not known with certainty how the list was used or whether any of the outlets or channels received payment for publications. The list is reproduced below:
Russian-language Israeli media targeted for work, including publication placements, comments, and expert opinions
- Novosti Israel — https://nikk.agency/
- Moskovsky Komsomolets — Israel — https://mkisrael.co.il/
- Novosti Izrailya — https://news.israelinfo.co.il/
- Isroil Information Center — https://isroil.info/
- ISRAland — Israeli News — https://isra.land/
Inauthentic comments were posted under messages in Telegram channels such as “Voice of Israel. Israel Now,” “Israel in Russian,” “Israeli Working Days,” and “Intellinews — Israel and the Middle East,” as well as channels run by political analysts Mikhail Pellivert, Mark Kotlyarsky, and David Eidelman.
As in SDA campaigns targeting Ukraine and various EU countries, for reporting purposes operators saved links to each posted comment and stored screenshots in a separate folder on Yandex Disk.
Russian émigrés in Israel as an influence target
The project produced several pitches aimed at shaping opinion among Russian émigrés who had left the country after the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Many of the proposals were likely approved, although perhaps not with full funding.
Particular attention was paid to the Russian diaspora in Israel. One internal proposal read:
“A significant group of émigrés settled in Israel. It is the only country where the number of ‘relocants’ can be reliably estimated on the basis of local official statistics.
Israel has received more than 60,000 Russian citizens since the start of the ‘special military operation.’ All these people now already have dual citizenship because, having Jewish roots, they exercised their right of return.
It is important to note that in Israel, new émigrés immediately found themselves in a specific environment with diverse political views.
The total number of Russian-speaking Israeli citizens is approximately 2 million to 2.5 million people, or more than 20% of the country’s population. This population has its own media, including several Russian-language television channels, radio stations, online media outlets, new media and Telegram channels.
Not all of these media can be considered anti-Russian. On the contrary, pro-Russian sentiment is quite widespread in Israel. According to a recent Pew Research Center poll, at least 16% of respondents in Israel trust Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Clearly, the goals of informational influence on the émigré community should be structured as follows:
1. Shift the attitudes of the majority of émigrés in a pro-Russian direction
- create a pro-Russian diaspora capable of influencing public opinion in host countries;
- increase the number of ‘frightened patriots’ who want and are prepared to return to the Motherland.
2. Discredit active anti-Russian émigrés in the eyes of the broader community of ‘relocated citizens,’ including by
- provoking divisions among the most active anti-Russian figures.
It appears that the best way to achieve these goals would be to create a group of media outlets aimed at émigré audiences.
These media outlets should not be formally connected to Russian state structures. Some of their representatives should themselves live in emigration and participate in events organized by émigré centers, conferences and so on.
Some of these media outlets should target Russian-speaking diasporas as a whole, while others should be geographically focused, above all on Israel, Turkey, Georgia, Armenia and Kazakhstan.”
How the Kremlin created fake “expert centers”
Participants in the Doppelgänger project proposed setting up nonprofit organizations in different countries that would resemble research institutes. The idea was to use them to recruit international experts and promote narratives useful to the campaign.
For example, the SDA requested $80,000 to launch a nonprofit in Israel, plus about 3 million rubles a month ($36,500) “for content creation, work with opinion leaders, and promotion.” It requested even more for an “Institute of Anti-Globalism, writing that “This project costs 5 million rubles a month” — upwards of $61,000.
Nikolai Tupikin also drafted what he called “a justification for strengthening and expanding the project with Israeli colonels from various intelligence services,” presenting the initiative as a form of Russian soft power.
In an apparent effort to justify the project to the Kremlin, the document stated: “Russian information warfare, through interference campaigns, helps Russia preserve its image as a superpower in a cost-effective way. The more Russia participates in active interference campaigns around the world, the stronger its image as a global power.”
An expanded presentation for the proposed Israeli institute said that “our narratives lack a legitimate source of information and a news hook,” but that “in Europe and other Western countries, the narratives we need already exist and enjoy sustained popularity.”
The project appears to have been approved by the Kremlin. In February 2025, someone acquired the domain ibi.institute (which had previously belonged to Instituto Iberoamericano), and used it to create a website for an entity called the International Burke Institute — IBI.
The website listed the United Nations office, UNICEF, UNESCO, the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), and the World Bank as partners. All of them told The Insider in response to inquiries that they were not and had never been partners of IBI.
The website, unsurprisingly, contained no reference to any connection between IBI and Russian experts. Nor did it provide an official address, information about its founders, or details about its financing.
As the disinformation specialists had promised in their pitch to the Kremlin, the site published “economic and political reviews of the country of the month.” In practice, however, reviews were produced for all countries at once in the form of a “sovereignty index.”
Judging by their style and language, the articles were generated using large language models and were almost certainly translated into English from Russian. They contained mistakes characteristic of machine translation or careless Russian-to-English work.
For example, an article about Russia referred to “Lugovoy’s Law (2020),” describing how “he consolidated…” — in English, unlike in Russian, a law would be referred to as “it,” not “he.”
Additionally, an article about the United States used the phrase “guerrilla struggle” where the intended meaning was “partisan struggle” — in the political sense of conflict between parties. The error reflects the fact that the Russian word partizansky can refer both to partisan politics and guerrilla warfare.
The reports also contained signs of AI-generated hallucinations, citing nonexistent UNESCO heritage sites such as “Gerngut” in Germany and “Imbargo” in the United States. Neither exists.
The IBI also claimed that Russia ranked 27th in a 2023 PISA study, even though no such PISA assessment was conducted that year. (The latest study available when the reports were prepared was conducted in 2022, and Russia did not participate.)
In August 2026, OpenAI published the results of an internal investigation showing that IBI content had in fact been produced using the company’s systems and that the operation was run by users in Russia. OpenAI blocked the group of ChatGPT accounts involved.
Although the IBI website was filled with generated content and false claims about institutional partners, the organization itself was indeed registered in Israel in July 2025. Its founders were Igor Kaminnik and Gabriel Mart, and board members with signing authority were Alexei Vilents and Roy Yaakov Yankelovich. The Insider has copies of the organization’s founding documents.
Igor Semyonovich Kaminnik is an Israeli citizen originally from Odesa, Ukraine. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, he was part of a circle of Odesa conceptual artists and belonged to the P. Fomsky collective, along with artist Pavel Fomenko. In the early 2000s, Kaminnik was involved in various civic organizations in Ukraine. In recent years, however, he has adopted a sharply pro-Russian position. “When he talks about Ukraine, it is nothing but Russian propaganda clichés,” a person who knows him personally told The Insider.
Kaminnik is listed as an expert with the Institute of the Newest States, a Russian organization founded by political analysts Modest Kolerov and Alexei Martynov.
Kolerov was the first head of the Kremlin’s Directorate for Interregional and Cultural Relations with Foreign Countries, created in 2005 as part of an effort to counter so-called “velvet revolutions,” the peaceful pro-democracy uprisings that had taken place across parts of the former Soviet bloc.
Martynov has spent about two decades in positions connected with Russian policy toward the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), a grouping of former Soviet republics. During that time, he has been declared persona non grata in Azerbaijan and Moldova.
Kolerov, meanwhile, has been barred for more than a decade from entering Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia, and Georgia.
In 2023, Kaminnik made repeated trips to Russia, including with his wife, Yulia Vasilyeva, and their daughter Tatyana.
Gabriel Mart sits on IBI’s audit committee and also serves with another organization, the Sholem Schwartzbard Memorial Foundation, named in honor of the Jewish writer and anarchist who assassinated Ukrainian political leader Symon Petliura in Paris in May 1926. In 2024, Mart participated in an IBI roundtable titled “The Heuristic Potential of Schizoanalysis,” where he was presented as a researcher at the Catholic University of the West. In one publication listing him as an employee of the university, The Insider found Mart’s other name: Innokenty Martynov.
Notably, Alexei Martynov’s real-life son — Innokenty Martynov — also works with Kaminnik. He travels frequently to Israel and has published several articles on psychoanalysis at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Anthropology and Ethnography under his Russian name.
Kaminnik also sits on the board of Israeli nonprofit Dor Moriah. The organization takes its name from a small street in Haifa near Kaminnik’s home and is registered at his residential address.
Dor Moriah also presents itself as a research center. Even its Russian-language website has a section labeled in English as a “think tank.” It contains articles with titles such as “Turkey is waging cognitive warfare against Israel in a format described in the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry’s communications strategy” and “How the opposition constructs a rejection of election results.”
Dor Moriah also publishes polling and sociological research, including on issues not obviously central to Israeli domestic politics, such as the Putin-Trump meeting in Anchorage.
Dor Moriah was founded in 2017, but it only began receiving substantial income — nearly 200,000 shekels annually ($64,000) — in 2023, the same year the SDA’s campaign in Israel began.
Its annual revenue in 2025 was almost 195,000 shekels, all of it from foreign donations. Israeli law requires disclosure only of donors who contribute at least 50,000 shekels during a reporting period.
In 2023, there were two such donors: Panagiotis Glazko, a Cyprus-based businessman with Greek citizenship, and a U.S. donor named Alan Licht.
In 2024, the only major donor was Israeli citizen Dan Piotkin. In other organizational documents, Piotkin is also listed as a member of Dor Moriah’s supervisory board and a co-author of its research.
Notably, Dor Moriah’s annual budgets vary substantially when measured in shekels. Converted into rubles at the exchange rate for each respective year, however, they come to roughly the same amount: 4.5 million rubles.
The governing party’s leading Russian-speaking rabbi
In April 2024, Dor Moriah announced the creation of a movement called Derech Eretz.
According to the official account, it was co-founded by Dor Moriah, the Sholem Schwartzbard Foundation, and an association called Turei Zahav, which has since been dissolved. Turei Zahav was headed by Rabbi Alexander Hayat, who in April 2024 became head of Derech Eretz.
Around the same time, Hayat posted several photographs with Kaminnik on Facebook.
Among Russian-speaking Israelis, Hayat is known primarily as head of the Russian-speaking branch of United Torah Judaism, one of Israel’s two ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties in the governing coalition. It is in that capacity that he gives interviews and participates in election events.
In Hebrew-language political circles, however, Hayat has been described as “the rabbi for immigrants from Russia in Likud,” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s party. In September 2025, the bar mitzvah of Hayat’s son was attended by Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, Justice Minister Yariv Levin, Environmental Protection Minister Idit Silman, coalition chairman Ofir Katz, Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee chairman Boaz Bismuth, and lawmakers Ariel Kallner and Osher Shkalim. Silman’s presence was not incidental: Hayat also serves as one of her advisers.
Meluhadim News, a Telegram channel close to Likud, regularly reports on Hayat’s work with the Russian-speaking community. In January 2026, he organized the enrollment of 100 Russian-speaking immigrants into the party. In the summer of 2025, he ran a campaign to recruit dozens of Russian speakers to Likud.
By May 2026, Hayat was being described as head of Likud’s Russian-speaking campaign headquarters. He led a meeting between Russian-speaking opinion leaders and Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, along with ministers Yariv Levin, Eli Cohen, Shlomo Karhi, and Zeev Elkin, and coalition chairman Ofir Katz.
Notably, by November 2025, Hayat was no longer attending internal Likud conferences in his personal capacity alone. By then, a group called Derech Eretz — “Russian Mobilization,” headed by Hayat — was participating in at least one such party conference.
Several independent sources confirmed Hayat’s cooperation with Igor Kaminnik to The Insider. One source said Kaminnik had claimed he paid Hayat a salary, an assertion that is indirectly supported by Dor Moriah’s reporting, which lists Derech Eretz activities among the organization’s work.
Dor Moriah’s 2025 annual report lists its areas of activity. In addition to conducting eight sociological studies, writing 15 analytical reports, and publishing 30 media pieces, the organisation also reported that “three open sessions and five working meetings were held in the Knesset devoted to promoting legislation regulating the activities of neighborhood councils in Israeli cities,” and it was also involved in ”development of the Derech Eretz movement, bringing together secular and religious Russian-speaking Israelis: eight working meetings with activists were held and recommendations were prepared for implementing projects at the local community level.”
In other words, work with the movement headed by Likud-linked Rabbi Hayat was listed as one of Dor Moriah’s core activities.
Both Kaminnik and the Burke Institute have also promoted Hayat’s work. Roy Yankelovich, head of the “institute” — and, in his day job, an Israeli sports journalist — wrote an opinion column about Hayat and Derech Eretz for TheJ.ca. Kaminnik, meanwhile, wrote about the movement in the Jerusalem Post, where he described his Dor Moriah nonprofit as Derech Eretz’s research center.
In the summer of 2025, businessman Yossi Prisman, from Samaria, helped Hayat establish a Derech Eretz youth organization. The two later fell out and are now suing each other. Prisman immediately recognized Kaminnik in a photograph.
“Hayat wasn’t paying his coordinators. When one of them asked him about the money, he pointed at Igor [Kaminnik] and said Igor would pay,” Prisman said.
One employee hired for the project has accused Hayat of failing to pay his wages. He told The Insider that the goal of the project was to create a nationwide Israeli political organization for young people with Russian roots. According to the source, Kaminnik attended one of the meetings. Another Dor Moriah representative, Alexei Vilents, a former municipal lawmaker in Moscow, also participated in events.
As part of the youth project, Derech Eretz organized a tour of Samaria for about 50 young people. It also held a wine evening with Russian-speaking businesspeople.
Lobbyists in the Knesset
Dor Moriah also works with sitting members of Israel’s parliament. In March 2025, the organization held a conference titled “Israel as an object of geopolitical confrontation.” Participants included Likud lawmaker Amit Halevi, Shas lawmaker Simon Moshiashvili, and Knesset Deputy Speaker Moshe Solomon of the Religious Zionism party. All three were members of the governing coalition at the time.
Lawmakers and other participants were told that “among world leaders capable of influencing the development of the Abraham Accords, aside from Donald Trump, Israelis primarily named representatives of BRICS countries: 28.9% named Vladimir Putin, 17% Xi Jinping, and 13.9% Narendra Modi.” They were also told that “70% of Israelis see a connection between the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the global confrontation between the West and the South.”
Coalition lawmakers even skipped a Knesset plenary session at which Netanyahu was speaking in order to attend the event. “The fact that these lawmakers left an important plenary meeting attended by the prime minister in order to attend a lobby meeting convincingly demonstrates the importance of the issues under discussion and the relevance of the initiatives being proposed,” Dor Moriah wrote.
The parliamentary lobby was registered by Amit Halevi. It is intended to promote three largely unrelated issues: creating neighborhood councils in Israeli citie, halachic banking (a system of financial services structured to comply with Jewish religious law, broadly analogous in concept to Islamic banking), and the idea of Israel’s future as “a bridge between the collective West and the Global South.”
The three open sessions and five working meetings in the Knesset mentioned in Dor Moriah’s annual report apparently referred to these initiatives.

articles.title: Zelenskyy accuses Russia of using cluster warheads in deadly strikes
articles.body:
Zelenskyy accuses Russia of using cluster warheads in deadly strikes hours after U.S. prisoner release
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of using cluster munitions overnight as it renewed strikes on Kyiv and multiple other locations.
At least four people were killed, according to Ukraine's foreign ministry. Another 34 people were injured, including five children, Zelenskyy said Thursday, hours after Russia released American Stephen Hubbard and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and called him a humanitarian.
"Last night, the Russians used, among other weapons against Kyiv, three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads," Zelenskyy wrote on X Thursday. "The distinguishing feature of these missiles is that they detonate in the air as they approach the target, striking everything within a 400-meter diameter."
More than 100 countries have banned the use of cluster bombs under the Convention on Cluster Munitions, an international treaty that was adopted in 2008. The munitions spread smaller "bomblets" over a wide area that can hit civilian locations indiscriminately.
Russia, like the United States, did not sign on to the treaty.
Russia's Defense Ministry said, meanwhile, that air defenses downed 808 Ukrainian drones overnight, and that two people were reported injured, The Associated Press reported. More than 600 drones were fired toward Moscow between late Wednesday and early Thursday, according to Mayor Sergei Sobyanin.
The developments came after Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted by Russian news agencies as saying Moscow would study proposals on the Ukraine war brought to St. Petersburg by Witkoff, but that the talks would take a long time.
"Almost immediately after another round of talks, Russia launched a pointed attack," Zelenskyy said. "This means there has been no real change in its attitude toward everything that is happening."
Twelve regions came under attack from Russia overnight, according to Zelenskyy, who said one attack hit Pechersk, Kyiv's historic center, and damaged monastery buildings, homes, shops, cafés and other civilian infrastructure.
Since Oct. 11, there have been 170 strikes on energy infrastructure sites across Ukraine, the Ukrainian president said.
Zelenskyy said earlier this week that if President Trump "cannot rein Putin in," he should provide long-requested interceptor missiles so Ukraine can defend itself. Secretary of State Marco Rubio later said that Mr. Trump has been "frustrated" by what he described as false accusations that "he is doing things to deliberately harm Ukraine." He insisted that nothing had been "deliberately denied to Ukraine," but added: "It's simply, it's a balance between our obligations to other partners and frankly our own ... requirements for our own facilities as well."

articles.title: U.S. and Israel prepare for a new war with Iran
articles.body:
- President Trump said the U.S. is not negotiating with Iran and that “something” will happen “fairly soon,” as plans for renewed strikes take shape.
- U.S. troops are leaving bases in Jordan, Qatar and Kuwait, and Israeli jets flew a mock strike mission to Iran’s border.
The United States and Israel are moving toward a new war with Iran within days, as President Donald Trump said Washington is no longer negotiating with Tehran and that “something” will happen “fairly soon,” while U.S. troops pull out of exposed bases across the Middle East and Israeli fighter jets rehearse a strike on Iran at the edge of its airspace.
The troop withdrawals, embassy staff cuts and large-scale air activity over the region closely resemble the buildup that came just before the war began in late February, and they put the next round of fighting on a timeline measured in days rather than months, with the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections now less than two weeks away.
“No, I think we’re not negotiating… we are going to have something, one way or the other. It’ll happen fairly soon,” said President Donald Trump on Oct. 21.
The remarks mark a sharp turn from Trump’s pledge on Oct. 8 that the United States would not attack Iran before the midterms, and they come as Washington and Jerusalem finalize plans for what officials described to The New York Times as a short but intensive operation against Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities and missile and drone arsenals. Options presented to Trump include strikes on tunnel entrances at nuclear sites such as Pickaxe Mountain and on the strategic islands of Kharg, which handles most of Iran’s oil exports, and Qeshm, NBC News reported, while officials quoted by the Times said there is a chance he could order strikes before the end of this month.
On the ground, the U.S. military has quietly moved troops out of bases in Jordan, Qatar and Kuwait in recent days, two U.S. officials and two people familiar with the matter told NBC News, and one official said getting forces out of harm’s way is part of planning as Trump weighs restarting major combat operations. The State Department has ordered staff reductions at the U.S. embassy in Saudi Arabia, citing Houthi attacks on the kingdom including strikes on civilian airports, and chiefs of mission at several other posts across the region have been told to operate with fewer personnel, in moves that sources compared directly with the drawdowns at the start of the war in February.
“We regularly move U.S. service members and assets to optimize mission readiness,” a U.S. Central Command spokesperson said.
Israel has already rehearsed the opening move of a new campaign, sending dozens of fighter jets and refueling aircraft along a route through Syrian and Iraqi airspace consistent with a strike on Iran and turning them back only as they approached the Iranian border, Axios reporter Barak Ravid reported, citing sources who described it as a massive power projection operation. Israel told Washington the flight was an exercise and a show of force, but the sortie was followed overnight by large-scale tactical aircraft activity over the region that defense writer Tyler Rogoway said looked like a dry run for a large integrated operation, in which commanders put much of the real strike force in position to rehearse before the order to execute is given.
Such rehearsals also force Iran to switch on its air defenses as if a full attack were coming, which lets U.S. and Israeli intelligence detect, classify and pinpoint radars and missile sites that would have to be suppressed, destroyed or avoided on the first night of an offensive, Rogoway noted, and that kind of targeting picture is far sharper when Iranian crews are on high alert than during routine surveillance.
Tensions are climbing at sea as well, after the naval arm of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said its forces hit four vessels it accused of illegal oil transfers in the northern Persian Gulf and that three more ships struck mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, warning that continued provocations could bring a wider response against U.S. bases in the region. Iran’s neighbors are bracing for the fallout, with Saudi Arabia already under a sustained Houthi missile and drone campaign that has led Britain to send Royal Air Force Typhoons to guard Saudi cities and Türkiye to prepare forces for deployment to the kingdom under its new defense pact with Riyadh and Pakistan.

articles.title: ‘Wrong and Unacceptable’: Zelensky Accuses Trump of Shifting Iran Blame to Kyiv
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky accused US President Donald Trump of shifting responsibility for Russia’s aggression onto Ukraine and diverting attention from problems surrounding Iran, in an interview published Thursday, Oct. 22.
Speaking to Steven Bartlett on The Diary of a CEO podcast, Zelensky rejected Trump’s argument that Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries were responsible for rising diesel prices in the US.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I think it’s wrong and unacceptable that he pins Russia’s aggression and Russia’s killings on me,” Zelensky said.
He argued that disruptions in the Middle East, particularly around the Strait of Hormuz, were at the heart of the energy problem. Zelensky accused Trump of redirecting the discussion toward Ukraine and making him personally the target of criticism.
Zelensky said he had repeatedly proposed a reciprocal halt to attacks on energy infrastructure. Such an arrangement would protect Ukrainian electricity supplies while allowing Russia to sell its energy exports.
But Putin had refused to agree to an energy ceasefire, Zelensky said, arguing that Trump was blaming Kyiv rather than confronting Moscow over that refusal.
He maintained that he had a good relationship with Trump but described the US president’s accusations as unfair.
Zelensky demands missiles and pressure on Putin
Zelensky said that if Washington could not secure an energy truce, it should provide Ukraine with the air defense missiles needed to protect its infrastructure.
Russian Shahed Drone Strikes Private Home in Zhytomyr, Injuring 8, Including 2 Children
He stressed that Kyiv was seeking deliveries financed by European partners, rather than asking for the weapons free of charge. He also complained that supplies had been directed toward the Middle East while Ukraine’s needs remained unmet.
The president argued that Trump could bring Putin to the negotiating table by directing the same forceful rhetoric toward the Russian leader that he used against Ukraine.
He pointed to sanctions approved by Congress as another instrument available to Washington. Asked why Trump had not applied greater pressure, Zelensky said he did not know, offering possible explanations without claiming to know the US president’s motives.
Dispute over Russian diesel and refinery strikes
The interview follows Trump’s criticism of Ukraine’s renewed attacks on Russian oil refineries, which he called a “disgrace” in an Oct. 15 interview with Newsmax.
Trump blamed Kyiv for higher energy prices and portrayed Zelensky as more difficult to negotiate with than Putin.
Ukraine had temporarily suspended refinery attacks at Washington’s request, but Zelensky said the pause could not continue while Russia kept striking Ukrainian energy facilities.
His position has been that any restriction on Ukrainian attacks must be matched by an end to Russia’s strikes on Ukraine’s electricity grid.
The dispute intensified after Trump agreed with Putin to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports. Zelensky has criticized that arrangement as economic relief for Moscow while its invasion continues.
Energy analysts have also questioned whether additional Russian diesel supplies would significantly reduce fuel prices, pointing instead to the disruption of shipments through the Strait of Hormuz during the US-Israel war with Iran.
Russian strikes follow latest diplomatic meeting
The interview’s publication also came after another major Russian missile attack on Kyiv, following Putin’s meeting with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday, Oct. 21.
Zelensky said Russia launched 21 ballistic missiles toward the capital in three waves overnight. Residential buildings, energy facilities, railway and metro infrastructure, shopping centers, and industrial sites were among the damaged locations.
Across Ukraine, he reported two deaths and 34 people wounded, including five children, in attacks affecting 12 regions.
The strikes followed a meeting at which the Kremlin signaled willingness to resume negotiations involving Ukraine, Russia, and the US. Witkoff also praised Putin as a humanitarian after Russia released an American detainee.
Responding to the attacks, Zelensky argued that negotiations must be accompanied by real pressure on Moscow. He called for stronger air defenses, faster missile deliveries, sanctions, and the capability to destroy Russian ballistic missile launchers.

articles.title: Russia Hits Central Kyiv With Cluster Missile
articles.body:
Russia used an Iskander ballistic missile carrying a cluster warhead against Kyiv’s historic center during its overnight attack on Thursday, Oct. 22, Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said.
Beskrestnov, known by the callsign “Flash,” said in a Telegram post that the missile carried a K5 warhead designed to disperse explosive elements over a wide area.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to him, the warhead operates above the ground and contains 58 explosive elements intended to strike people and equipment across an area measuring approximately 400 by 400 meters (437 by 437 yards).
He reported civilian injuries and destruction, accusing Russia of deliberately attacking the historic part of the capital.
“The aim was to destroy part of the old city and injure as many people as possible,” Beskrestnov said.
Beskrestnov identified the K5 warhead and assessed the attack’s intended target. He did not provide a separate casualty count attributable specifically to that missile.
Homes, monastery and emergency vehicles damaged
The statement followed successive waves of Russian missile and drone strikes across Kyiv, which killed one person and injured at least 24 others, according to morning updates from Ukrainian authorities.
The Kyiv City Military Administration said at 9:21 a.m. that 16 of those injured had been hospitalized.
Emergency services reported damage in six districts, including residential neighborhoods, transport facilities and civilian businesses.
Sloviansk Expands Forced Evacuation Zone for Families With Children to Entire Community
In the central Pecherskyi district, buildings and a monastery sustained damage. Eight people were injured there, including three children, according to the State Emergency Service’s district-by-district account.
Mayor Vitali Klitschko separately confirmed damage to an ambulance station and six emergency medical vehicles. He said no medical personnel were injured.
In the Dniprovskyi district, one person was killed, homes and vehicles were damaged, and fires broke out in residential and non-residential buildings. Six people were injured in the Holosiivskyi district, while two others were hurt in the Obolonskyi district.
A restaurant complex and another non-residential building caught fire in the Sviatoshynskyi district. Transport infrastructure was damaged in the Darnytskyi district.
Zelensky reports 3 waves of ballistic strikes
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia launched 21 ballistic missiles toward Kyiv in three waves during the overnight attack.
He reported damage to residential buildings, energy facilities, railway and metro infrastructure, shopping centers and industrial enterprises.
Zelensky said 12 regions across Ukraine came under attack. His morning statement reported two deaths and 34 people wounded nationwide, including five children.
The bombardment came after Russian President Vladimir Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday for discussions about ending the war.
Zelensky argued that the strikes demonstrated no genuine change in Moscow’s approach despite the diplomatic contacts. He called for greater pressure on Russia, stronger air defenses and faster deliveries of interceptor missiles.
Ukraine’s Air Force said Russia also launched 210 drones during the broader overnight assault. By 9 a.m., Ukrainian defenses had shot down or suppressed 181, while Russian weapons struck 32 locations and intercepted-drone debris fell at eight others.
Missile attacks leave further hazards
The latest barrage follows earlier ballistic missile strikes that left unexploded warheads near homes in the capital.
On Oct. 8, the National Police reported disposing of two unexploded Iskander-M warheads from an attack the previous day.
The warheads, each weighing approximately half a metric ton (1,102 pounds), had fallen near residential buildings in the Shevchenkivskyi and Darnytskyi districts.
Police bomb technicians and emergency service specialists used specialized equipment to remove the fragments to a temporary demolition site for destruction. That earlier operation involved separate missiles from the cluster-warhead strike Beskrestnov described on Thursday.

articles.title: Russia Turns to Its Rarest Fighter as Ukrainian Deep Strikes Keep Coming
articles.body:
