Russia Turns to Its Rarest Fighter as Ukrainian Deep Strikes Keep Coming
Ukraine’s long-range drone campaign is forcing Russia to throw even its rarest fighters into the defense of its own territory, with MiG-35s—a fleet of just six aircraft—now hunting incoming Ukrainian UAVs.
Russia has begun using its extremely small fleet of MiG-35 fighters to intercept Ukrainian long-range drones striking targets deep inside Russian territory, according to Defense Express on October 22.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Russian Aerospace Forces officially have around 86 MiG-29-family aircraft of various versions, but only six MiG-35s—four single-seat and two two-seat aircraft.
Despite their rarity, the newer fighters are now reportedly being used more actively against Ukrainian deep-strike UAVs.
Just six MiG-35s exist
The assessment is based in part on information published by the aviation-focused Soniashnyk OSINT community, which shared an image apparently taken by a Russian pilot from inside a MiG-35 cockpit during what was described as an interception mission against Ukrainian drones.
Defense Express notes that the actual combat readiness of Russia’s much larger MiG-29 fleet remains unclear. There is no reliable public estimate of how many of those older aircraft are currently operational or available for air-defense missions over Russian territory.
That makes the reported deployment of MiG-35s particularly notable. Russia has only six examples of the aircraft, all produced as part of an experimental batch that took five years to complete between 2018 and 2023.
A fighter that never became a real fleet
Russian officials first claimed that MiG-35s had been used in combat against Ukraine in 2023, at a time when the manufacturer was seeking additional Defense Ministry orders.
Those orders never materialized on anything approaching the scale needed to make the aircraft a significant component of Russia’s tactical aviation.
The MiG-35 is an advanced development of the MiG-29. Russian specifications claim roughly 50% greater range than earlier variants and a maximum weapons load of up to 6,500 kilograms across nine hardpoints.
Built for air combat, now hunting Ukrainian drones
The aircraft can carry R-73, R-27, and R-77 air-to-air missiles, giving it several options for intercepting aerial targets. Strike configurations can also include Kh-29, Kh-31, and Kh-38 air-to-surface missiles.
Russian promotional material has portrayed the MiG-35 as a lower-cost alternative to the US F-16 Block 70/72, although Defense Express notes that such comparisons have not been backed by meaningful evidence.
What matters more now is how Moscow is using the handful of aircraft it actually possesses.
Ukraine’s deep strikes stretching Russia’s air defense
Ukrainian long-range drones have repeatedly reached military facilities, oil refineries, data centers, airfields, and other strategic targets hundreds of miles inside Russia, forcing Moscow to dedicate an expanding range of assets to homeland air defense.
The reported use of MiG-35s suggests that the burden is now reaching aircraft Russia possesses only in extremely limited numbers.
With just six MiG-35s available, every fighter committed to chasing Ukrainian drones represents a comparatively scarce combat aircraft being diverted to defend Russia’s rear rather than performing other missions.
Earlier, reports emerged that Russia was turning to artificial intelligence developed by its largest bank to help design future aircraft, potentially including fighter jets, as Western sanctions continue to restrict access to engineering software previously used by the country’s aerospace industry.

articles.title: Occupiers attack energy infrastructure 170 times since October 11, taking advantage of delays in air defense supplies – Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Russian occupiers are taking advantage of delays by partners in supplying air defense systems to Ukraine and have intensified their attacks, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported.
“Russia is clearly taking advantage of the slowdown in air defense supplies from our partners. It is equally clear that when some partners ease the pressure on Russia, it only reinforces Putin's belief that his goals are within reach. We need different signals and different steps – stronger ones. I have instructed the Ministry of Defense, together with the military command and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, to brief our partners on every aspect of the real situation and the threats we face, based on intelligence data. It is important to speed up deliveries of defense packages that have already been approved,” Zelenskyy said on X Thursday.
According to him, more than 170 strikes on critical energy infrastructure in Ukraine have been recorded since October 11, and this despite the fact that a significant number of Shahed drones and some missiles have been successfully shot down.
The President also reported that, on Thursday night, the enemy targeted Kyiv with three ballistic missiles equipped with cluster warheads; these detonate in the air as they approach their target, striking everything within a 400-meter radius.
“One of them struck Pechersk, Kyiv's historic center, hitting the area between the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra and the Holy Presentation Monastery. Monastery buildings, homes, shops, cafés, and other civilian infrastructure were damaged. This is another extraordinarily revealing strike – revealing because it was no accident. The choice of weapon was deliberate, the choice of target area was deliberate, and so was the intent to inflict as much loss and damage on civilians as possible. There was no military target nearby, not even in theory, and the weapon was designed to cause widespread destruction. Russia has not changed the way it wages this war, and it is taking no steps that would signal a genuine desire to end it,” Zelenskyy emphasized.
As previously reported, a massive Russian strike on Kyiv during the night of Thursday, October 22, caused damage in six of the capital’s ten administrative districts. One person was reported killed and 24 others injured, 16 of whom were hospitalized. In total, 12 regions of Ukraine were targeted by Russian strikes that night; two civilians were killed, and 34 people, including five children, were injured.
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Russian occupation forces launched a massive, combined-arms strike against Ukraine overnight, employing Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon, and Oniks missiles, alongside 210 attack UAVs and decoy drones. Kyiv was the primary target. As of 9:00 a.m., air defense systems had intercepted or neutralized 181 enemy UAVs (including 87 jet-powered drones); however, hits were recorded at 32 locations, and debris fell at eight other sites.
Serhiy (Flash) Beskrestnov, an advisor to the President of Ukraine on defense technologies, reported that the Russian forces used an Iskander ballistic missile equipped with a cluster warhead to strike the center of Kyiv overnight into Thursday. He expressed his conviction that this action was not taken for military purposes, but rather with the intent to inflict the maximum number of casualties among civilians.
Ihor Klymenko, Secretary of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine (NSDC), believes that the overnight attack on Kyiv by Russian forces serves as a response from the Russian leadership to Ukraine’s peace initiatives. He has called on international partners to increase support for the development of Ukraine’s air defense capabilities and to step up sanction pressure on the Russian Federation.

articles.title: Russia Hid a Buk-M1 in the Trees—Autumn Gave It Away to Ukrainian Drones

Russia Hid a Buk-M1 in the Trees—Autumn Gave It Away to Ukrainian Drones
Ukrainian drone operators have struck a Russian Buk-M1 surface-to-air missile system on the Huliaipole axis, where Moscow has been moving additional air defenses forward to counter increasingly active Ukrainian aviation, Ukraine’s 7th Rapid Response Corps of the Air Assault Forces reported on October 22.
The strike was carried out by operators from the 433rd Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Footage released by the corps shows the Russian Buk-M1 being detected and hit after it was positioned in the area to help protect Russian rear positions from Ukrainian airstrikes.
During a subsequent mission, the drone crews also located and struck another camouflaged air-defense target, although the exact type of system has not yet been identified.
Russian forces have been attempting to conceal their air-defense equipment inside tree lines, but Ukrainian troops say the changing season is increasingly working against them as vegetation thins and large military systems become easier to detect from the air.
“The occupiers carefully camouflage their air defenses in forest belts. However, autumn is not working in their favor: the greenery is gradually disappearing, and hiding expensive equipment is becoming increasingly difficult. Coordinated interaction between units under the operational command of the 7th Air Assault Corps and effective intelligence sharing are producing results,” the corps said.
The Buk-M1 is a medium-range air-defense system designed to engage aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles, and other aerial targets. Its deployment on the Huliaipole axis reflects Russia’s effort to strengthen protection of rear areas as Ukrainian aircraft continue striking military targets behind the front.
But moving such systems closer to the battlefield also exposes them to Ukrainian reconnaissance and strike drones—especially as the natural cover Russian crews rely on begins disappearing with the onset of autumn.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces identified and struck a Russian Buk-M3 medium-range surface-to-air missile system valued at approximately $45 million.

articles.title: Iran threatens to strike oil and AI facilities across Gulf if US and Israel renew attacks
articles.body:
Iran will strike oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities across as many as seven countries in the Gulf in the event of a fresh US-Israeli attack, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, has said.
Mehdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Mohammad Ghalibaf, the hardliner who led Iran’s negotiations with the US to end the conflict between the two countries, said Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu had agreed in principle on an attack, but could not guarantee a successful outcome. He added: “We see the next conflict as an existential threat. The third war in two years means a threat to existence. Our strategy is ‘zero red lines’.”
Mohammadi said: “We break the temporal and spatial dimensions of the conflict. The war will continue longer and in a wider geographical area than the enemy anticipates.”
Iran’s ability to mount such operations, including any unofficial help it receives from China or Russia, will be a key factor in any American decision to restart the war.
Iranian media reported that Rezaei had declared: “In the event of a war, cables, datacentres and artificial intelligence facilities could also be targeted. If the conflict breaks out again, we will have a broader plan.
“There can be no arrangement in which Iran’s economic lifelines come under attack while the economic architecture enabling those attacks is considered untouched and immune.”
According to recent reports in US media, US military advisers have drawn up a detailed list of targets for a fresh joint US-Israel assault on Iran to be implemented after the US midterm elections on 3 November.
Foreign ministers from three European countries, as well as Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt, will meet in Istanbul on Friday to establish agreed policies on the linked Iranian, Yemini and Palestinian crises. There is alarm that a further war is now the working assumption in Tehran and Washington.
The naval services of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) claimed to have simultaneously struck four commercial ships seeking to navigate through the strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. The ships were said to be transferring oil from ship to ship.
The IRGC claimed a further three ships had been struck when they hit mines in the strait. There was no independent verification that this number of ships were hit, but Brent crude oil was trading at $113.4 a barrel, a recent high, propelled by US reports of the imminent renewed joint Israeli-US assault on Iran.
Trump has backed away from striking Iran again seven times in the past four months. However, a deadlock in diplomatic negotiations has led US government officials to brief about a potential new military campaign that would target missile sites, oil installations and nuclear sites.
The sabre-rattling by both sides has coincided with extended joint-training manoeuvres by the US and Israel, including practice runs over Iraq. Dozens of Israeli planes also flew close to the Iranian border earlier this week, according to the news site Axios. A big fire at a large aluminium factory in Arak in central Iran suggests sabotage operations may be under way inside the country.
Netanyahu met the US secretary of defence, Pete Hegseth, in Israel on Monday to discuss the timing and purpose of a joint attack, including the possible political implications for Netanyahu’s chances of re-election.
Netanyahu would prefer it if Iran attacked first, he reportedly told Hegseth.
A US military buildup is due to be completed by early November, before a possible newly Democrat-inclined Congress or Senate take their seats in January. Trump intends to have stationed three aircraft carriers, thousands of marines, fighter jets and special operations forces in the Middle East by November.
Reza Nasri, an international lawyer close to the Iranian foreign ministry, said: “A third wave of war would not stay contained. Power grids, desalination plants, refineries and ports across the region would burn. Tens of millions would be left without water or electricity, and a massive wave of refugees would move from Arab countries towards Europe.
“Hormuz would close completely, oil would spike, and the global economy would tip into recession. Israel’s economy, already bled by mobilisation and missile fire, would not survive a prolonged war of attrition. And Trump would be trapped in a crisis that consumes the rest of his presidency and leaves a wreck for his successors,” Nasri said.
Fars news agency, which is close to the IRGC, said Iran had issued directives to its various military and operational units “stipulating that in the event of a new widespread war, involving the assassination of Iranian officials and the killing of civilians, the Iranian response will not be limited to military targets, but will also include political targets”.
Mediators from Iran and Pakistan this week again explored familiar if reconfigured options for a ceasefire, including proposals that Iran receive billions in frozen assets in return for lifting its blockade of the strait, allowing UN weapons inspectors to view its bombed nuclear sites and to export its stockpile of highly enriched uranium to a third country.
Iran has offered to end the Hormuz blockade within seven days and start talks on its nuclear file, but only if preconditions are first met, including lifting US sanctions.

articles.title: Denmark to purchase long-range missiles amid growing Russian threat - media
articles.body:
Denmark to purchase long-range missiles amid growing Russian threat - media
Kyiv • UNN
Denmark will acquire Joint Strike and Anthem long-range missiles to strengthen offensive capabilities and deter Russia. The deal includes weapons for F-35s.
Denmark plans to spend billions of kroner on high-precision, long-range missiles for its armed forces, including weapons for its F-35 fighter jets, fulfilling a promise to add offensive capabilities as the Scandinavian country strengthens its defenses against Russia. UNN writes about this, citing Bloomberg.
Details
The government in Copenhagen will purchase missiles from two suppliers, according to sources familiar with the deal. The package includes Joint Strike missiles manufactured by Norway's Kongsberg Gruppen ASA, as well as Anthem missiles from Covenant, which are produced in Germany, the sources said.
The German government is also negotiating the details of a procurement contract with Covenant, according to the sources.
TV2 reported on the deal earlier and said that Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus would brief the press later on Thursday. His ministry declined to comment. Spokespeople for Covenant and Kongsberg also declined to comment.
Denmark's acquisition comes after last year's decision to add longer-range missiles and drones to the country's arsenal, a move that Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called at the time a "paradigm shift" for a country that had focused on defensive weapons.
The country's government said at the time that the new systems would enable Denmark not only to counter air threats but also to strike threats far from its territory. Frederiksen said the goal was to strengthen deterrence and avoid war, as Russia has adopted an increasingly aggressive stance toward Europe.
Denmark sharply increased military spending after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine changed Europe's security environment, investing in everything from air defenses and fighter jets to drones and ammunition.

articles.title: The view from Russia: The Ukraine conflict is entering its final phase
articles.body:
The view from Russia: The Ukraine conflict is entering its final phase
Andrey Sushentsov, dean of the Faculty of International Relations at MGIMO and a member of the Scientific-Expert Council under the Security Council of the Russian Federation, discusses why Western Europe is so afraid of a direct confrontation with Russia, how the US is shifting the burden of the Ukraine crisis onto the EU, why the “pyramid of trust” surrounding Kiev is crumbling, and when the Ukraine conflict might come to an end.
His interview, first published in Russian by TASS, was translated and edited by the RT team.
America sails away, Europe gets the bill
Evgeny Kuznetsov: You have noted that the US is seeking to extricate itself from the Ukraine crisis by shifting the burden onto Western Europe. If Washington does indeed distance itself, are these Europeans prepared, politically and economically, to assume the role of Ukraine’s principal “security guarantor”?
Andrey Sushentsov: The US strategy in the Ukrainian crisis initially reflected its archetype as a maritime power employing a “continental sword” in its confrontation with a major continental power. This involves a neighboring country with military resources, which the maritime power supports in order to weaken its rival.
Ukraine was well suited to this role, as a large state with substantial armed forces, motivated to confront Russia. But the limitation of such a strategy is that you can’t fully control the behavior of the “sword.” Nor is it entirely resource-efficient, there’s a limit to the resources that can be allocated to it, and if no turning point is reached in the confrontation, further support yields no additional gains in effectiveness.
The Americans realized early on that many of their interests in this crisis had been achieved and prepared to withdraw. They did what a maritime power usually does when it decides to turn its attention elsewhere as they sailed back to their own region. The main difference between a maritime power and a continental power lies in the freedom to choose where to deploy military forces. A maritime power can choose where to deploy them and launch strikes across various parts of the world’s oceans. This is usually carried out in the form of raids, as large-scale expeditionary campaigns rarely prove successful. The US decided it was time to leave.
But they didn’t want the withdrawal to be accompanied by the collapse of the Ukrainian regime. The US incorporated its withdrawal and the reorientation of its priorities towards East Asia into its policy towards its NATO allies. It handed over responsibility for supporting Ukraine to them and assumed the role of “moderator” as a negotiator who, rather than being the instigator of the crisis, is steering it towards a resolution. US strategic documents state an interest in bringing the Ukraine crisis to an end.
Yet the US behaved treacherously toward both Ukraine and its European allies, saddling them with this burden without warning. The Western Europeans lack military resources, technological capabilities, strategic thinking, and awareness of their own interests comparable to those of the Americans, qualities that enable them to weigh up causes and consequences, to discern what is achievable and what is not by military means, and to identify where their bloc’s interests lie in this crisis.
These Europeans currently have a financial instrument of considerable weight at their disposal, in essence, the only one they can draw upon. They are using it wastefully, given the domestic debt of most major European states is approaching or exceeding 100% of GDP. They can’t obtain external compensation for their military expenditure, and there’s no hope of a Ukrainian victory.
If there were any hope, they would be counting on recouping their losses through Russian resources, through new deals with Russia on new terms. None of these hopes is being realized.
Moreover, due to a lack of strategic experience, lost as a result of American patronage and the nuclear umbrella, these Europeans are beginning to deny their own geography. To deny that Russia is on the continent alongside them.
Geography is a constant, an immutable part of the foreign policy system. Governments and historical circumstances may change, but geography remains unchanged.
The course towards a long-term confrontation with their largest neighbor, a source of many benefits for the Western European economy, which they have now lost, demonstrates the narrowness of their vision. Domestic political processes in the EU suggest that, following the Americans’ example, it is time for these Europeans to reflect on what their interests are, which of these are achievable in the course of the Ukraine crisis, which are not, and what the possible trajectory might be. So far, the Western Europeans haven’t made any good moves.
When there are no good moves, it is better to pass a turn and stop making mistakes. So far, as our President [Vladimir Putin] put it, it looks like a series of mistakes, one after another.
Big spending, little strategic power
Evgeny Kuznetsov: Won’t they get tired of playing this game?
Andrey Sushentsov: Western Europeans states don’t possess the full strategic autonomy enjoyed by Russia and the US, and are not entirely capable of acting collectively from a unified position. Every major decision requires the consensus of nearly 30 countries.
The European Commission doesn’t have a very substantial budget of its own but relies on the budgets of the nation states. Despite the single currency, debt is measured separately for each country.
There is no unified army. It’s a far cry from even the most loosely organized confederation. They would carry strategic weight if they were capable of acting in unison, but there’s no sign of this. Western Europeans are terrified of being directly drawn into a military crisis with Russia. Speculation about sending troops into Ukraine always ends with the caveat that this will only happen once a lasting peace and a ceasefire have been achieved.
In part, their enthusiasm is fueled by what they perceive to be the relatively low cost of supporting Ukraine and this proxy conflict. They have no qualms about Ukraine. They are indifferent to what will become of it, its borders or its population. They express rhetorical outrage, flock to summits, pose for “family photographs,” and make categorical statements. But in essence, this is a gathering of onlookers who are not directly involved in the military crisis.
The tool at their disposal is debt financing at Ukraine’s expense, amounting to nearly $500 billion. An astronomical sum which has failed to deliver the strategically necessary results, whilst worsening their own position. All that money has gone up in smoke.
Russia as the glue holding Europe together
Evgeny Kuznetsov: The EU is not abandoning its plans to impose ever more restrictions on Russia. Incidentally, Brussels has also added you to its sanctions list. At the same time, some European leaders are calling for dialogue with Russia. Is that possible at present?
Andrey Sushentsov: Western Europeans are using the Ukraine crisis as a platform for unity, to become a more cohesive entity. Their strategic lack of autonomy, the prominent role of the Americans, and their internal fragmentation mean that the only platform for solidarity is an anti-Russian one.
The relevance varies from country to country. For Southern Europe, it’s not so obvious. For Spain, despite its anti-Russian government, Palestine and the Middle East are more important. The Baltic states and Northern Europe have an alarmist and militaristic outlook. Some share a border with us. The people in charge are a peculiar lot; one can expect all sorts of things. But no one wants to involve their armed forces in the Ukraine crisis, as North Korea has done on our side.
They are using Ukraine to strengthen their own agency and take steps towards coordinated action. These steps are not particularly effective. However, joint plans are being drawn up and substantial funding is being allocated.
One unresolved issue is the restructuring of the Western European defense industry; it’s fragmented and produces around 15 different types of main battle tank with guns of varying calibers. Standardization is a major and difficult challenge. A catalyst is needed. In other words, they are, to some extent, tackling an internal challenge.
Peace alongside Russia – or a strategic dead end
Evgeny Kuznetsov: Do the NATO Europeans want to sit at the negotiating table with Russia, representing a “united Europe,” in order to compensate for their strategic lack of autonomy?
Andrey Sushentsov: Their tactics for establishing agency include providing financial aid to Ukraine, the theft of Russia’s gold and foreign exchange reserves, the withholding and disposal of revenues, and an attempt to share the blame for this crime amongst everyone. If it’s a crime, then it’s a collective one, so that no single country is held solely responsible. And they are resolving many technical issues.
The US doesn’t resolve such issues, nor does Russia. We can afford to take strategic, autonomous, purposeful and consistent action. These Europeans take a step back, a step forward, two steps back; they look over their shoulders and seek consensus.
It’s in Russia’s interests to invite them to the negotiating table only if it is clear that these Europeans prioritize a stable world on the continent, based on the principle of “peace alongside Russia,” rather than against Russia. The “peace against Russia” approach is inherently unstable and a dead end for Western Europe. It dooms them to fall behind, to strategic defeat, and to never becoming a true player on the world stage. The more internal contradictions there are within the bloc regarding priorities, the more fragile it becomes, and the Russian question is gradually becoming precisely such an issue.
Ukraine’s ‘pyramid of trust’ is crumbling
Evgeny Kuznetsov: You said that the “pyramid of trust” surrounding Ukraine will soon crumble. When will this finally happen?
Andrey Sushentsov: From the Russian perspective, the logic behind this crisis is that we are waging a war to wear down our opponents and deplete their resources. We are targeting their rear lines and breaking their “continental sword.”
We are demonstrating that their strategy is irrelevant; its objectives are unattainable. And the resources they are expending will, over time, be needed in ever-greater quantities. The existing ones are becoming obsolete, as are the systems for utilizing them on Ukrainian territory. They need to be replenished and rebuilt.
Building infrastructure is extremely costly; in wartime conditions, it is simply impossible. In time, Western countries themselves will realize the unviability of this strategy. The opposition within those countries is already openly voicing its outrage and stating that this is a dead end.
[Friedrich] Merz’s visit to Kiev was heavily criticized by the entire opposition, at a time when Germany’s national debt is rising, the chancellor travels to Kiev and once again promises money and resources, essentially at the expense of the German people. The scale of the resources being invested is becoming so significant that the question arises as to what justifies it. What are Berlin’s objectives, what is it achieving, and what is it failing to achieve?
There are increasingly insistent calls for the Ukrainian leadership to take a realistic view of the situation and understand what is achievable and what is not. The “pyramid of trust” is crumbling. One after another, the parties involved are adopting an increasingly detached stance on this issue.
Their primary and secondary hopes have not been realized. Now they are almost left high and dry. We must admit, it was a mistake.
No one wants to take responsibility for it. It has not only a political but also a financial dimension. Who should be held to account for the hundreds of billions of euros spent on a strategically futile venture that has antagonized Russia and undermined security on the continent?
That is why we are talking about a short-term historical perspective. It may come to an end in the coming months, or perhaps in the coming years. But we are not talking about a decade-long war. The point is that this will still remain a crisis with its own distinct phases, and we are currently in the final phase of its resolution.

articles.title: ‘No change’ in Russia’s attitude on war shown by deadly attacks, Zelensky says
articles.body:
‘No change’ in Russia’s attitude on war shown by deadly attacks, Zelensky says
Russia’s latest attacks on Ukraine show there has been “no real change” in Moscow’s attitude towards the war, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Thursday. The deadly strikes came just hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin told US envoy Steve Witkoff his country was ready to resume trilateral talks with Washington and Kyiv.
Ukraine on Thursday accused Russia of failing to change its position on the war by firing a wave of ballistic missiles just after US envoy Steve Witkoff met President Vladimir Putin to discuss the resumption of peace talks.
Air raid sirens sounded throughout the night and into the day in Kyiv, where two people were killed and more than 30 other people wounded, city authorities said.
Two women aged 50 and 60 were killed and dozens more people were wounded in an attack on a crowded market in the eastern city of Lozova. Two were wounded in the Moscow region after Ukraine launched its own large-scale drone attack.
The strikes came after the Kremlin said it was willing to restart trilateral talks with Kyiv and Washington next month, but dismissed new ideas brought by Witkoff that were developed with European countries and Ukraine.
In all, a dozen Ukrainian regions were hit overnight, including residential houses, energy sites, shops, cafes and a monastery damaged in Kyiv, where strikes have intensified before winter sets in.
Read moreUkraine’s Pavlohrad refuses to yield to Putin despite unrelenting bombardment
All families and children were told to evacuate the frontline towns of Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk in the east after a spate of attacks killed dozens of civilians.
Zelensky said the onslaught began “almost immediately” after Witkoff and Putin held hours-long talks in Saint Petersburg, scoffing at US President Donald Trump’s envoy’s description of the Russian leader as a “humanitarian”.
“This means there has been no real change in its attitude towards everything that is happening,” he added.
Emboldened
Ukraine has repeatedly called on its allies, including the United States, to supply it with advanced US-made Patriot interceptors to shoot down missiles and fast-moving attack drones.
Zelensky warned of more strikes to come and suggested that Moscow – emboldened by an easing of sanctions pressure – was “clearly taking advantage of the slowdown in air-defence supplies from our partners”, in a clear nod to Washington.
In Brussels, NATO said it was allowing Ukraine to buy weapons through the alliance’s central procurement agency on a “case-by-case basis”.
Trump sought an optimistic tone as his envoy returned from Russia and on Wednesday said negotiators were “maybe now the closest we’ve been” to ending the war.
But in Kyiv and European capitals, hopes for a breakthrough were slim, with many worried the White House was siding with Moscow.

articles.title: Trump cannot get Putin to halt strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, so he blames Ukraine instead, Zelenskyy says
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has failed to reach an agreement with Russian ruler Vladimir Putin on halting strikes against Ukraine's energy infrastructure. However, Trump is trying to shift the blame for this failure onto President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, he said on The Diary of a CEO podcast.
His words came amid Russia's four record waves of ballistic missile attacks, after US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff described Putin as a "humanitarian." Previously, US officials cut Kyiv off from US intelligence and lowered a speed cap on Starlink to pressure Ukraine into stopping strikes on Russia's oil refineries that bring Moscow revenue for its war.
Trump pins the problem on Kyiv, not Putin
Zelenskyy explained the behavioral pattern behind Trump's recent actions and statements. At first, Putin rejected his proposal for a ceasefire. Then, the US president blamed it all on him, explaining to his people that world fuel prices are rising because of him, which is not true at all, said the Ukrainian leader.
He pointed to the blocked Strait of Hormuz shipping chokepoint, not Ukraine’s refinery campaign, as the driver of higher prices.
He also noted that the volumes of diesel allowed by the US are insufficient to lower global oil prices.
Even so, Zelenskyy said he keeps a working relationship with Trump. What he will not accept is being cast as the villain in Russia’s war: by his account, the US president is rewriting the context, turning Ukraine’s leader into the target for a problem that starts in Moscow.
Earlier, experts said the diesel deal was unlikely to meaningfully lower diesel prices. For Putin, the agreement itself was a win.
A former senior State Department official says it hardly matters whether the fuel arrives, because Putin “has already achieved the result he wants,” with Trump believing he has a pre-election card that could move markets.

articles.title: Ukraine faces a new Russian cruise missile called Filin
articles.body:
- Ukrainian military intelligence published a 3D model and component breakdown of Russia’s Filin cruise missile, first used against Ukraine in late summer 2026.
- The ground-launched missile has a claimed range of up to 1,200 km and contains 35 American and 22 Chinese components.
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency has published a detailed breakdown of Filin, a new Russian ground-launched cruise missile that Moscow began firing at Ukraine in late summer 2026. According to the agency, the missile combines a composite airframe and a Russian jet engine with onboard electronics built largely from American and Chinese parts.
The Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine’s Defense Ministry, known as HUR, released an interactive 3D model of the missile, its main assemblies and a catalog of its electronic components on the agency’s War & Sanctions portal. The agency did not say how many Filin missiles Russia has launched, which targets they hit or how investigators obtained the parts they examined.
Filin, Russian for “eagle owl,” is made by AO NPO Molniya, a company within Russia’s state-owned Tactical Missiles Corporation. HUR described the missile as the latest product of a Russian effort to build relatively cheap jet-powered strike weapons that launch from the ground instead of from aircraft or warships.
The missile is 3.5 meters (11.5 feet) long and has a wingspan of 3 meters (9.8 feet), with a maximum launch weight of 210 kg (463 pounds). Its fuselage is made of carbon fiber and fiberglass composites, and some of its parts are produced by 3D printing, an approach that can cut manufacturing time and cost compared with traditional machined components.
Russia claims Filin can reach a top speed of 800 km/h (497 mph) and fly up to 1,200 km (746 miles), although HUR’s specification sheet gives the range as 600 to 1,200 km (373 to 746 miles), which suggests the figure depends on the configuration. The missile can fly at very low altitude, where ground-based radar has a harder time detecting incoming threats, or climb as high as 6 km (19,700 feet).
Filin comes in versions with either a 50 kg (110-pound) or a 100 kg (220-pound) warhead, and HUR lists three warhead types: high-explosive fragmentation, penetrating and thermobaric. A thermobaric warhead first disperses an explosive cloud and then ignites it, producing a longer and more powerful blast wave than a conventional charge of similar weight.
The missile is fired from a ground launcher with the help of a solid-fuel booster, which pushes it up to flying speed before its small jet engine takes over for the cruise to the target.
HUR’s investigation also links Filin closely to Russia’s long-range attack drone program. The missile’s onboard equipment is produced by OOO PLAZ, which also makes equipment for the Garpiya, or “Harpy,” drone, a modification of the Geran-2 built in several series by the Izhevsk Electromechanical Plant Kupol. The Geran-2 itself is Russia’s version of the Iranian-designed Shahed-136, and HUR said electronic units from Filin and Garpiya share a similar layout and similar markings.
For guidance, Filin relies on a Chinese-made inertial navigation system, which tracks the missile’s position using onboard motion sensors without any outside signal. It works alongside a 16-channel Kometa satellite navigation module, a jam-resistant receiver made by Russia’s VNIIR-Progress that has repeatedly turned up in Russian drones and guided bombs recovered in Ukraine.
HUR said Filin’s electronics resemble those found in other Russian missiles and drones, but with a larger share of Chinese parts and with the same design solutions reused across different units and circuit boards. Investigators counted 35 American components and 22 Chinese ones in the missile’s onboard equipment.
The identified suppliers include Texas Instruments, Analog Devices, NXP Semiconductors and STMicroelectronics, along with Chinese firms such as WinChipHead and Mornsun. Production markings on some parts date from 2021 and 2022, including an Ethernet switch chip made in May 2022, three months after Russia launched its full-scale invasion.
Filin’s engine, by contrast, is Russian: an R500 turbojet built by OOO Reynolds. HUR had previously identified the same engine in Russia’s S-71K Kover air-launched cruise missile and in the S-71M Monokhrom.

articles.title: Germany arrests Ukrainian national suspected of spying for Russia
articles.body:
Germany's Federal Criminal Police arrested a Ukrainian citizen in the state of Brandenburg, surrounding Berlin, for suspected espionage on behalf of a Russian intelligence agency, Germany's Federal Prosecutor's Office said on Oct. 22.
The suspect, identified as Vadym Y., was arrested in the Oder-Spree district of Brandenburg a week after an investigating judge issued a warrant on Oct. 15, the prosecutor's office said.
Vadym Y. had been in contact with Russian intelligence through an interlocutor since at least July 2025, the prosecutor's office said. He allegedly collected relevant information in connection with Russia's war against Ukraine, including on the production of armored vehicles, ammunition, and explosives, as well as on military personnel and facilities on NATO's eastern flank.
While some of the information was publicly available, according to the prosecutor's office, the suspect allegedly also obtained details by deliberately approaching people working in the European defense industry.
The information on the suspected spy comes primarily from Germany's domestic intelligence service (BfV).
This incident comes a day after Germany's military for the first time classified Russian sabotage threats against its troops and facilities as "significant," German news outlet Sueddeutsche Zeitung reported on Oct. 21.
Reviewing internal documents from Germany's armed forces, Sueddeutsche Zeitung reported that this is the military's second-highest threat classification.
"We are noting that we face a significant sabotage threat overall for [Germany's armed forces]," said a defense ministry spokesperson, according to Reuters.
Germany's reclassification of Russian threats comes as experts warn Russia is testing how far it can push Europe without triggering open war — from drones crossing NATO airspace to sabotage and cyberattacks across the continent. Europe has strengthened its defenses since 2022, but key gaps remain, including in air defense, communications, intelligence, and joint command, experts say.
On Oct. 5, Martin Jaeger, head of Germany's foreign intelligence service, told lawmakers that Germany is in a "shadow war" with Russia and risks being drawn into a violent conflict with Moscow.

articles.title: Zelensky: Russia used three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads in attack on Kyiv
articles.body:
Zelensky: Russia used three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads in attack on Kyiv
According to Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky reported this on Facebook.
“There were reports on the cleanup efforts following the Russian attacks on our cities and communities. Last night, the Russians launched, among other weapons, three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads against Kyiv. What makes these missiles unique is that they explode in the air as they approach their target, striking everything within a 400-meter radius,” Zelenskyy said.
According to him, one of these missiles struck Pechersk—the historic center of Kyiv—specifically the area between the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra and the Holy Vvedensky Monastery. The strike damaged monastery buildings, homes, stores, cafes, and other civilian infrastructure in the city.
“This is yet another extremely telling strike—telling in that it is not accidental. It is a deliberate choice of weapon, a deliberate choice of target area, and a deliberate attempt to inflict as many casualties and as much damage as possible on civilians. There wasn’t even a single military facility nearby, even in theory, and the weapon was designed to cause widespread destruction. Russia has not changed its approach to waging this war and is not taking any steps that might indicate a genuine desire to stop the war,” Zelenskyy emphasized.
He added that air raid alerts and strikes continue throughout the day in Kyiv and many other cities. In Kharkiv, a commuter train was hit. Dnipro, Marhanets, Mykolaiv, Kherson, and cities and villages in the Kyiv, Zhytomyr, Donetsk, Kharkiv, Chernihiv, and Rivne regions were all targeted.
Attacks on the energy sector continue. Since October 11, there have been more than 170 strikes on critical energy infrastructure—and this, Zelensky noted, despite the fact that a significant portion of the “Shaheds” and some of the missiles are being shot down. The president thanked all of Ukraine’s friends who are helping with the restoration of the energy sector.
“We know from our intelligence that the Russians have set priorities for further terror against Ukrainians in the coming weeks. Clearly, Russia is taking advantage of the slowdown in the delivery of air defense systems from our partners. And it is equally clear that the easing of pressure on Russia by certain partners only convinces Putin that his goals are seemingly achievable. We need different signals, different steps—stronger ones,” Zelensky emphasized.
He instructed the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense, together with the military command and the Ukrainian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, to inform partners about all aspects of the actual situation and existing threats, based on information provided by intelligence agencies.
“It is important to expedite the delivery of defense aid packages that have already been agreed upon. Thank you to all the leaders and countries that are helping!” Zelensky noted.
As reported by Ukrinform, Russian invaders launched strikes on 12 regions on the night of October 22, killing two people and injuring 34.

articles.title: Press review: Russia-US-Ukraine peace hopes rise as Moscow offers Iran-US mediation
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. The prospects for peace and trilateral talks between Russia, the US and Ukraine following the October 21 St. Petersburg meeting; Moscow’s willingness to mediate between Tehran and Washington; and Russia’s potential agreement with the US to start shipping fertilizers alongside diesel. These stories topped Thursday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Media: Chances of peace and Russia-US-Ukraine talks following St. Petersburg meeting
US efforts to end the conflict between Russia and Ukraine have resumed, perhaps the main visible and indisputable outcome of the October 21 talks between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US special presidential envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg. The envoy left Russia with news of the release of an American citizen from a Russian prison and Moscow’s assurances that the proposals he brought would be reviewed. In addition, Putin expressed readiness to launch trilateral talks in the Russia-US-Ukraine format. The talks are scheduled for mid-November, after the US congressional elections, which are likely to bring significant changes.
Witkoff’s visit to St. Petersburg wrapped up a busy diplomatic round, international affairs expert Nikolay Novik told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. The St. Petersburg talks were preceded by consultations in Oslo. Witkoff and Kushner, who participated remotely, met with Zelensky, European leaders, and EU and NATO representatives there, the expert recalled. "It is likely that Witkoff presented an updated plan to end the conflict and a proposal for direct talks involving Trump and Zelensky. There may also have been discussions about a meeting between Putin, Trump, and Xi Jinping in China during the APEC summit on November 18-19: Washington doesn’t need a technical pause, but rather an outcome from the summit that can be presented as a tangible result," Novik said.
At the same time, the package of conditions that the US envoy might have brought - if these were the ones recently mentioned in the Western media - does not suit Russia, Russian International Affairs Council President Dmitry Trenin told Vedomosti. According to the expert, Moscow agreed to discuss not so much the settlement itself as possible ways to establish a security framework for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends. "By 2027, we will most likely still be in the midst of ongoing hostilities, though the US administration had certainly hoped to achieve tangible results by the end of this year," Trenin noted. The expert stressed that the future prospects of the negotiation process, including the development of specific terms, will be determined by the actual situation on the battlefield.
The current round of talks differs from previous ones because the agenda will include the issue of security guarantees for both Russia and Ukraine, an issue that was not included in negotiations with Kiev following the Istanbul consultations, Nikolay Silayev, a leading researcher at the MGIMO Institute of International Relations, said. However, the expert does not expect the upcoming negotiations with Ukraine to conclude any differently from the previous ones. "The main reason for the lack of confidence in a breakthrough is the public statements made by Ukrainian and European officials. Their position remains the same: an unconditional ceasefire," he stressed.
Izvestia: Russia ready to mediate between Tehran and Washington
Moscow is prepared to act as a mediator in settling the conflict between the US and Iran, provided both parties are interested. Talks between Washington and Tehran have reached an impasse, partly due to the unresolved question of Iran’s nuclear program. Russia previously proposed transporting Iran’s enriched uranium to its territory, but this initiative has yet to receive support.
The eight-month conflict between the US and Iran has stalled. Washington’s initial plan to quickly topple the country’s government has failed. Passage through the Strait of Hormuz remains difficult, and diplomats have yet to make progress toward resolving the conflict. Under these circumstances, Russia could assume the role of mediator. Moscow is ready to take such a step, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko told Izvestia. "If all parties express interest, then we are ready [to act as mediators]," he noted. "We previously offered our services regarding how the Iranian nuclear program could be resolved, but our proposals have not yet been supported," the senior diplomat said.
Thanks to its good relations with both Iran and Israel, Russia occupies a unique position as a universal intermediary in the Middle East, political analyst Alexander Kargin said. Moreover, Moscow is currently pursuing a negotiating track with the US as well. The expert noted that Pakistan, another potential mediator, has no diplomatic relations with Israel at all, whereas Russia does not face this problem.
Russian mediation would at least help establish a ceasefire, paving the way for a comprehensive resolution of the crisis, Kargin said. The analyst expects that, ultimately, the practical necessity of Moscow’s involvement will prevail, and the parties will bring Russia into the negotiations. At the same time, according to him, the parties to the conflict have diametrically opposed views on the nuclear program. While Russia’s proposal to remove the uranium would be ideal, heightened tensions in the Middle East are preventing the parties from making even the smallest compromises, Kargin stressed.
Izvestia: Russia may begin exporting fertilizers to US alongside diesel
Russia is ready to supply mineral fertilizers and fuel to the US, but expanding fertilizer exports would require a reallocation of shipments: currently, about 69% of fertilizer production is exported, experts said. Russian President Vladimir Putin has discussed the prospect of supplying fertilizers to the US market on a significant scale. In addition, the first shipment of 40,000 metric tons of Russian diesel fuel is scheduled to leave for the US on October 22, with other countries set to receive shipments by the end of the year.
During a meeting with US special presidential envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on October 21, Russian President Vladimir Putin said that Moscow could supply fertilizers to the American market in large quantities. However, it is difficult to gauge potential export volumes, since a significant portion of Russian production is already under contract with foreign buyers, Denis Prikhodko, an equity market analyst at Alfa-Capital Asset Management, told Izvestia. According to him, shipments will increase gradually, primarily through the redistribution of export flows among foreign markets rather than through higher production.
Increasing fertilizer and diesel fuel shipments to the US market could help bring down prices for these products both in the US and globally, which is especially important for agricultural producers. Such agreements with Russia would benefit both the Donald Trump administration and the Russian authorities, Igor Yushkov, a leading analyst at the National Energy Security Fund, stressed.
The European factor is also relevant. According to political scientist and German studies expert Yegor Belyachkov, the current leadership of most European countries will likely react negatively to an agreement between Russia and the US on fertilizer supplies, just as they did with the diesel deal. This approach directly reflects European countries' policy in recent years, under which the slightest compromise between Moscow and Washington prompts EU nations to attempt to block such agreements. Brussels could do so by tightening sanctions against Russia and coordinating with American Democrats, the expert said.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Possibility of routing Persian Gulf oil around Strait of Hormuz
New pipelines that bypass the Strait of Hormuz and lead to seaports outside the Persian Gulf will address the problem of supplying Middle Eastern oil to the global market. In five years, the strait may become obsolete for oil trade as shipments are redirected along new routes. This is not the first attempt to find alternative ways to deliver oil from Persian Gulf countries. Previously, this idea was also proposed by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. According to him, the construction of oil pipelines will render the Strait of Hormuz "a worthless piece of water" in as little as two to three years.
Bypass routes are currently more profitable, not because transporting oil via pipeline is inexpensive, but because of the increased costs linked to transit through the Strait of Hormuz, Maxim Malkov, a Kept partner and head of the firm’s oil and gas practice, told Rossiyskaya Gazeta. Before the crisis, tanker transit cost the same as or less than pipeline transport, while now, that balance has reversed, the expert noted. However, maritime transport is cheaper in peacetime. The cost of pumping oil through a pipeline is up to five times higher than the cost of moving it by oil tanker per kilometer, Oleg Abelev, head of the analytical department at the Rikom-Trust investment company, pointed out.
Existing alternative routes do not resolve the problem because their combined capacity is less than half of the volumes that previously passed through the Strait of Hormuz, Malkov emphasized. Moreover, the Red Sea poses its own risks, such as Houthi attacks, and there are virtually no alternatives to tankers for transporting refined petroleum products, the expert noted. But even if the existing infrastructure that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz is expanded and new oil pipelines are built in parallel, the economic viability of these projects will be questionable, economist Boris Kopeikin stressed. If the situation in the region stabilizes in the long term, oil will once again follow the traditional route, through the Strait of Hormuz, he said.
At the same time, the main advantage of alternative routes is the diversification of risks. They reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz and allow exports to continue in the event of shipping restrictions, but they do not guarantee complete supply security, Ivan Timonin, a senior manager at the Implementa consulting firm, said. According to Abelev, pipelines are no safer than maritime transport. They are vulnerable to drone and missile attacks, and protecting them along their entire length is quite difficult. Unlike seagoing vessels, a pipeline is stationary and its location is precisely known. It cannot be replaced or rerouted. Maritime transport offers greater flexibility. Oil pipelines for the Persian Gulf states are an expensive insurance policy, not a cheap alternative, the expert stressed.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: French authorities trying to ease protests with talks and concessions
Ahead of another round of large-scale protests scheduled for the weekend, the authorities are trying to reach a deal with the protesters. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu met with union representatives on October 21. The meeting produced no results; the government did not receive any promises to call off the protests. In fact, a general strike has been announced.
Nevertheless, Lecornu remains undeterred. The government has proposed an aid program for businesses affected by the unrest. Following his trip to the Persian Gulf states, President Emmanuel Macron issued a statement saying that he had secured additional fuel shipments to bring down prices in the country. The authorities are hoping these measures will have a rapid effect.
Rather than resorting to force, the French authorities have decided to address the wave of protests sweeping the country through persuasion. They have chosen to respond to the demonstrators’ main demands. Perhaps there is no other option: last weekend, more than half a million French citizens took to the streets across the country. The protests are no longer limited to schoolchildren and their parents who are dissatisfied with the education system. Labor unions are actively participating in the protests, which are directed against the rising cost of living and ultimately against the economic policies of the current president and government.
At the same time, the situation in the country is gradually returning to normal, although this will take some time, Tatyana Zvereva, a professor at the World Economy and World Politics Faculty of the Russian National Research University Higher School of Economics, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. "The composition of the protesters is complex. It includes high school students, members of the ‘Yellow Vests’ movement, and others, including members of fringe political organizations," she noted. According to the expert, the French authorities are pursuing two main lines of action. On the one hand, they are restoring order, which society as a whole expects. The far-right National Rally party has been particularly vocal in demanding this. On the other hand, the authorities are negotiating with moderate protesters.
"The logic is this: the most aggressive protesters must be held accountable, and positive-minded citizens must be reached out to by addressing their socio-economic demands. However, the second point is much more difficult to achieve. Therefore, it seems unlikely that we can expect quick results from the negotiations. But dialogue can help defuse the situation and let off some steam," Zvereva emphasized.

articles.title: Russia hit Kyiv with missiles carrying cluster warheads, Zelensky says
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump called Elon Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starlink, the Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday, citing US officials.
The Starlink system was working more normally on Thursday, shortly after the Trump-Musk conversation, according to US and Ukrainian officials cited by the WSJ.
Some Ukrainian officials told the newspaper the system was not restored to full functionality but was working at higher speeds than under the cap.
President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said earlier on Thursday that Starlink speed had not been restored for Ukraine, adding that he hoped for talks with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in the coming days.
Trump told Musk he was frustrated the system's speeds remained capped at around 100 mph (160 kph), the Journal said, citing officials.
Rubio said on Wednesday that decisions regarding Ukraine's access to Starlink were up to its parent company SpaceX and its CEO Musk, not the White House.
Starlink restrictions hamper Ukraine's drone operations
Ukraine uses Starlink for battlefield communications and drone operations. Restricting the satellite service hampered the country's attack and air defense drone missions against Russia.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday that Russia hit Kyiv overnight with three ballistic missiles carrying cluster munition warheads.
Zelensky said the missiles were designed to detonate in the air as they approached their targets, spreading damage across an area 400 meters wide. He added that one of them struck Kyiv's historic district, hitting the area near the monastic buildings of Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry reported at least four deaths in the strikes, while President Volodymyr Zelensky said 34 others were wounded, including five children, according to CBS News.
The attacks came just hours after Russia freed American citizen Stephen Hubbard and US special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom he described as a humanitarian.
Ukraine's energy facilities hit over 170 times since October 11
He also said that Russia had kept targeting Ukrainian energy infrastructure with more than 170 strikes on critical energy facilities since October 11.
Cluster munitions are prohibited in more than 100 countries under the 2008 Convention on Cluster Munitions. The weapons release multiple smaller explosives across large areas, putting civilians at risk both during attacks and afterward, when unexploded bomblets can remain dangerous. Neither Russia nor the US is a party to the treaty.

articles.title: Britain undersells its nuclear contribution to NATO
articles.body:
Britain is unique among allies in declaring its existing nuclear forces to NATO, but despite nuclear capabilities consuming over a fifth of the defence budget the Ministry of Defence does not maximise the political and economic value of that commitment, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, examined nuclear deterrence in the High North as part of its inquiry.
Dhesi said: “The High North poses a major strategic challenge for the UK’s security. This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage.”
Its conclusion states: “The United Kingdom has committed to acquiring a sub-strategic nuclear capability to enhance deterrence, although how this aligns with the security of the High North is less clear. To ensure the capability is effective it will probably be necessary for the RAF to occasionally rehearse forward deploying the nuclear-capable F-35A aircraft to the High North. Recipient countries will, therefore, need to be fully aligned and supportive of Britain’s extended deterrence strategy. Uniquely, the UK already declares its existing nuclear forces to NATO, but despite consuming over a fifth of the defence budget the MOD does not maximise the political and economic value of this considerable financial and military commitment.”
According to the most recent departmental annual report and accounts cited by the committee, spending on nuclear capabilities accounts for £14.45 billion of the total defence budget of £69.61 billion.
Britain agreed in 2025 to purchase twelve F-35A fighter aircraft for the Royal Air Force, giving it a sub-strategic nuclear capability and joining NATO’s Dual Capable Aircraft programme, with the Defence Investment Plan allocating £2.1 billion up to 2030 for the total British F-35 fleet. The committee notes that while the aircraft will be flown by RAF pilots, approval to use the nuclear weapons carried by those jets would in any crisis remain under American control.
The report asks how Britain will operate the new capability, including whether the aircraft would deploy to allied countries during peacetime to practise their wartime nuclear role, and how concern about the enduring level of American commitment to European security is addressed by carrying a weapon that remains under American sovereign control during any crisis.
France and Britain each hold around three hundred nuclear warheads, against an American stockpile the report puts at around 3,700 operational weapons. Under the July 2025 Northwood Declaration the two countries agreed to create a Nuclear Steering Group to provide political direction and coordinate across nuclear policy, capabilities and operations, and President Macron announced changes to French nuclear doctrine in March 2026 which included moving towards forward deterrence.
That resulted in bilateral agreements with NATO countries including Denmark and Norway in the High North, allowing French nuclear aircraft to deploy temporarily to their territory for exercises and joint missions. French nuclear assets will not be shared and French nuclear decision making will remain sovereign.
The committee records that France has generated considerable publicity around its agreements, strengthening its international profile on security matters and offering a platform to engage on wider issues including defence export sales.
Its recommendation asks the department to provide the committee with a classified briefing on how it intends to enhance nuclear deterrence through the new sub-strategic capability, including any discussions with regional allies on extended deterrence in the High North and the forward deployment of the capability, and states that given the financial burden of operating the deterrent the department should remind allies more frequently of the unique nuclear capability Britain declares to NATO.

articles.title: Congressmen urge Trump, Musk to give Ukraine ability to destroy missile launchers in Russia – media
articles.body:
American congressmen, including 16 members of the Democratic Party and seven members of the Republican Party, have signed a letter urging U.S President Donald Trump and SpaceX founder Elon Musk to grant Ukraine access to Starlink satellite systems to detect missile launchers on the territory of Russia.
"We are writing to urge you to ask Elon Musk to let Ukraine use the Starlink satellite internet system to hunt for missile launchers inside Russia. With one phone call, you could both save lives and give Vladimir Putin greater incentives to negotiate," reads the text of the letter sent on Wednesday, as cited by The Hill.
Among the Republicans who signed the letter are Joe Wilson (South Carolina), Brian Fitzpatrick (Pennsylvania), Don Bacon (Nebraska), Carlos Gimenez (Florida), Jeff Hurd (Colorado), Andy Harris (Maryland), and Max Miller (Ohio).
"Mr. President, we all share the goal of ending the war in Ukraine and the devastating loss of life it has caused... If Ukraine cannot reliably intercept Russian arrows, it must be able to strike the archer. The Starlink system, operated by Mr. Musk's SpaceX, could help with this," the letter states, with the congressmen noting that Vladimir Putin "currently has no intention of stopping the bloodshed."
As reported, Ukraine began using StarShield in 2024. Standard StarLink (Starlink Mini), installed on drones, has a limited speed of up to 160 km/h, which is insufficient to perform certain missions. To make an aircraft fly faster, it is necessary to gain access specifically to the military version of StarLink – StarShield.
SpaceX, without warning the Ukrainian Defense Forces on the night of October 14, unilaterally restricted the operation of StarShield terminals; this complicated the work of UAV missions, in particular interceptors and middle strikes. By the end of that same day, the operation of terminals at speeds of 160 km/h resumed, but Ukraine received confirmation that the 160 km/h restriction applies only within its territory.
On the same day, Musk stated that decisions regarding restrictions on the operation of military StarShield systems are made by the U.S military and the president, and commercial StarLink cannot be used for offensive military actions. However, Trump later stated that Washington was not involved in slowing down StarShield for Ukraine, and U.S Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that StarShield was allegedly unavailable to Ukraine and the White House had nothing to do with disruptions in StarLink's operation. U.S Secretary of War Pete Hegseth reported that his department refrained from issuing any directives regarding restricting StarShield's operation. Later, the British newspaper The Telegraph, citing its own sources, reported that Musk personally appealed to Trump with a proposal to limit StarLink's operating speed for the Ukrainian military.
Following this, a number of senators and congressmen stated the unacceptability of such actions, Musk's influence on the course of the war in Ukraine and U.S security, and that they would demand an investigation into the restrictions on the operation of StarShield systems in Ukraine and hold those responsible accountable.
On October 20, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that the American side had restored the operation of Ukraine's early warning system for Russian ballistic missile launches and announced a conversation with Rubio, while Rubio himself stated that he had nothing to do with decisions made by Musk and SpaceX regarding the operation of StarLink and StarShield.
The European Commission stated that SpaceX's restrictions on StarLink services for Ukraine contradict agreements, and the company must ensure full access for Ukraine.

articles.title: Russia Deploys New Filin Missile: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine Reveals Its Specifications and Components
articles.body:
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has published detailed information on Russia’s new Filin cruise missile.
The information, interactive 3D model, list of components, and electronic component database are available on the War&Sanctions portal.
According to Ukraine’s intelligence, Russian forces began using the weapon against Ukraine in late summer this year.
The missile was developed by Russia’s Molniya Scientific Production Association, a joint-stock company that is part of the Tactical Missiles Corporation.
The emergence of the Filin missile continues Russia’s military-industrial complex’s trend of developing low-cost, ground-launched, jet-powered strike weapons.
The missile’s 3.5-meter-long fuselage and 3-meter wingspan are made of composite materials, including carbon fiber and fiberglass. The developers used 3D printing to manufacture some structural components.
The 3D model shows that the Filin cruise missile has an elongated fuselage with a pointed nose, a straight wing of moderate aspect ratio, a tail assembly with a vertical fin and horizontal stabilizers, and a rectangular air intake on top of the fuselage.
The maximum speed claimed by the Russians is 800 km/h, with a range of up to 1,200 km at altitudes from extremely low to 6 km.
The missile is launched from a ground-based launcher using a powder booster. Its warhead weighs either 50 or 100 kg, depending on the variant.
The onboard equipment is manufactured by PLAZ LLC, which is also involved in producing Harpy UAVs. The guidance system uses a Chinese inertial navigation system and a 16-channel Kometa CRPA antenna, which provides resistance to electronic warfare interference.
The electronic component database contains a higher proportion of Chinese elements (22 identified units compared to 35 from the United States) and standardized circuit boards.
The missile is powered by the Russian R500 engine manufactured by Reynolds LLC, which has previously been identified in the S-71 Kover and Monoсhrome cruise air missiles.
