articles.title: Russia, Ukraine exchange strikes as US envoy leaves after talks
articles.body:
Russia bombs Kyiv and Ukraine fires drones towards Moscow, despite talk of renewing negotiations
KYIV, Oct 22 - Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow overnight as the warring sides kept up a barrage of attacks despite the latest US push to end the conflict.
Russia said on Wednesday it was ready to resume US-mediated talks with Ukraine next month, after President Vladimir Putin hosted US envoy Steve Witkoff for talks in St Petersburg.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said he hoped negotiations, which would be the first since February, would take place early in November.
Ukraine said Russia fired at least 21 ballistic missiles in three waves, and Zelenskiy said three of them carried cluster munitions — "bomblets" that disperse over a wide area and are banned by many countries because of the danger they pose to civilians. Russia's defence ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Russia said Ukraine launched 630 drones towards Moscow during the night.
The two sides held an exchange of war dead, with Moscow handing over 252 bodies and Ukraine handing over 25, according to the Belta state news agency in neighbouring Belarus. Such exchanges have accompanied moves towards talks in the past.
But while Witkoff spoke of "some degree of momentum" after meeting Zelenskiy and European and NATO officials in Oslo earlier in the week, the Kremlin expressed doubts.
"The Americans sensed some new nuances (in Oslo) and told us about this. But these nuances, so to speak, do not entirely satisfy us," Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said.
A senior Russian official, briefed on the results of the Putin-Witkoff talks, said they were relatively short and not substantive. The American brought a set of proposals drafted in Oslo and handed them to Putin for review, the person said.
Another source close to the Kremlin said the US proposals included a scenario where Ukraine would cede all of its Donbas region to Russia in return for receiving a guarantee of its future security from NATO.
Russia says it launched the war, the deadliest in Europe since World War Two, in part to prevent Ukraine from joining NATO. It has repeatedly said it would not end fighting unless Ukraine cedes more land, limits the size of its forces and is permanently barred from forming alliances.
Ukraine, which says the invasion was an unprovoked war of conquest, has long dismissed Russia's conditions as a demand for capitulation that would leave it defenceless against future Russian attacks.
US PRAISE FOR 'HUMANITARIAN' PUTIN GOES DOWN BADLY WITH KYIV
Zelenskiy's meeting with Witkoff was aimed in part at smoothing over a deterioration in relations with Washington this month, after President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and lifted sanctions on Moscow.
Kyiv says Washington failed to provide early-warning data on Russian missile launches, throttled the SpaceX satellite system used to guide Ukrainian drones, and withheld missile defence systems bought on its behalf by Europeans. Washington denies any shift in policy to intentionally hamper Ukraine's forces.
Trump has repeatedly rebuked Ukraine for attacking Russian oil refineries while saying little about far deadlier Russian attacks on Ukraine. He called for Zelenskiy to be replaced and said Russia's actions in Ukraine have been "fine".
Zelenskiy, who long avoided any criticism of the Trump administration, has increasingly pushed back against what he describes as a shift towards sympathy with Moscow.
On Thursday Zelenskiy snapped back at Witkoff for saluting Putin as a "humanitarian" during his visit to Russia, when the US envoy thanked Putin for releasing a 74-year-old American captured by Russian forces in Ukraine.
"Three waves of ballistic missiles have been launched at Kyiv by Russian 'humanitarians' since yesterday evening," Zelenskiy posted on X. "They used 21 missiles. Unfortunately, numerous sites across the city have been hit and damaged."
He said 2 people were killed and 34 injured, including 5 children, in attacks on a dozen Ukrainian regions.
Russia said it carried out a "massive strike" overnight on port infrastructure in Ukraine's Odesa region, as well as on vessels used by the Ukrainian military.
In Russia, two people were wounded near Moscow by drones launched towards the capital during the night, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram. Most of the drones were downed at long range, he added.
In the Russian border region of Belgorod, one man was killed and another wounded by Ukrainian drones, local officials said.
With the frontlines of the war largely static, both sides have escalated long-range air strikes this year. Russia has particularly targeted the Ukrainian power grid, while Ukraine has aimed at Russian oil refineries. Both have struck data centres, commercial warehouses and Black Sea shipping.
The war has ground on for more than 4-1/2 years, defying Trump's pledge during his 2024 election campaign that he could end it in a day. No breakthrough emerged from three short meetings in Istanbul last year and three rounds of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi and Geneva at the start of this year. REUTERS

articles.title: Is Iran ready for another major US attack after midterm elections?
articles.body:
Is Iran ready for another major US attack after midterm elections?
October 22, 2026
Officials in Tehran are preparing for renewed strikes
following media reports that the United States and Israel have been examining new options for escalating their war against Iran.
The US midterm elections on November 3 and Israel's October 27 election have injected a political factor into how both countries are approaching the conflict, which they launched in late February.
Polls show that high energy prices brought on by the Iran war are hurting Donald Trump's Republican Party. On October 8, the president posted on social media that the United States would not attack Iran before the midterms, citing "productive discussions" with Tehran. The United States last launched strikes on Iran in early September.
After the elections are over, however, Trump may feel less politically constrained.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has campaigned on a platform of regime change in Iran.
Report: Plans in place for 'short' US-Israeli operation
Citing senior US officials the New York Times reported on Wednesday that the United States and Israel have "developed specific plans" for a "short but intensive operation" in Iran that would include targets such as nuclear facilities, energy infrastructure, and the country's arsenal of missiles and drones.
One official told the newspaper that the goal would be to force Iran into making "diplomatic concessions" by further weakening its economy, as negotiations to end the conflict have gone nowhere. The United States has also maintained a blockade of Iranian oil exports in the Strait of Hormuz that has sapped Tehran's oil revenues.
Other outlets have reported similar plans in recent weeks. In early October, Axios reported that the Pentagon has instructed US Central Command "to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran."
There are currently two US aircraft carrier strike groups in the Arabian Sea, with a third expected to arrive by late November.
On October 15, Trump told the right-wing broadcaster Newsmax that he was considering a strike on Pickaxe Mountain, near the Natanz nuclear complex, where US officials say Iran may have moved sensitive nuclear-related material underground.
A day later, CNN reported that Trump is considering using a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb on Iranian targets. As the MOAB creates a humungous blast wave above ground, its effectiveness in targeting underground facilities such as Pickaxe would be limited.
Has Iran learned from earlier attacks?
Iranian officials say they are prepared for another attack, with a broad response that would include strikes on US bases and energy facilities in the Gulf.
Ali Asghar Shafieian, a media adviser to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, told DW that, although the United States retains a significant technological and military advantage, Tehran's strategy is based on preserving the regime's hold on the country rather than matching US strength.
"The United States has the upper hand in military power and technology, but Iran's strength is in how it deals with a crisis," Shafieian said.
Shafieian pointed to the rapid replacement of senior officials killed in previous attacks as an example of how Tehran has tried to make its political structure more resilient. Iran has also been rebuilding missile and drone capabilities that were hit during the massive wave of strikes during the first weeks of the war.
Citing Iranian officials, the Reuters news agency reported this week that Iran is "preparing for renewed Israeli and US attacks, not for a deal with America to end the war," adding that Tehran was prolonging negotiations to try to weaken Trump ahead of the midterms.
Iran has told regional governments that US military bases and critical infrastructure could become targets if neighboring countries assist another US or Israeli operation.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has warned that participation or cooperation by regional states would result in a "decisive and proportionate response."
"Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if we see strong evidence of a sincere desire by US to build trust & reach a just solution," Araghchi posted on X Wednesday. "But, if US chooses war over diplomacy, it'll certainly result in an even greater strategic failure."
How Iran prepares for new strikes?
Rahman Ghahremanpour, a Tehran-based political analyst, told DW that Iran's preparations extend beyond missiles and drones to prioritizing internal security.
That includes confronting armed opposition groups, preparing for possible protests and developing plans to prevent external military pressure from combining with domestic unrest.
Another conflict, he said, could bring renewed internet restrictions and a stronger mobilization of government supporters in public spaces.
"In the government's asymmetric-war strategy, the ultimate objective is to convince the United States that regime change through military action is impossible," Ghahremanpour said.
Ghahremanpour added that some factions within Iran have supported returning to a negotiated agreement. But he believes that Washington's demands are now considered so extensive that even Iranian officials who favor compromise struggle to build domestic support for them.
"For now, we are facing a deadlock," Ghahremanpour said. "Iranian officials do not appear optimistic about reaching an agreement."
Talks continue to snag on Iran's nuclear program, which US officials say must top the agenda.
Iran's latest proposal to the United States, sent through Qatari mediators, included an offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under Iranian control, in exchange for the US's lifting its maritime blockade, releasing frozen assets and ending military actions.
Citing data from the ship tracker Kpler, the Wall Street Journal reported this week that oil flows through Hormuz are approaching prewar levels as the US military escorts tankers and shipping companies are more willing to take risks for a bigger payoff. This raises questions about whether Iran's leverage over oil flows might be weakening.
Fear of war inside Iran
An escalation in the confrontation would come at a moment of severe economic pressure and growing political polarization for Iranians.
A doctor in Tehran told DW that she fears what would happen should fighting resumed. Speaking with the media in Iran remains very dangerous, and she spoke under condition of anonymity.
"The economic situation has become extremely bad," she said. "Even if you have a good income yourself, you don't feel good living among so many people struggling with poverty," she added.
She expects authorities to restrict internet access again if fighting resumes.
A woman in Tehran described anger toward regime supporters and said another war combined with domestic protests could increase the risk of confrontations on the streets.
Asked about possible attacks on underground nuclear sites, she said the issue felt increasingly detached from her everyday problems.
"What do the nuclear sites have to do with us?" she said. "They are inside mountains."
Edited: Emmy Sasipornkarn

articles.title: Putin agrees to resume three-way peace talks with Ukraine and US
articles.body:
Putin agrees to resume talks on Ukraine war with Kyiv and Washington, Kremlin says
In short:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as soon as next month.
The Russian leader has met with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg.
What's next?
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he supports the proposal, and is hopeful the three-way talks will take place in early November.
The Kremlin says Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume three-way negotiations next month with Washington and Kyiv aimed at ending the war in Ukraine.
The Russian leader met US envoy Steve Witkoff for talks in a grand imperial palace in St Petersburg.
Mr Putin's foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said the focus would be on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends".
The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February before the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran.
Mr Witkoff's talks with Mr Putin about Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine took place as US President Donald Trump pushed Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has insisted that only a leaders' summit can break the impasse.
Latest proposals have little of value, Kremlin says
The Kremlin said the discussion in St Petersburg lasted about three hours and came a day after Mr Witkoff met Mr Zelenskyy and some European leaders in Norway's capital, Oslo.
Mr Ushakov said the proposals from the Oslo meeting "contained little of real value in the context of resolving the Ukrainian crisis".
However, he later told Russian state TV that while Moscow was not "fully satisfied" with the Oslo proposals, they were a step in the right direction.
Mr Zelenskyy said he supported the proposal for three-way talks.
"We have received feedback that … Russia supports a trilateral meeting at the level of our [negotiating] teams," he said.
"The American side has proposed holding it as soon as possible and we support that …The Ukrainian side has been in contact with its American partners. They will do everything to ensure that the meeting takes place as early as possible, in November. I think no later than early November."
Mr Zelenskyy said that Kyiv supported "any proposals for a ceasefire, an end to the war, an energy ceasefire as well as humanitarian initiatives".
Witkoff sees 'some degree of momentum' in peace efforts
Mr Witkoff and Mr Putin met at St Petersburg's Constantine Palace, with Mr Ushakov and Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev also at the table.
Mr Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined the discussion via a video link.
Before the meeting, Mr Witkoff said that there was "some degree of momentum" in talks.
In televised opening remarks, Mr Witkoff thanked Mr Putin for agreeing to send diesel to the US after Mr Trump lifted a ban despite anger from some US lawmakers, adding that the fuel would help reduce prices for American farmers and truckers.
Mr Putin said he was ready to consider restoring US-Russia economic ties and was prepared to discuss the US-led conflict with Iran.
He said Moscow stands ready to use its relationship with Tehran to help bring peace.
Mr Ushakov said that "large-scale joint economic projects that offer significant prospects for cooperation" between Russia and the US were discussed in detail with Mr Witkoff.
"Some of these are, in fact, nearing the implementation stage," he said.
Russia resumes attacks on Ukraine
Just as Russia indicated its readiness to join the trilateral peace talks, officials in Ukraine reported the capital Kyiv had been attacked with ballistic missiles on Wednesday evening, local time.
Homes, a petrol station and transport equipment were damaged and six people were injured.
Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram there were strikes in two districts on the east side of the Dnipro River bisecting the city, and posted on social media:
"Explosions in the capital. Kyiv is under ballistic attack.
"Stay in shelters!"
The city remained under a drone warning for more than two hours after the initial alert was declared.
Russian authorities also said they downed most of the 630 drones heading towards Moscow overnight.
Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram that two people were injured in the attack outside of the city.
AP/Reuters

articles.title: Ukraine’s military admits it fails to intercept any single Russian ballistic missile again
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. Ukrainian air defenses failed to intercept a single Russian ballistic or cruise missile last night, as follows from the data of the country’s General Staff analyzed by TASS.
This is not the first time that Ukrainian air defenses have failed to intercept a single Russian missile overnight launched at military facilities and sites used by Ukraine’s military.
Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky has regularly called on the West to supply new interceptor missiles for Patriot air defense systems. Kiev has repeatedly complained that weapons deliveries from partner countries have declined amid the US-Israeli war against Iran. Zelensky argues that Ukraine must receive interceptor missiles individually from countries willing to supply them.
Russia’s Defense Ministry reported on the morning of October 22 that Russian forces had launched a massive overnight strike against Ukraine’s military-industrial sector involved in the production and storage of cruise missiles, long-and medium-range unmanned aerial vehicles, transport infrastructure in Kiev, port infrastructure in the Odessa Region, and vessels at sea supporting the Ukrainian army’s operations.

articles.title: Vance: Starlink Use Depends on US Policy Toward Kyiv, Moscow – Not Musk
articles.body:
US Vice President JD Vance said on Thursday, Oct. 22, that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk should not be at the center of the dispute over restrictions on Ukraine’s satellite service, framing the issue instead as a matter of US policy toward the war in Ukraine.
Vance spoke to reporters before departing for a rally in North Platte, Nebraska, a day after senior US special envoy Steve Witkoff held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Well, I think that fundamentally Elon Musk runs a private corporation, and I think it’s completely understandable that he doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the US government effectively directing him on what to do,” Vance said.
“So I don’t think this is about Elon,” he continued, leaving unanswered who ordered the restrictions – a decision for which both Musk and the White House denied responsibility while pointing to the other.
Vance turns criticism on European leaders
Asked by a reporter whether he supported Republican calls for an investigation, Vance turned to European governments instead of answering directly.
He said it was ironic that countries with nothing comparable to SpaceX’s technology had spent years targeting the company with regulation and licensing restrictions, now relying on the company.
Currently, the EU is negotiating Ukraine’s access to its secure satellite communications program that could expand the system with commercial services in early 2027.
Russian Shahed Drone Strikes Private Home in Zhytomyr, Injuring 8, Including 2 Children
“Now they’re all running to SpaceX saying, ‘Please do what we need you to do,’” he said, arguing that the situation proved a point that US President Donald Trump has long made; that European countries rely on American technology, businesses and military power.
At the same time, Vance claimed that “European political leaders love to bash the US allies that they depend upon so much.”
The remark comes amid European criticism of Trump’s abrupt Oct. 9 diesel deal with Putin, which eased US sanctions on Russian fuel and effectively cleared the war for over 4.8 million tons of Russian diesel to reach the global market.
While Europe has sanctions imposed on Moscow since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, Trump has waived new sanctions on Russia which he signed into law just three weeks before striking a deal with the Kremlin leader.
On Monday, Oct. 19, a member of Trump’s Republican party, US Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, warned that anyone who tries to restrict Ukraine’s use of Starshield will face accountability, including a full investigation, public hearings and steep budget cuts.
Fitzpatrick also pledged to introduce bipartisan legislation, the “Roland Reagan Peace Through Strength Act,” blocking all purchases of Russian oil.
‘A tall mountain to climb’
One of the reporters pointed out that Ukraine has repeatedly agreed to negotiations, while Russia has not, and asked what gives Vance confidence that the current peace negotiations, led by Witkoff, will be different.
Vance claimed that both countries have agreed to join the negotiating table, adding that “the reason why we haven’t struck a peace deal is because they’ve [Kyiv and Moscow] just been too far apart on some of the details of that negotiation.”
According to him, Witkoff re-engaged the process.
“I mean, the nature of these things is you take a swing at it, you see how much progress it can make, and you’re back at it. And sometimes it works and sometimes it doesn’t,” he said, praising Witkoff and Trump’s administration for taking on difficult work, knowing that they “have a tall mountain to climb.”
So far, the Kremlin rebuked every proposition for a direct meeting with Ukraine, as well as proposals for a ceasefire.
In September, during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York, 51 countries issued a joint statement supporting Ukraine and urging Russia to accept an immediate ceasefire.
During the same summit, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, who represented Putin, said that the Kremlin will not pause its “special military operation” even during negotiations. He also blamed Europe for “engaging in their shenanigans,” saying Ukraine would have kept its 1991 borders if they hadn’t.
At Witkoff’s request during their three-hour meeting on Wednesday, Oct. 21, Putin said he would be willing to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine and the US in November.
During the same visit, Witkoff praised Putin as a “humanitarian” for releasing an American prisoner held in Russia, drawing sharp criticism from both Republicans and Democrats.
Starlink dispute deepens rift between Kyiv and Washington
The Starlink (Starshield) controversy is just one of the latest strains in diplomatic relations between Ukraine and the US.
Tensions began when Trump announced the controversial diesel deal while the Ukrainian delegation was in Miami with US officials, hoping for a breakthrough in Russia’s war.
Kyiv later said it had been warned that Washington could restrict intelligence sharing if Ukraine kept striking Russian oil refineries. Around the same time, Trump also called for Ukraine to elect a new president, claiming Putin was easier to negotiate with.
Overnight on Oct. 13-14, Ukrainian military units lost connectivity on terminals moving at roughly 160 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour) or faster, without prior warning. The disruption crippled several types of drones Ukraine uses, including interceptor drones used against Russia’s jet-powered Shaheds.
On Oct. 14, Musk claimed that limits on the military Starshield service were set by the US military, and ultimately the president himself, while Trump denied involvement.
“I don’t know if it was somebody, because it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said.
Since then, reports have pointed in both directions. While Reuters reported on Oct. 15 that the order originated inside the White House, The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, Oct. 20 that Musk ordered the restrictions himself.
On Oct. 21, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Musk determines Ukraine’s access to Starlink under a private commercial contract.
The episode has even drawn criticism from within Trump’s own party. Besides Fitzpatrick, Republican Senator Thom Tillis and Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen led nine senators in asking the Pentagon’s inspector general on Oct. 15 to investigate the disruptions.
Following a meeting with Witkoff in Oslo, Norway, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 20 that US intelligence sharing with Ukraine for early warnings of Russian attack is working again, adding that Ukraine could see results within the next 48 hours on Patriot interceptors and Starlink restrictions.

articles.title: Turkish army gets more Tayfun ballistic missiles
articles.body:
- Türkiye delivered a new batch of Roketsan Tayfun Block 2 ballistic missiles to its Land Forces Command, following earlier deliveries in May and June 2026.
- The Tayfun Block 2 has a range of more than 500 km and a reported accuracy of under 10 meters.
Türkiye’s Ministry of National Defence has delivered a new batch of Roketsan Tayfun Block 2 ballistic missiles to the Turkish Land Forces Command, adding to a missile force that began entering service only five months ago.
The delivery was reported on Oct. 22, 2026, and in line with previous handovers, the ministry kept the number of missiles classified. The new batch is at least the third known delivery this year: the ministry announced on May 20, 2026, that Tayfun Block 2 missiles had been accepted into the Land Forces inventory for the first time, and a second batch followed on June 25.
Tayfun, Turkish for “typhoon,” is the longest-range ballistic missile Türkiye has developed on its own. Roketsan, the state-owned missile maker, describes the Block 2 as having a range of more than 500 km (310 miles) and designed to strike high-value targets deep behind enemy lines, including air defense systems, command and control centers, aircraft hangars and other critical military facilities.
The missile is about 6.5 meters (21.3 feet) long and 610 mm (24 inches) in diameter, with a launch weight of 2,300 kg (5,070 pounds). It is fired from a wheeled transporter-erector-launcher, a truck that carries, raises and launches the missile and holds two rounds, which allows crews to move quickly between firing positions.
Roketsan says the Tayfun Block 2 lands within 10 meters (33 feet) of its target, measured as circular error probable, the radius within which half of the missiles fired are expected to land. It uses coordinate-based guidance, meaning it flies to a fixed point programmed before launch, and the company says it is highly resistant to GPS jamming and can operate day or night in poor weather. The missile carries a pre-formed fragmentation warhead, which breaks into a pattern of fragments on detonation.
Türkiye first test-fired Tayfun in October 2022 from Rize-Artvin Airport on the Black Sea coast, when the missile flew 561 km (349 miles) in 456 seconds before striking a target area off Sinop. That distance was roughly twice the 280 km (174-mile) range of Roketsan’s earlier Bora missile, previously the longest-range ballistic missile in Turkish service. Further test firings followed in May 2023 and in later years as the program moved toward serial production.
Roketsan has continued to expand the family alongside the Block 2 deliveries. In July 2025, the company unveiled the much larger Tayfun Block 4 at the IDEF defense fair in Istanbul, a missile about 10 meters (33 feet) long and weighing roughly 7,200 kg (15,900 pounds), which Roketsan presents as a hypersonic ballistic missile system. In July 2026, Roketsan released footage of a Tayfun Block 3 striking an unmanned boat at sea, which the company said was the first time a Tayfun had been used against a naval target and the first use of a seeker on the missile.
With three batches delivered since May, the Tayfun Block 2 is now steadily building up inside the Turkish Land Forces, while the Block 3 and Block 4 versions continue through development and testing at Roketsan.

articles.title: Inside the institution where Ukraine races to counter Russia's evolving drones
articles.body:
Inside the institution where Ukraine races to counter Russia's evolving drones
From a Canon camera to a magnetometer, wreckage reveals how Russian weapons keep advancing and why Ukraine’s countermeasures struggle to keep pace.
The aftermath of a Russian Geran-5-type jet-powered drone strike on a Ukrnafta petrol station is seen in the Holosiivskyi district of Kyiv, Ukraine, on Sept. 15, 2026. (Kostiantyn Liberov / Libkos / Getty Images)
In a government office, researchers of drones and electronic warfare gather around a small metal device recovered from a Russian Geran drone. Its purpose — to measure the Earth’s magnetic field for navigation.
"This is the most recent component we found, about a week or two ago," said one of the researchers.
Outside, a Russian drone’s jet engine roared — a sound that has become almost constant in Kyiv in recent months as advances in drone technology allow Russia to strike farther, more often and with greater precision. The small metal sensor on the table could make that threat even more vicious.
If it works as the researchers suspect, it could keep drones on course even when their satellite navigation is jammed, making the prospect of a winter under near-constant Russian attack even grimmer.
The researchers work at an institution under Ukraine’s Defense Ministry, and its work is rarely seen by outsiders. Here, specialists dismantle Russian weapons recovered from the battlefield or attacks to identify vulnerabilities, help develop countermeasures, and anticipate what Russian engineers might try next. The Kyiv Independent was given rare access on the condition that neither the institution nor the people inside be identified.
Their work is a race against time. The researchers estimate that developing an effective countermeasure usually takes four to six months, while Russia can introduce further modifications after two or three.
Regarding the sensor they found — in technical terms called a magnetometer — the researchers said they were still investigating its purpose and whether Russia might deploy it at scale.
But finding a new component is not the same as understanding it, and understanding it is not the same as having a way to counter it. And the Russian engineers who put the magnetometer in the drone face a similar gap. Fitting it to a handful of drones is not the same as being able to deploy it at scale.
What Russia’s drone wreckage reveals about the threats ahead
Inside the institution, the fluorescent-lit hallways were filled with pieces of missiles, drones, fuzes, and motherboards, all neatly organized and labeled. People move in and out, some in camouflage, others in jeans and plain shirts, some carrying paperwork, others pieces of military hardware.
There is the nose of a North Korean missile, taller than a grown man, and a large section of a Russian Oreshnik missile, its cylindrical body roughly as wide as a passenger car. On the other side of the hallway were several Russian Geran drones, their triangular bodies resembling black paper airplanes enlarged to more than three meters long (9.8 feet), with wings spanning roughly three meters.
Outwardly, the Russian Gerans still resemble the Iranian drones Russia began using to terrorize Ukrainian cities in the fall of 2022. Inside, however, successive modifications had made them markedly different from those early aircraft, and even from the first Russian-made Gerans that appeared by the summer of 2023.
To trace the drones' evolution, the researchers work backward from the ones they recover. They begin by identifying and documenting each drone’s basic features, then dismantle it to map its internal systems, trace its components to their manufacturers, and reconstruct how each part contributes to the aircraft’s operation.
The researchers explained that changes inside the drones often reflected the success of Ukraine’s defenses. A navigation system that had once guided an aircraft to its target could become vulnerable to jamming, prompting Russia to try something else.
"When the Russians see that the effectiveness is decreasing, they introduce other technologies," one researcher said.
But the two sides don't take turns. Russia can introduce another modification while Ukraine is still working out how to defeat the previous one.
On one of the tables lies a Canon camera recovered from one of the first iterations of Russian drones from late 2022 used for attacks on Ukrainian cities. Still in its original casing, it looked much as it would in a shop, except that its settings had been glued in place against the vibrations of flight.
read also
The next example they recovered a few months later, a Sony, had been stripped of its casing, leaving its lens and colorful wiring exposed. "You can already see that it’s quite a development compared to the first sample," a researcher said.
Such details helped the specialists judge how far an adaptation had progressed. You can tell a lot from the workmanship and the way it’s put together, one researcher explained. Specialists look for whether a part was improvised and attached to a drone or whether the drone was built to carry it — a sign that an experiment might be entering regular production.
Sometimes the clue is simpler. Sometimes there are letters "E" or "EE" on a drone’s tail fins, which the researchers believe stands for "experiment."
Other clues had been deliberately erased. The researchers showed antennae chips with their identifying markings scratched off, an effort, they said, to hide the supply chains bringing American and European electronics into Russian weapons despite sanctions.
"Removing markings does not make identification impossible," one researcher said. But it can turn what might have been a glance at a label into an investigation requiring specialized equipment and scarce time.
Reconstructing Russian technology can take months or even years, hampered by a lack of specialized equipment, resources, and expertise in Ukraine, and even with help from foreign partners, some electronic components remain nearly impossible to decipher without access to manufacturers’ proprietary information, which they are often unwilling to share.
A threat long in the making
Hanging in the stairwell was a completely intact Geran-3 that had reached the institution in 2025, well before this autumn’s urgent calls to accelerate production of interceptors capable of catching jet-powered drones. It had run out of fuel and landed in sand without detonating.
At its rear was a silver jet engine, roughly the size of a large melon, replacing the propeller-driven engine that gave earlier iterations of these drones their familiar moped sound. Faster flight and higher operating altitudes made jet-powered variants harder for mobile teams armed with machine guns to engage.
A message written on the black body of the drone in white marker read "greetings to Serhii from the engineers." The researchers believed it was addressed to Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky on defense technology. One researcher found a small consolation: the Russians had misspelled "engineers."
The same recovered aircraft had carried another indication of what was coming this summer beyond the jets: a camera and a mesh modem. "(That meant it was) able to send back video footage and receive control signals," a researcher said.
The researchers have a collection of the palm-sized mesh modems in their office, which they identify as Chinese-made. Mesh modems allow drones to relay video and control signals through one another, extending communications beyond an individual aircraft’s direct connection to its operator.
One researcher compared the technology to repeaters used to extend Wi-Fi coverage through a house. Here, the repeaters are other drones. This allows operators to change targets during flight and pursue even moving targets, such as trains, rather than simply sending a drone toward fixed coordinates, the researchers said.
The video feed allows the Russian operator to watch a civilian building draw closer while continuing to steer the drone toward it. He is far from the people inside but can see who he is targeting.
"If it is a civilian site, he knows what he is hitting and how," one researcher said.
read also
The next unknown
The institution has possessed evidence of Russian attempts to implement jet engines and mesh relays since last year. But what a single recovered aircraft could not establish last fall was how soon or whether at all the same hardware would appear in large numbers.
Half a year later, it did. Since this summer, jet-powered drones have targeted Ukraine, particularly Kyiv, on a daily, constant basis, with the sound of explosions a regular occurrence in the capital throughout the day.
The researchers described the interval before an effective response to a modification became available as a "window of opportunity" for Russia. Once a change proved useful, Russia could concentrate resources on producing and deploying it while Ukraine was still developing a countermeasure.
"They don’t wait for us to come up with a countermeasure," one of the researchers said. The engineers attribute this problem mostly to scale. Russia likely has institutions similar to theirs, just several times larger with more resources.
The magnetometer the researchers recently recovered was still at an earlier stage of their investigation. "We can’t say for sure what it is, until we’ve completed all the necessary research," one said.
It might prove a modest refinement rather than a breakthrough. To become a widespread threat, its integration would need to be refined and its production scaled up.
But even a slight edge could be enough, helping more aircraft stay on course and tilting the balance of the war further in Russia's favor.

articles.title: Estonia provides additional EUR 10 mln in aid to Ukraine through PURL – Foreign Ministry
articles.body:
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna has said the country has contributed EUR 10 million in defense aid to Ukraine under NATO's Priority List of Ukraine's Needs (PURL) initiative.
"Today, Estonia decided to contribute another EUR 10 million through NATO's PURL initiative, bringing our total contribution through this mechanism to EUR 31 million. This will help Ukraine obtain urgently needed air defence and ammunition," Tsahkna said on X social media platform on Thursday.
According to him, Estonia's military aid to Ukraine this year amounted to 0.3% of the country's gross domestic product.
The minister said Russian strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure have left hundreds of thousands of people without electricity, and with winter approaching, this support is vital for protecting lives and ensuring the functioning of essential services.
"The stronger Ukraine can defend itself, the less Russia can dictate the terms of peace. We must keep supporting Ukraine and increasing pressure on Russia," Tsakhkna said.
The Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) is a joint initiative of the U.S., NATO, and partner countries, launched in the summer of 2025 to rapidly deliver critically important U.S.-manufactured weapons and ammunition to Ukraine. Ukraine compiles a list of priority needs (primarily air defense and artillery), which is coordinated with the United States and NATO. Partner countries (NATO members and other states) make voluntary financial contributions to joint funding packages. With the funds received, the United States will transfer the necessary weapons to Ukraine directly from its own stockpiles

articles.title: The Price of Faustian Bargains with Trump
articles.body:
For the past week, President Donald Trump and his aides have traded accusations with Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, over who restricted Ukraine’s access to a military-grade version of Starlink, SpaceX’s satellite network product that Ukrainian forces depend on to intercept incoming Russian projectiles and target Russian launchers.
Musk blamed Trump and the U.S. military for the decision, writing on X, “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.” Trump insisted that his administration did not disrupt Ukraine’s access to the network. Secretary of State Marco Rubio argued that decisions about Ukraine’s access to the network were in the hands of SpaceX and Musk and not the White House. The Wall Street Journal and CBS News reported that the decision had been Musk’s.
On Mar. 9, 2025, Musk had promised that, whatever his disagreements with U.S. policy toward Ukraine, “Starlink will never turn off its terminals. We would never do such a thing or use it as a bargaining chip.” Critics have raced to blame Musk alone, casting him as the puppeteer behind the throne, the first business titan to achieve what William Randolph Hearst, Marcus Alonzo Hanna, and J.P. Morgan only aspired to: a latter-day Cornelius Vanderbilt, who is reputed to have scoffed, “Law? What do I care about the law? Hain’t I got the power?”
That gets the story backward. Musk’s businesses are uniquely dependent on the blessings of Washington: a fifth of SpaceX’s revenue comes directly from federal agencies, its satellites require federal authorization to launch and operate, and the possible merger of Tesla and SpaceX will live or die by the decisions of federal regulators.
Confronted with a White House that appeared determined to squeeze Ukraine, whatever its public denials, Musk faced a familiar choice for anyone dependent on political patronage: capitulate, resist, or retreat into ambiguity. He chose ambiguity, revealing the limits of his power. The wealthiest man in the world still answers to someone else.
The finger-pointing creates a haze of ambiguity, giving both men plausible deniability. The apparent aim is to force Ukraine into a settlement by depriving it of the means to resist: a way to secure a quick, short-term peace and lower oil prices at the expense of Ukrainian sovereignty and international law.
But that calculation mistakes capitulation for stability. Rewarding President Vladimir Putin of Russia could encourage him to test NATO’s resolve in the Baltic states, Poland, Finland, or Sweden, raising the risk of a direct confrontation with the alliance. It would also signal to other U.S. adversaries that sufficient pressure can fold Washington’s commitments.
For now, Trump could claim to have brokered peace between Russia and Ukraine, even if the peace he delivers is the silence of a defeated country. Musk can evade responsibility by presenting himself as merely one supplier among many across the defense industry whose failures have weakened Ukraine’s defenses. He could point to weapons manufacturer RTX, whose Patriot interceptors are so scarce that Ukraine reportedly ran out of them this month, or to delays in delivering F-16s manufactured by Lockheed Martin that were promised two years earlier.
Faustian bargains
Beneath the public quarrel lies a familiar pattern: surrender political independence and retain the freedom to accumulate extraordinary wealth. The historians who have studied Putin’s Russia most closely would recognize the pattern instantly. Timothy Snyder has written that Russia’s oligarchs “were tamed, but not by a neutral state.” Rather, “Putin himself became the head oligarch, the boss of bosses.” Anne Applebaum echoed the insight and described Putin as making himself “godfather to all of the other oligarchs.”
Putin laid out the terms of that bargain on Jul. 28, 2000, when he met with 21 of Russia's richest men in the Kremlin, less than three months after his inauguration. The message was simple. The fortunes they had amassed in the chaos of the 1990s were theirs to keep, as long as they stayed out of politics entirely. Keep your distance from power, and the state would leave you alone.
Those who refused the deal faced immediate reprisals. Boris Berezovsky and Vladimir Gusinsky, whose television networks refused to bend the knee, were driven into exile within the year. Gusinsky’s NTV was seized by state-controlled Gazprom. Mikhail Khodorkovsky, then Russia’s richest man, funded opposition parties and lectured the Kremlin on corruption. In Oct. 2003 he was pulled off his plane at a Siberian airport and arrested. He spent a decade in prison and watched his oil company, Yukos, dismantled and its assets transferred to state-controlled companies.
Those who accepted the deal are the ones who got rich, and they have never been richer. Forbes counted a record 155 Russian billionaires this year, the fourth straight year that number has grown, with a combined fortune of $696.5 billion—up 11% from the previous year, even as Putin’s war against Ukraine entered its fifth year. Their collective wealth reportedly now exceeds the bank term deposits of the rest of Russia’s population: 155 oligarchs with fortunes greater than the savings of roughly 146 million ordinary Russians.
“Oligarchies are unstable,” Snyder has observed. “Members disappear.” For those who might have forgotten the terms of Putin’s bargain, an instructive reminder came in 2023, when Yevgeny Prigozhin, the head of the Wagner Group, did the one thing the bargain forbade: he challenged the Kremlin’s authority. Prigozhin seized a military headquarters in Rostov-on-Don and sent his forces toward Moscow. His column advanced to within 125 miles of the capital before he agreed to stand down under a deal brokered by Aleksandr Lukashenko, the Belarusian dictator.
Putin publicly called the mutiny treason, then appeared to forgive him. Two months later, on Aug. 23, 2023, Prigozhin’s private jet crashed north of Moscow, killing everyone aboard. The Kremlin denied involvement, the U.S. intelligence concluded that the plane had been blown up, and The Wall Street Journal later reported that the operation had been ordered by Putin’s Security Council chief. Putin’s eulogy, delivered the next day, described Prigozhin as a man who had “made serious mistakes in life.” No oligarch in Russia needed the rest of the sentence spelled out.
Prigozhin’s fate is only the most spectacular entry on a longer, murkier list. Since the invasion of Ukraine began in 2022, at least 85 Russian businessmen and officials have reportedly died in unexplained or violent circumstances, many of them figures in the energy industry. Among the dead are three Lukoil executives: board member Alexander Subbotin, who died in May 2022 after a visit to a “shaman” outside Moscow; chairman Ravil Maganov, who fell from a sixth-floor window that September; and vice president Vitaly Robertus, who was found dead in his office in March 2024.
In April 2022, two former energy and banking executives were found dead alongside their families. Vladislav Avayev, a former Gazprombank vice president, was found shot dead in his Moscow apartment with his wife and 13-year-old daughter. Sergei Protosenya, a former Novatek executive, was found hanged at a rented villa in Lloret de Mar, Spain, with his wife and daughter stabbed to death inside. Catalan police concluded that Protosenya had killed his family, then himself. His son rejected that finding, insisting that his father had been in good spirits and had no reasons to kill them and himself.
Transneft vice president Andrei Badalov fell from a 17th-floor window in July 2025. The Moscow Times has counted 18 such fatal falls from windows since 2002. Three days later, Russia’s transport minister, Roman Starovoit, was found shot dead in his car hours after Putin fired him. Another transport official died of supposedly acute heart failure the same day.
A shadow over America
Putin’s Russia offers an extreme and grotesque example of the bargain. Yet some critics see an emerging American version, in a far less violent form. Snyder and Applebaum have warned that Western billionaires risk repeating the mistakes of Russia’s oligarchs under Boris Yeltsin, believing they can manage a strongman for profit, only to discover that he is managing them.
Musk spent more than $277 million to help elect Donald Trump, took a desk in the West Wing, and ran the Department of Government Efficiency like a man who believed he was co-president. When that arrangement flamed out in May 2025, he tried to exercise independent political power by turning against Trump, calling his signature legislation, the Big Beautiful Bill, a “disgusting abomination.” Musk threatened to form a third political party and then briefly launched one. He even taunted Trump about Jeffrey Epstein, posting that the president “is in the Epstein files.”
After Trump publicly mused about terminating his contracts, Musk quickly retreated. He deleted the posts, and conceded that they “went too far.” He returned to the fold, shook Trump’s hand at Charlie Kirk’s memorial, accepted the National Medal of Science from him this month, and became the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterms, giving at least $366 million to Republican groups. He has grown vastly richer in the process: SpaceX’s June IPO made him the world’s first trillionaire, while the company remains the U.S. government’s dominant launch provider, with competitors such as Blue Origin winning only a fraction of the contracts.
Musk’s retreat illustrates the bargain: surrender the freedom to oppose the president and preserve the ability to enrich yourself. By that measure, Musk’s political defeat has come with an extraordinary financial windfall. He won by losing. The throttling of Starlink in Ukraine appears to fit this pattern. Last week, after Trump demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian refineries and Kyiv did not comply, its access to a military-grade version of Starlink was restricted and responsibility disappeared into a haze of accusation and denial.
The costs of such Faustian bargains fall on everyone excluded from them. In Russia, soldiers die at the front by the hundreds of thousands while politically compliant billionaires accumulate obscene fortunes. In Ukraine, drone operators lost contact with their interceptors in mid-flight last week while Russian missiles were in the air; the consequences of a disrupted connection are immediate and potentially fatal. Other customers face the question: can a contract with Starlink be relied upon?
In America, democratic government rests on the principle that neither political office nor private places anyone above the law. Businesses must be free to challenge a president without fearing retaliation, and their owners must remain accountable for their conduct. Those protections help distinguish America from an authoritarian dictatorship like Putin’s Russia.
The Starlink saga does not suggest that America has become Russia. But it raises a troubling question: is political obedience becoming the price of commercial success in America? Putin’s oligarchs struck that bargain in 2000 and have been collecting on it ever since. Whether Americans accept a version of it will depend on how forcefully our institutions and business leaders defend our freedom to say no.

articles.title: Drones reportedly hit a Russian weapons plant near Moscow that Washington and Kyiv sanctioned
articles.body:
An explosion hit the 75th Arsenal, a Russian army plant in Serpukhov south of Moscow, overnight on 22 October, Russian Telegram channel Astra reported. Russian officials also claimed drone attacks on the Moscow region, Tula, and Lipetsk that night.
As Russia presses its full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s long-range drones and missiles keep hitting military plants and refineries deep inside Russia. Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi says this plant specializes in repairing Buk and S-300 air defense systems. Astra describes it more broadly, as making weapons and ammunition and repairing military equipment. If Militarnyi is right, the blast hit a site that fixes Russian air defenses. It came the night Moscow’s mayor credited air defenses with stopping hundreds of drones.
Blast at the arsenal
An Astra OSINT analyst placed the explosion inside the site from a video, the channel said. Residents claimed in local chats that blasts followed passing drones, then at least three missiles. Astra did not confirm the missile count. Serpukhov lies about 99 km south of Moscow. Ukraine has sanctioned the plant, and the US Treasury has listed it too. As of the morning of 22 October, no Russian official had confirmed the blast.
630 drones, by Moscow’s count
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed that 630 drones flew toward the Moscow region from 20:30 on 21 October to 04:00 on 22 October. He claimed most were destroyed far out and 163 were neutralized on approach to Moscow. Two people were injured in Voronovo, in New Moscow, he stated.
Tula Oblast Governor Dmitry Milyaev claimed air defenses downed 70 Ukrainian drones over his region. Private homes were damaged in Tula and the Zaoksky district, he stated.
Lipetsk governor claims homes and a clinic damaged
Earlier in the night, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ posted footage of commotion in Lipetsk after explosions. Lipetsk Oblast Governor Igor Artamonov claimed a drone strike damaged homes, apartment blocks, and a closed polyclinic. A man born in 2001 was injured and hospitalized, Artamonov claimed.
In May, Ukrainian intelligence said Russia was deploying more regiments against strike drones. In September, Ukrainian units hit more Russian air defense systems and radars than in any month since 2024, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said. Analyst Oleksandr Kovalenko counted 76 destroyed in September with days of the month still to go and argued Russia cannot replace such losses. If Militarnyi’s description holds, losing repair capacity would deepen that gap.
Read also

- Ukraine destroys record 76 Russian air-defense systems this month, losses analyst says Russia “will never be able to restore”
- Russia reportedly rushes four regiments and 162 batteries to defend Moscow from Ukrainian drones

articles.title: U.S., Russia, and Ukraine discuss resuming trilateral peace talks in November as missile and drone strikes continue
articles.body:
Three-way talks between the United States, Russia, and Ukraine could resume in November. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed this, following statements from the Kremlin that it was ready for such talks.
“We’ve received feedback that Russia supports a three-way meeting between our teams. The American side is proposing that we hold it as soon as possible. We support that,” he said late on October 21.
Zelensky gave no specific dates for the possible meetings, saying only that the United States was “doing everything possible” to arrange them sooner. “I think no later than early November,” he said.
Zelensky said that, alongside ending the war and bringing peace closer, the negotiators’ main task would be to prepare for a meeting between the leaders. He said Kyiv would support any ceasefire — full or partial — at the talks.
Yesterday afternoon, after U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said talks could begin in mid-November. Russia, he said, was ready to resume negotiations “on the main issue,” which “concerns establishing a security framework for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends.” Ushakov said the talks could begin in mid-November, immediately after the U.S. congressional midterm elections.
Ushakov said, however, that the “new approaches” Witkoff presented to Putin, which had been announced ahead of the meeting, contained “not all that much that was useful for resolving the Ukrainian crisis.” But when later asked whether the war was nearing an end, he suggested that “things are heading that way.”
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said today that the talks could take place in Abu Dhabi. Asked whether Russia would prepare any documents for signing at the meeting, Peskov said: “You’re getting ahead of yourself. Don’t do that.”
Witkoff flew from St. Petersburg to Oslo, where he briefed allies on his conversation with Putin. He then wrote on social media that three-way talks would “continue at the technical level.”
Commenting on Witkoff’s visits to Oslo and St. Petersburg, U.S. President Donald Trump said he believed an end to the war was now “perhaps closer than ever.” He said he had spoken to Putin about it himself “the other day.”
Despite both sides’ statements that they were willing to negotiate, they continued exchanging strikes overnight. Russia attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles, killing one person and injuring more than 20 in Kyiv. Zelensky said the attack showed there had been no “real changes in [Russia’s] attitude toward everything that is happening.”
Ukraine, in turn, launched drone strikes on several Russian regions, including Moscow and the surrounding Moscow region. Two people were injured in the Novaya Moskva district.

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. articles.title: Russia, Ukraine exchange overnight strikes, one killed in Kiev
articles.body:
Russia and Ukraine reported overnight drone and missile attacks on Thursday, with Ukrainian authorities saying one person was killed and 22 were injured in Kiev, while Moscow said air defences had intercepted 630 drones approaching the Russian capital.
Russian forces launched ballistic missile strikes on six districts of Kiev overnight, causing fires and destruction, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said in a statement.
"Kiev: one person was killed and 22 injured, including four children, as a result of Russian shelling," it said.
Meanwhile, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said the Russian capital and the surrounding region were also under attack overnight, with 630 drones having flown towards the Moscow region.
Most of the drones were intercepted by air defences at long range, while 163 were destroyed on approach to Moscow, Sobyanin added.
In a separate statement, the Russian defence ministry said its forces had carried out a large-scale overnight strike using precision-guided ground-launched weapons and unmanned aerial vehicles.
According to the ministry, the strikes targeted Ukrainian military-industrial enterprises involved in the production and storage of cruise missiles and medium- and long-range drones, as well as transport infrastructure in Kiev and port infrastructure in the Odessa region.
The ministry also said vessels used in the interests of the Ukrainian armed forces had been targeted.
The claims by both sides could not been independently verified.

articles.title: Danish military orders long-range missiles, drawing Russian ire
articles.body:
Denmark buys long-range US, Norwegian missiles, drawing Russian ire
- Denmark bought long-range missiles from US and Norwegian firms to deter Russia. Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus said the aim is to strengthen Denmark and NATO deterrence.
- The deal includes Norwegian strike missiles for F-35 jets and US Anthem missiles for land use. Bruus gave no number, cost, or delivery date.
- Moscow condemned the move and warned of “inevitable disastrous consequences”. Denmark also signed a US deal to boost maritime cooperation and shipbuilding.
AI generated
COPENHAGEN - Denmark said on Oct 22 it had bought long-range missiles from US and Norwegian manufacturers, after announcing a year earlier it would acquire such weapons to deter Russia.
The move drew condemnation from Moscow.
“We have bought two different missile systems: Norwegian strike missiles from Kongsberg, which can in particular be launched from our F-35 fighter jets, and Anthem missiles from the American company Covenant, which can be fired from land,” Danish Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus told a press conference.
Bruus did not specify the number of missiles or the costs, nor when deliveries would begin.
In September 2025, Copenhagen announced it was planning on acquiring long-range missiles capable of reaching targets inside Russia, stressing that the threat from Russia would weigh on Europe for a long time to come.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen at the time called it “a paradigm shift in Danish defence policy”.
“We are facing a security situation where no one can predict what will happen tomorrow,” Bruus told reporters on Oct 22.
The minister stressed that this situation required Denmark to possess new military capabilities to strengthen both its own and NATO’s collective deterrent force.
Denmark announced it had also signed an agreement with the United States aimed at strengthening maritime cooperation, particularly in the area of shipbuilding.
The Russian embassy in Copenhagen, in a written statement, said Denmark’s missile policy aims at confrontation with Moscow and warned of “inevitable disastrous consequences”.
“Copenhagen is enthralled by the dangerous illusions that purchasing offensive high-precision long-range weapons to pose a military threat to a nuclear power will help strengthen Denmark’s security and defence,” the embassy said. AFP, REUTERS

articles.title: Committee questions whether attack submarines put to sea
articles.body:
Evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines raises serious questions about whether Britain can meet its High North commitments before new capabilities enter service, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, records reporting that all five of the Astute class nuclear attack submarines then in service had recently been tied up in dockyards at the same time, with none deployed.
Dhesi said: “The UK needs to be willing to address a hard truth: it does not currently have all the capabilities to operate successfully in the High North. Russian submarine and sabotage forces in the High North pose direct risks to the North Atlantic and the UK, including the nuclear deterrent. Despite this, the Ministry of Defence has accepted a serious anti-submarine warfare gap. Publicly available evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines calls into question whether the UK can meet its commitments in the High North.”
Professor David Blagden of the University of Exeter told the committee: “[i]t was reported in the media quite recently that a French SSN [attack submarine] had been seen in Faslane around the time that one of [our] SSBNs sailed on its patrol… [i]s this the French now doing ‘delousing’ for a UK nuclear deterrent submarine going on patrol? Is that great alliance solidarity or is it, ‘Oh my god, we can’t get one of our own SSNs to sea to do one of the highest missions?'”
Delousing is the activity in which an attack submarine sanitises the waters around a ballistic missile submarine to ensure it is not being tracked or tailed by an adversary as it leaves on or returns from a deterrent patrol.
The Rt Hon the Lord Case, chair of Team Barrow, told the committee in November 2025 that the government is saying to the defence industry “[p]lease, how quickly can you build our nuclear submarines for us? We are having to make up for decades of neglect.”
Retired Rear Admiral Philip Mathias, a former Director of Nuclear Policy at the Ministry of Defence, said in December 2025 that one consequence of a lack of investment in the submarine fleet was that the duration of patrols for Vanguard class crews, which were seventy days during the Cold War, were now more than two hundred days, and that there was a shockingly low availability of submarines to counter the Russian threat in the High North.
The committee’s conclusion states: “The Royal Marines’ Arctic expertise is a significant national strength, but it cannot compensate for shortfalls in the naval platforms needed to deploy, protect and sustain operations in the region. The UK’s ability to deter and respond to threats in the High North depends not only on future programmes, but also on the readiness of the Royal Navy’s existing ships, submarines and specialist forces. Russian submarine and seabed warfare capabilities based in the High North pose direct risks to the North Atlantic, UK waters and the nuclear deterrent. Evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines therefore raises serious questions about whether the UK can meet its High North commitments before new capabilities enter service.”
The committee asks the government to provide a plan setting out how the department will improve the availability of the Royal Navy’s frigates, destroyers and attack submarines before 2030, noting that the update might be presented at a classified level but that it expects a version to be made publicly available.
Ministers have consistently declined to disclose submarine availability, and Luke Pollard MP told Parliament this week that it is British policy not to disclose the operational availability or deployment details of submarines, as doing so would be likely to prejudice the capability, effectiveness or security of the armed forces.

articles.title: What Russians are told — and not told — about Ukrainian strikes
articles.body:
What Russians are told — and not told — about Ukrainian strikes
A woman rides on a bus as smoke rises from the area of Gazprom Neft’s Moscow oil refinery in Moscow, Russia, on Sept. 20, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
Andrii Sukharyna
Head of analytics at Join Ukraine
On the night of Sept. 12, Ukrainian drones attacked Taganrog. Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) reported hits on an FPV drone production facility, two drone storage sites, a Pantsir air defense system, and a radar.
Local authorities, as usual, listed something else: 16 commercial buildings, five cars, a football club, and a Svetofor store.
Regional social media channels summed it up in a single sentence about "drone debris" that set a store and several non-residential buildings on fire.
Under a post by a Rostov community on VKontakte, one commenter clarified: "One big-box store selling aircraft tires has been burning since 4 a.m. and is still burning."
They were referring to a military airfield where, judging by satellite imagery, fuel tanks caught fire.
Three days later, missiles struck the city.
Ukraine's General Staff reported explosions and a fire at the Atlant Aero plant, which manufactures Molniya strike drones. Russian authorities listed broken windows, a gas pipe, a grocery store, and an Ozon warehouse. The regional communities we monitor published 178 posts about the two strikes on Taganrog. Only one identified the target. Atlant Aero was not mentioned once.
The case of Taganrog offers a clear picture of how Russia's audience is structured. It is divided into segments, each seeing a different war.
Most people get their news from television and local online communities: television remains the main source of information for 61% of Russians.
Those interested in the war also read pro-war bloggers, known in Russia as Z-war bloggers. The smallest group reads independent media run by Russians abroad.
A month ago, using Novorossiysk as an example, we wrote that Russians do not see strikes on military targets. In September, we expanded our monitoring beyond 1,000 regional communities on Telegram and VKontakte to include more than 40 major nationwide channels, giving us a broader picture.
The first group gets the authorities' version.
On Sept. 9, the Ukrainian Navy said a Neptune missile had hit the Admiral Essen frigate in Novorossiysk.
Of 246 regional posts about that night, only one mentioned ships, while nearly 100 posts reported deaths: according to Russian authorities, four people were killed in the city.
Regional Russia knows about the civilian deaths, but not the frigate.
On Sept. 22, Ukraine's General Staff reported a strike on a base near the village of Tsymbulovo in Oryol Oblast, from which Russia launches jet-powered Geran drones.
Over the following month, the village's name did not appear in any of the thousand communities we monitored, including those in Oryol.
The shutdown of the Moscow oil refinery after a Sept. 20 strike, reported by Reuters, appeared in just six of 407 posts. The state-run channels in our sample, Solovyov and Komsomolskaya Pravda, simply repeated official statements in nine out of every 10 posts.
This feed creates the impression that air defenses shoot down hundreds of drones and debris falls on residential buildings.
Readers of Russian military bloggers know much more.
On Sept. 12, the Voyennyy Osvedomitel channel identified a military airfield as the likely target in Taganrog. On Sept. 18, it published a satellite image of damaged Atlant Aero workshops.
Overall, military bloggers identified the target in nine of 16 posts about Taganrog.
On the Moscow oil refinery, Z-blogger Fighterbomber wrote: "Let me remind you, this is the most heavily protected oil refinery in the country. Perhaps even in the world. I predict it will be attacked more than once."
But this knowledge is one-sided. The same channels report Russian strikes on Ukraine far more frequently and in greater detail.
Some 92% of reactions to such posts are positive. And Voyennyy Osvedomitel presented the strike on Tsymbulovo as a story of resilience: the shelters are sturdy, and the launchers are cheap to replace.
Independent media and those run from abroad provide the most comprehensive coverage of the strikes: they identified the target in 14 of 20 posts about Taganrog. Yet they have the smallest audiences.
In our sample, a typical military blogger's post about a strike on Russia receives 73,000 views, compared with 14,000 for a post by an independent media outlet.
Everything changes when a strike hits close to home.
The official account then clashes with what people heard during the night, and they start asking questions.
Under a post about Taganrog, people write: "Your Telegram channels say it wasn't just the store" and "When will they finally learn to tell the truth?"
In Oryol, a woman asked the governor about nighttime explosions during a live broadcast. She heard an explanation about a "piece of a drone" and recounted it in the comments: "Short and clear. Yes, that piece fell with such a bang that almost the whole city heard it."
The same community debunked a deepfake in which the governor supposedly admitted that the region lacked air defenses. The comments under the debunking post read: "This fake is telling the truth" and "I'd vote for the fake."
In Salekhard, the capital of the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, people reasoned this way after a gas plant in Novy Urengoy was hit: "How did it happen that the attack was repelled, the drone was turned into debris, and the facility it attacked is on fire? So the attack wasn't repelled, and this wasn't debris. It hit exactly what it was supposed to hit."
The numbers reflect this pattern, too. In communities based in the region that was hit, 34% of substantive comments question the effectiveness of defenses and the official figures. Another 23% describe what people saw and heard themselves or ask their neighbors about it.
They do not always find the right answers.
Novy Urengoy lies nearly 3,000 kilometers (about 1864 miles) from the Ukrainian border, and drones reached the city for the first time. The neighboring Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug banned the publication of anything about drones that same day.
The most popular comment about the strike in our databases reads: "It's been obvious for a long time that they aren't being launched from Ukraine."
Where the authorities stay silent, Russians find their own answers, and they are not always right.
Ordinary Russians in the regions know little about this war. They are told about downed drones and damaged buildings, and as long as the explosions are far away, that is enough.
Questions emerge when a strike hits their own city. In September, Yamalo-Nenets appeared on our map for the first time, and communities in 24 regions posted about the strike.
Questioning the authorities does not necessarily mean wanting the war to end. In the aftermath of the month's largest attack, the one on Moscow, 59% of substantive comments blamed the authorities and air defenses, while 16% blamed Ukraine and the West. Yet only one in 12 called for the war to end.
To sum up, here is what ordinary Russians were not told in the news in September: a strike drone factory and a military airfield in Taganrog; a frigate carrying Kalibr missiles in Novorossiysk; a launch base for jet-powered Geran drones; the shutdown of the capital's main oil refinery; and a gas plant in Yamalo-Nenets.
Russians in the regions continue to be shielded from learning by accident that the war is not going as victoriously as Putin claims. The results are rather underwhelming.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

articles.title: US lawmakers urge Trump to ask Musk to let Ukraine use Starlink to strike Russian ballistic missile launchers
articles.body:
US lawmakers urge Trump to ask Musk to let Ukraine use Starlink to strike Russian ballistic missile launchers
A bipartisan group of nearly two dozen members of the US House of Representatives has urged President Donald Trump to ask Elon Musk to give Ukraine access to Starlink systems to target missile launchers on Russian territory.
Source: a letter sent on Wednesday and obtained by The Hill, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The signatories are seven Republican members of the House of Representatives and 16 Democrats.
"We are writing to urge you to ask Elon Musk to let Ukraine use the Starlink satellite internet system to hunt for missile launchers inside Russia. With one phone call, you could both save lives and give Vladimir Putin greater incentives to negotiate," the lawmakers wrote.
"If Ukraine cannot reliably intercept Russian 'arrows', it must be able to shoot the 'archer'. The Starlink system run by Mr Musk's company SpaceX could help with that," they added.
The Republican signatories are staunch supporters of Ukraine: Joe Wilson, Brian Fitzpatrick and Don Bacon, as well as Carlos Gimenez, Jeff Hurd, Andy Harris and Max Miller, who represents a district with a sizeable Ukrainian population.
"Mr President, we all share the goal of bringing an end to the war in Ukraine and the devastating loss of life it has caused. Unfortunately, Putin presently has no intention of stopping the bloodshed," the lawmakers wrote.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has also called for greater US assistance in striking missile launchers on Russian territory.
The bipartisan letter comes as growing numbers of Republicans are expressing their outrage over disruptions to Starlink and its military version, Starshield, in Ukraine.
Background:
- The Wall Street Journal reported that Elon Musk had ordered Starlink services to be slowed down. It is unclear to what extent Trump was involved in discussions about the slowdown.
- US Republican Senator Thom Tillis is seeking an investigation into the Pentagon's actions with regard to problems with Starlink satellite communications systems encountered by the Ukrainian Armed Forces.

articles.title: Russia has intensified its attacks with cluster ballistic missiles and continues to destroy Ukraine’s energy infrastructure — Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Russia has intensified its attacks with cluster ballistic missiles and continues to destroy Ukraine’s energy infrastructure — Zelenskyy
Kyiv • UNN
At night, the Russians struck central Kyiv with cluster ballistic missiles, and during the day attacked Kharkiv, Dnipro and Kherson. Since October 11 more than 170 strikes on energy facilities have been recorded.
Overnight, the occupiers fired cluster ballistic missiles at central Kyiv, damaging residential buildings and structures near the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in his address, UNN reports.
Details
"This is a deliberate choice of weapon, a deliberate choice of the area of use, and a deliberate desire to inflict as many civilian casualties and as much damage as possible," the President stressed.
The shelling continued during the day: in Kharkiv, the Russians hit a city commuter train, while Dnipro, Kherson, and six other regions also came under fire.
Separately, the enemy is targeting electricity and heating — since October 11, more than 170 strikes on energy facilities have been recorded. According to intelligence, Moscow has already planned new attacks for the coming weeks, taking advantage of delays in the delivery of Western air defenses.
"Obviously, Russia is taking advantage of the slowdown in the delivery of air defenses from our partners. And it is equally obvious that easing pressure on Russia by certain partners only convinces Putin that his goals are supposedly achievable," Zelenskyy emphasized.
For this reason, the Ministry of Defense and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs were instructed to immediately provide the allies with intelligence data on new threats and demand that the delivery of already approved defense assistance be expedited.
