articles.title: U.S. Reportedly Considering Major Strikes on Iran After Midterms
articles.body:
The U.S. and Israel are reportedly developing plans for major strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections in November.
Citing people familiar with the deliberations, the New York Times reported on Wednesday that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussed the possibility of renewed strikes on Iran with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel this week. Possible targets of the strikes reportedly include Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
U.S. officials have repeatedly asserted that the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps are teetering on the edge of collapse but are deliberately prolonging the war in an effort to meddle with Republican prospects in the midterm elections. Once the elections are over, President Donald Trump promised last month, the Iranian regime would quickly capitulate.
“I think the war is going to end immediately after the election,” Trump said. “They can’t hold out any longer.”
Renewed strikes could complicate that outlook.
Some officials have reportedly argued that resuming attacks for an intense but limited campaign would hasten Iran’s economic collapse, especially as the country has been squeezed by an ongoing U.S. blockade on Iranian ports and economic sanctions campaign. The officials hope the blow will make Iran more amenable to negotiations.
Trump has at times shared that view.
Last week, Trump told Newsmax he was considering additional military action in Iran, including a possible strike on Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a nuclear facility deep underground. His comments came amid reports that he was weighing deploying a 22,000 GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, also known as the “mother of all bombs.”
The President added the war would end soon, be it through negotiation or escalation.
“Do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he said in a speech to the United Nations General Assembly last month.
“But I believe we’ll make a deal,” he added, “right after the election.”
Will the U.S. renew strikes on Iran?
Intensified fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthi rebels and the Saudi and Yemeni governments has threatened to create a broader regional crisis that could be harder to disengage from. The State Department on Wednesday ordered nonemergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia amid escalating attacks by the Houthis on Saudi infrastructure.
Houthi attacks on Saudi airports and Aramco facilities, as well as their attempts to disrupt shipping through Bab El-Mandeb, which has become an important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz for energy trade, could prompt direct U.S. strikes in support of Saudi Arabia, analysts have said. Trump said earlier this month that the U.S. “may” join Saudi strikes on the Houthis, although that has yet to transpire.
Israel’s Oct. 27 election could also raise the stakes of additional military action. Netanyahu, whom Trump has endorsed, would remain in office until a new government is formed, even if his bloc loses the election, and his government would retain the authority to order strikes during that transition. But renewed strikes before the election, or after an electoral defeat, could invite scrutiny. “One ordered in the last weeks of a deadlocked campaign would be judged in Israel as politics as well as strategy,” Gregg Roman, executive director of the Middle East Forum, wrote in a September analysis.
Nevertheless, the forum assessed that a large-scale Israeli strike on Iranian territory, with or without U.S. participation, was probable before the end of the year. Analysts told the Times Netanyahu could use the prospect of joint strikes to form a unity government that could allow him to stay in power.
“The larger constraint,” Roman argued, “is Washington.”
Trump has not yet approved the proposed strikes, the Times reported.
Trump has also called off plans to renew attacks on Iran before. He reportedly blocked an Israeli plan for a multi-day offensive against Iran earlier this month, and rejected five proposals for major operations against Iran or the Houthis in recent months.
The U.S. and Iran have not exchanged major fighting in recent weeks. The last reported U.S. strikes on Iran were on Sept. 8, even as Iranian attacks on commercial shipping have continued. Earlier this month, Trump ruled out attacking Iran before the midterms.
How might Iran respond to new strikes?
Tehran’s reluctance to make concessions to the U.S. appears to have strengthened, rather than weakened, over the course of the war. Iranian leaders reiterated this week that they will not directly negotiate with the U.S. unless Washington accedes to certain demands, which include ending its naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian funds.
The initial U.S. and Israeli bombing campaign on Iran that began the war on Feb. 28, as well as June 2025 attacks during an earlier round of U.S.-Iran nuclear diplomacy, also hardened the Iranian view that the U.S. is not serious about negotiating. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in March that the previous disruptions of negotiating rounds had increased distrust in Washington.
Last month, the IRGC published an open letter appealing to American voters to “wrest control” from their government. In the letter, the IRGC said: “Despite all the hardships that our enemies impose on us, we will continue fighting, as we have done for the past 47 years.”
Both the U.S. and Iran appear to believe they hold enough leverage to achieve their goals, and those “dueling perceptions” have impeded progress towards a deal, according to an Oct. 1 analysis by the New York-based nonpartisan research organization The Soufan Center.
Iran’s key point of leverage is its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway vital to global energy trade. Iran’s militarization of the strait has disrupted global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, leading to soaring energy prices and inflation.
Analysts previously told TIME that the higher prices are politically costly for Trump. In recent weeks, a growing number of Republicans have broken with Trump on Iran. The President has also seen his lowest approval ratings of his second term.
Iran’s ability to choke off regional oil exports, however, appears to be waning. Middle East oil exports topped prewar levels last week as shipping companies use alternative routes to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. HSBC Group Chief Executive Georges Elhedery also projected that Hormuz could be “redundant” in five years thanks to investment in alternative logistics routes.
Iranian officials told the Times that they are aware of the U.S. and Israel’s war planning and are developing their own tactics.
Earlier this week, IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi told the Tehran Times that “even a limited” attack from Washington would provoke a “serious energy crisis” for the world. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said that an attack on Pickaxe Mountain would be met with a response “just as hard,” if not “stronger.”
And earlier this month, Iranian officials said Iran had prepared potential retaliatory operations that would depart from the U.S. and Israel’s assumptions. Security Chief Mohsen Rezaei told Press TV that Iran could respond to renewed attacks by targeting new targets, including U.S.-linked data centers and AI facilities in the Gulf, as well as subsea communications cables. Last month, Iran threatened to retaliate against any further U.S. attacks by targeting U.S. oil and gas assets in the Gulf.
In a post on Telegram on Sunday, Mahdi Mohammadi, a senior adviser to Iran’s negotiator Gen. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said, if the U.S. and Israel attack, “they may want to keep it short, but we will not allow it.”
He added on Wednesday: “The war will continue longer and across a wider geography than the enemy calculates.”

articles.title: Yemeni army launches airstrikes on Houthi missile launchers, weapons depots in Taiz
articles.body:
Mohammed Sami, Ikram Kouachi and Sahin Demir
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The Yemeni army launched airstrikes on Houthi missile launchers and weapons depots in Taiz province in the country’s southwest on Thursday, according to state television.
Yemen Satellite Channel said the attacks hit several Houthi positions, including missile launchers, radars, military communications systems and weapons depots in the western, southern and eastern parts of Taiz.
Taiz has seen rising escalation since July amid fighting between government forces, backed by a Saudi-led coalition, and Houthi fighters.
Separately, Yemen’s Interior Ministry said Thursday that Houthi shelling caused extensive damage to a mosque and a school in Taiz province.
In a statement posted on US social media company X, the ministry said Houthi forces fired shells at a mosque and a school in Al-Najd village in the Mashra’a Wa Hadnan district, south of Taiz.
The ministry reported significant material damage but did not specify whether there were any casualties.
The official Saba news agency, citing a local source, said several shells struck the Omar al-Tayyar Mosque and School in the village.
Meanwhile, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed Thursday that the group had carried out four military operations targeting sites in Saudi Arabia with ballistic missiles and drones over the past 48 hours.
In a statement posted on US social media company X, Saree said the attacks targeted the Saudi Defense Ministry building in Riyadh, King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu and Abha International Airport.
He claimed that the strikes directly hit their targets, disrupted operations at Dammam airport and caused a fire at the Aramco facility in Yanbu.
Saree also claimed that Saudi forces had carried out more than 2,900 airstrikes and missile attacks over the past 100 days, killing or injuring more than 562 people.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several other provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.
The Houthis control much of northern and western Yemen, while government forces and their allies hold Aden and large parts of the country’s southern and eastern provinces.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Russia strikes area between Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra and monastery with ballistic missile carrying cluster warhead
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: Russia strikes area between Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra and monastery with ballistic missile carrying cluster warhead
On the night of 21-22 October, Russian forces used, among other weapons, three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads against Kyiv, one of which struck the historic centre of the Ukrainian capital.
Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter)
Details: Zelenskyy said he had received reports on dealing with the aftermath of Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities and districts.
According to the Ukrainian authorities, on the night of 21-22 October, the Russians used, among other weapons, three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads against Kyiv. These missiles detonate in the air as they approach their target, striking everything within a radius of 400 m.
One of the missiles struck Pechersk, Kyiv's historic centre, specifically the area between the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra and the Holy Presentation Monastery. Buildings belonging to the monastery, residential buildings, shops, cafés and other civilian infrastructure in the city were damaged.
Quote: "This is another extraordinarily revealing strike – revealing because it was no accident. The choice of weapon was deliberate, the choice of target area was deliberate, and so was the intent to inflict as much loss and damage on civilians as possible. There was no military target nearby, not even in theory, and the weapon was designed to cause widespread destruction. Russia has not changed the way it wages this war, and it is taking no steps that would signal a genuine desire to end it."
Background:
- Zelenskyy reported that shortly after they had a meeting with the US special representative and discussions regarding peace and negotiations, the Russians attacked Kyiv with 21 missiles, killing at least two people and injuring more than 30.
- Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian president and a radio technology expert, said that on the night of 21-22 October, Russia struck Kyiv with an Iskander missile equipped with a K5 cluster warhead, which is designed to inflict maximum casualties.

articles.title: What a Russian Satellite Stalking a Commercial Spacecraft Means for the Space Force
articles.body:
Over a two-week period beginning in late September and culminating in mid-October, a Russian satellite maneuvered dangerously close to a commercial Finnish satellite currently providing intelligence to the Ukrainian military.
The apparent provocation has experts wondering why Russia made the move—testing new capabilities, collecting intelligence, or trying to intimidate the Finnish company—and what, if anything, the U.S. Space Force could or should do about these types of events in the future.
While the incident did not involve a U.S. asset, the Russian action highlights the growing importance of commercial space assets to military operations and how those relatively defenseless assets could be vulnerable in or before a conflict.
Between Oct. 15-19, a Russian satellite dubbed COSMOS 2612 performed deliberate, fuel-intensive maneuvers to close in on the Finnish ICEYE-X36 satellite, according to a report by LeoLabs, which the company shared with Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Instead of a somewhat standard flyby, COSMOS matched, shadowed, and orbited around the ICEYE satellite, coming as close as 500 meters to it, according to the report.
The Russian satellite spent months adjusting its orbit, then rapidly closed the distance with the ICEYE satellite, continuously maneuvering around it before COSMOS abruptly ended its movements and distanced itself Oct. 18-19.
The LeoLabs report characterizes the event as a “red” on “blue” engagement in orbit and calls it a planned, highly coordinated rendezvous and proximity operation, which required precise navigation and onboard sensing.
An ICEYE spokesperson declined to provide a detailed response to a query from Air & Space Forces Magazine about the incident.
“We are aware of the situation and tracking it closely. Our constellation architecture is designed for continuity and resilience,” the spokesperson said in an email.
The Center for Strategic and International Studies held an online event Oct. 21 to discuss the incident and its implications for the U.S..
Neither of the two experts at the CSIS event claimed to understand Russia’s goals with the stunt, but Greg Gillinger, senior vice president of strategy and development at Integrity ISR, called it unusual and said it indicated Russia’s intent to send a message to the Finnish company.
“I still scratch my head about what the Russian endgame is with this,” Gillinger said.
Clayton Swope, deputy director of the CSIS Aerospace Security Project, said the event certainly was not “benign.”
“I don’t think we have enough information right now to know whether or not Russia achieved the objectives it wanted to achieve here,” Swope said.
The COSMOS/ICEYE incident comes about a month after Space Force leadership publicly announced that the force has on-orbit offensive space weapons at its disposal and under Guardians’ control.
“Today, we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenge of evolving threats wherever they exist,” Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink said during the opening keynote at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference on Sept. 14. “This is why the Space Force now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.”
The timing of the satellite maneuvers, following Meink’s comments, could be a Russian signal, threat, or influence campaign meant to deter outside, commercial support for Ukraine—or even a bluff, retired Air Force Col. Jennifer Reeves, the senior resident fellow for Space Studies at the Mitchell Institute, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
What USSF Can Do
In 2025, USSF’s Rapid Capabilities Office kicked off a project to field threat-awareness sensors that communicate close hazards to space asset operators. Such sensors would presumably alert operators if a Russian satellite came as close as it did to the ICEYE bird.
Beyond sensing and communicating, though, an April report from the Secure World Foundation noted that more nations are starting to fund “bodyguard” capabilities for their space assets, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported at the time. Germany, India, France, and Japan are all either building or planning to acquire such space-based bodyguards, which could protect and counterattack any space-based incursions.
Swope, speaking on the COSMOS/ICEYE incident, said spacefaring nations need clearer expectations for behavior in space, and predicted events like the recent incident would likely happen again.
“I just feel like it’s not a question of if; it is a question of when we see these satellites do something that we’re going to say is hostile again,” Swope said.
He also said any use of bodyguard satellites needed to include a clearer explanation of what they will accomplish in orbit.
Reeves likewise said the Space Force needs to be prepared to both understand and respond to future incidents like this one. While the service has been building its space domain awareness capabilities in recent years, that’s only one piece of the larger puzzle, she said.
“There’s a big difference between knowing where something is and understanding what it’s doing,” she said.
The force has made “tremendous progress” in tracking orbits and objects with a sophisticated sensor network and other tools, she said. But the Pentagon must put more “rigor” into protecting both military and commercial assets in space, Reeves said.
“The Space Force needs to be running through these scenarios on the regular, and hopefully they are,” Reeves said. “I’m going to trust that they are in their wargames and exercises.”
Those exercises need to include both allies and commercial partners, Reeves added.
“We’ve got to determine how quickly we can determine what happened,” she said. “Can we distinguish an accident from something deliberate? How confident are we in attribution?”
Both Reeves and Swope separately noted that any counterattacks or deterrence to space-based provocations don’t have to involve space-based retaliation or actions.
Reeves pointed to the U.S. ability to strike ground-based facilities to sever links to satellites. Swope noted increased pressure on Russia’s oil “shadow fleet,” a network of an estimated hundreds of old tankers used to export oil while evading sanctions, could be a lever to nudge Russia away from space tomfoolery.
Necessary Guidance
Ultimately, while the Space Force will be the entity dealing with satellite harassment or attacks, the force’s role needs clearer definitions on what constitutes aggression and merits a response, especially given the long-term consequences of space debris and other factors involved in kinetic actions in orbit, Reeves said.
“I don’t think it’s necessarily the Space Force itself that should be determining that,” Reeves said. “I think it should be our national leadership that’s coming up with that. … Because at this point in time, we don’t have that coming from the national-level leadership.”
That lack of guidance has placed the burden on military leadership to decide what the U.S. believes hostile actions in space look like and how the military should respond.
“We don’t want to be doing this thought work when we’re living it in real time,” Reeves said. “There are dire consequences in space if the wrong action is taken or a hostile action is taken.”

articles.title: IDF denies Trump halted Iran strike, warns of dangerous miscalculation: 'Attack was never on the table'
articles.body:
Senior IDF officials say U.S. President Donald Trump did not block an Israeli strike on Iran, contradicting reports that Washington had intervened to prevent a renewed military confrontation ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
"Trump did not stop us from attacking Iran because an attack was never on the table. There was an increase in alert levels and heightened military readiness, in line with American preparations," the officials said. According to them, there is no reason to strike Iran before the elections unless Israel detects preparations by Tehran to launch an attack.
However, alongside the military preparations, senior defense officials are concerned about statements coming from Israel's political leadership. At a time when the IDF is trying to maintain a high state of readiness without triggering an escalation, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz continue to speak publicly about the possibility of an attack.
On Wednesday, Netanyahu said Iran was "once again trying to develop its bombs of death," while Katz said Thursday that "Bennett, Lapid or Golan will be responsible for any terrorist attack or strike." The military is uncomfortable with such statements. Commanders have no control over the messages issued by political leaders, yet they will be responsible for managing any consequences on the ground.
Iran, meanwhile, is also listening. Public statements about a possible Israeli attack could prompt Tehran to raise its own alert level and prepare for retaliation. Israel could then interpret those Iranian preparations as a warning sign and respond by increasing its readiness further, creating a potentially dangerous cycle of action and reaction. In such circumstances, a misunderstanding of the other side's intentions could lead to an escalation that neither country necessarily intended. That is precisely the danger of miscalculation.
Preparations within the Israeli Air Force are continuing. According to published reports, dozens of fighter jets participated this week in a training mission simulating an attack on Iran, flying as far as the vicinity of the Iranian border.
Such exercises are part of routine operational preparations intended to maintain the Air Force's capabilities, assess enemy vulnerabilities, identify effective flight routes and preserve the element of surprise. While they demonstrate continued readiness, they do not, in themselves, indicate that a decision has been made to launch an attack before the elections.
Trump: Iran is 'fabricating fake attacks'
For now, Trump appears unwilling to launch an attack on the Islamic Republic, at least before the November 3 U.S. midterm elections. In a new social media post Thursday, the president did not threaten military action. Instead, he accused Iran of "fabricating fake attacks."
"Iran is doing everything it can to drive up oil prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections," Trump claimed. "They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more oil is now passing through the Strait of Hormuz than even before the conflict began."
Iranian state television claimed Thursday that seven oil tankers had been struck or hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz overnight. If confirmed, the incidents would apparently represent the largest number of vessels damaged in the strait in a single day since the war with Iran began on February 28.
Citing a statement from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' navy, the Iranian report said four tankers had come under attack and three others had struck naval mines. It also warned that the Revolutionary Guards could target U.S. military bases in the region if Washington attempted to facilitate tanker traffic through alternative routes in the strait.
Lloyd's List Intelligence, a company specializing in shipping data and analysis, said tanker operators willing to risk the passage have been transporting oil from Gulf states through the strait at night. The vessels reportedly use a route near Oman's coast protected by the U.S. military, with their tracking systems and mobile phones switched off. The oil is subsequently transferred to other tankers waiting in the Gulf of Oman before being shipped to customers in Asia.
Iran unveils what it calls a 'suicide drone production line'
Alongside its warning that American military bases could be targeted, Iran's state broadcaster released footage carrying another implied threat. The video purportedly showed what it described as the Iranian military's "suicide drone production line," unveiled for the first time. Iranian army commander Amir Hatami appeared in the footage, which authorities claimed featured the country's most advanced drone.
The developments follow a Financial Times report published Wednesday claiming that Trump had blocked an Israeli attack on Iran ordered by Netanyahu for the weekend of October 10, nearly two weeks ago.
According to the report, the IDF had prepared for several days of fighting against Iran, with planned targets including civilian infrastructure such as power stations, nuclear facilities and other sites associated with the Iranian regime. The operation, which Netanyahu had reportedly pushed for, was ultimately halted because Trump opposed a resumption of hostilities before the U.S. midterm elections. Netanyahu has denied the report, while senior IDF officials now say no such attack was planned. 
Meanwhile, the New York Times reported overnight that the U.S. and Israeli militaries have developed detailed plans to resume strikes on Iran after the American midterm elections, including a "short and intense" operation. According to assessments cited in the report, a three-day assault could inflict enough economic damage on Iran to push it back into negotiations.
Iranian officials, however, said they were aware of the American and Israeli military plans and were developing new targets and tactics of their own.
Among the potential targets threatened by Iran are data centers and undersea internet cables. Iranian officials have also warned that any renewed confrontation "will not be short."
Peyman Salehi, a political commentator in Tehran, said that if Iran were attacked, "some of its response plans would include striking major oil refineries in Saudi Arabia, including facilities belonging to the national oil company Aramco, because such a move would lead to an immediate and sharp increase in oil and energy prices."
"The war has made it clear to us that the best leverage against Trump is to drive up oil and energy prices, because that would hurt the American people," he added.

articles.title: Ukraine Destroys Elusive North Korean Koksan Supergun in Operation Vivaldi
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Destroys Elusive North Korean Koksan Supergun in Operation Vivaldi
Ukrainian drone operators from the 3rd Army Corps destroyed a North Korean-made Koksan self-propelled artillery system in the Donetsk region during Operation Vivaldi, according to footage released by Ukraine’s 60th Separate Mechanized Brigade on October 22.
The strike was carried out by operators from the brigade’s Fatum unit, which published a new compilation showing attacks on Russian equipment and personnel.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Hellish autumn notes of ‘Vivaldi.’ Operators of Fatum from the 60th Separate Mechanized Brigade burned a North Korean Koksan self-propelled gun, as well as several vehicles. In addition, quad bikes and buggies were destroyed, along with enemy infantry moving on them. The pilots of the Troika continue to erase the enemy,” the brigade said.
The Koksan is North Korea’s longest-range conventional tube-artillery system and one of the most unusual weapons Pyongyang has supplied to Russia. Western intelligence first identified the system in 1979 near the North Korean city of Koksan, which later gave the artillery piece its commonly used Western name.
The original M1978 Koksan can reportedly strike targets at ranges of up to roughly 40 kilometers with standard ammunition and as far as 60 kilometers with rocket-assisted shells. Its rate of fire is relatively slow at around one to two rounds every five minutes, but its long reach allows it to operate well behind the immediate front line.
The weapon’s gun is mounted in an open configuration, providing little protection for its estimated four-to-six-person crew.
The earlier model also requires a separate vehicle to carry ammunition because of the size of the weapon and its shells, while the later M1989 variant can carry around 12 rounds onboard.
The Koksan has combat history dating back decades. North Korea supplied the system to Iran, where it was used during the Iran-Iraq War and gained a reputation as an effective long-range counter-battery weapon.
Earlier, Ukrainian drone operators destroyed four North Korean–made M1989 Koksan self-propelled artillery systems deployed by Russian forces.
The mission was carried out by the 412th Nemesis Regiment, which used both bomber drones and FPV drones to strike the weapons.

articles.title: Russia kept sneaking troops through gas pipes behind Ukrainian lines. Now Ukraine has gone more than 15 km underground to do the same to Russia
articles.body:
Ukraine's Defense Forces advanced more than 15 km through underground utility tunnels into Russia's rear on the Kupiansk axis in Kharkiv Oblast, the Khartiia Corps of Ukraine's National Guard reported on 22 October. The corps called it Operation Veles. The underground advance was paired with attacks on the surface and drone strikes, hitting Russian forces from two directions, the corps told Militarnyi.
Russian troops have repeatedly crawled through gas pipelines around Kupiansk to get behind Ukrainian lines, even after Ukraine reported confident control of the city in February. This time, Ukraine went underground itself. The operation took away Russia's chance to get into Kupiansk's rear, the corps said.
The corps reported more than 30 Russian soldiers captured and Russian losses of more than 100. Militarnyi, citing the unit, put the number of Russian troops killed at over 100.
Khartiia studied how Russian troops moved through pipes before going underground itself, the corps commander, Brigadier General Ihor Obolenskyi, said.
"We watched how the enemy works underground and studied how they do it. The Russians intended to use gas pipelines to get into the rear of our troops. So we went underground ourselves. We anticipated the enemy's actions and mastered the tactics of underground combat," he said.
For the operation, troops trained physically and psychologically to fight in confined spaces, sappers and engineers prepared the underground route, and special communications, navigation, silent logistics, and life-support systems were put in place, Khartiia told Militarnyi. The operation was named after Veles, the Slavic pagan god of the underworld.
Khartiia's brigade, the R.U.H. assault regiment, the Lava drone regiment, the Achilles drone brigade, and units of Ukraine's military intelligence, including the Freedom of Russia Legion and the Russian Volunteer Corps, took part, the corps said.
Russia has used pipelines to infiltrate before
By September 2025, Russian forces had used pipelines to move troops behind Ukrainian lines three times, Ukrainian monitoring project DeepState reported on 12 September 2025. The first was in Avdiivka, the second near Sudzha, and the third near Kupiansk, where groups crossed the Oskil River through a gas pipe.
Near Sudzha in March 2025, Russian special forces walked through a pipeline that until recently had carried Russian gas to Europe, the Associated Press reported. A pro-Kremlin blogger claimed they covered about 15 km and that some spent several days inside.
Russian troops kept using the pipeline near Kupiansk this year. On 27 September, Khartiia's reconnaissance drones recorded Russian forces leading nine civilians, including children, elderly people, and a person on crutches, through the gas pipeline out of the Kupiansk community. Men of military age in civilian clothes walked alongside them, and the corps believes they were Russian soldiers using the group as cover to withdraw. Ukrainian troops held fire because of the civilians, the corps said, adding that the case has been documented for a war crimes investigation.
Why the war is moving underground
Drones, constant surveillance, and AI-assisted targeting have made the battlefield surface transparent and deadly, argue John Spencer, chair of urban warfare studies at West Point's Modern War Institute, and Col. Drew Craig, principal military engineering staff officer at NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. In an August analysis, they write that soldiers in Ukraine describe a "death zone" of some 30 km, where moving above ground can draw an attack within minutes. When firepower makes the surface too dangerous, armies have historically gone underground, as they did in World War I and Vietnam, and more recently in Gaza and Lebanon.
"Armies that cannot survive above ground must adapt below it," the authors write.
Fighting in tunnels brings its own requirements, the authors write: detecting the enemy by sound and vibration, and specialized unmanned systems that cannot rely on GPS or stable radio links. Long stretches underground also take a severe psychological and physical toll on soldiers.
Western militaries are not ready for this, Spencer and Craig write. No NATO partner maintains even general capabilities for large-scale underground warfare, and US and British efforts focused mainly on detecting and clearing tunnels rather than occupying and operating in them.

articles.title: U.S. Congress Urges Trump to Allow Ukraine to Use Starlink for Strikes on Russia
articles.body:
Twenty-three members of the U.S. House of Representatives have urged President Donald Trump to allow Ukraine to use the Starlink satellite network for military operations inside Russia.
According to The Hill, the lawmakers believe that such authorization would help Ukraine detect Russian missile launchers in a timely manner and strike them on Russian territory.
The initiative was led by Republican Joe Wilson. The letter was signed by 16 Democrats and seven Republicans, who urged Trump to personally contact SpaceX founder Elon Musk to secure the lifting of the relevant restrictions.
“We urge you to ask Elon Musk to allow Ukraine to use the Starlink satellite internet system to locate missile launchers on Russian territory. One phone call could save lives and increase Vladimir Putin’s incentives to negotiate,” the lawmakers wrote.
According to lawmakers, if Ukrainian forces cannot reliably intercept Russian missiles, they should be able to strike the launchers from which those missiles are fired.
The letter also noted that Ukraine had already approached Elon Musk with a request for an exemption from the restrictions preventing the use of Starlink for such operations inside Russia.
The lawmakers believe that Donald Trump could help secure the decision.
In July 2026, during closed-door talks at the White House, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reportedly asked the U.S. President Donald Trump to authorize the use of Starlink to guide long-range drones toward ballistic missile launchers on Russian territory.
In August 2026, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk held talks with former Ukrainian Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
According to reports, the talks proved ‘extremely unsuccessful,’ after which Musk reportedly became firmly inclined to deny Ukraine permission to use Starlink for such operations.
Following his departure from office on August 7, Fedorov said he was continuing negotiations with Musk but did not specify their subject or outcome.

articles.title: Pentagon extends Raytheon deal for missile defense radars
articles.body:
- The Missile Defense Agency extended Raytheon’s AN/TPY-2 radar sustainment contract by two years, raising its ceiling from $2.6 billion to nearly $3 billion.
- The ordering period now runs to Oct. 31, 2028, with $112.3 million obligated at award.
The Missile Defense Agency has extended Raytheon’s contract to operate and maintain the U.S. military’s AN/TPY-2 missile defense radars for two more years, adding $394 million to the deal and lifting its ceiling to nearly $3 billion, the Department of War announced.
The sole-source modification raises the maximum value of the contract from about $2.6 billion to $2.999 billion and keeps the ordering period open until Oct. 31, 2028, with $112.3 million in fiscal 2027 operations and maintenance, research and development, and procurement funds obligated at the time of award.
The AN/TPY-2 is a transportable X-band radar that sits at the heart of the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense system, better known as THAAD, and also serves as a standalone early warning sensor for U.S. ballistic missile defense. The radar can work in two ways: deployed far forward to spot ballistic missiles shortly after launch and pass tracking data to other defenses, or as part of a THAAD battery to track an incoming warhead and guide interceptors to hit it as it descends.
Under the extension, Raytheon will continue to run and support the radars from its facility in Woburn, Massachusetts, and at radar sites in the United States and overseas, where the company’s field teams help keep the sensors operating around the clock. The work combines cost-plus-incentive-fee, cost-plus-fixed-fee and firm-fixed-price contract items, and the Missile Defense Agency at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, is also extending the task orders that fund individual radar sites.
The U.S. Army fields eight THAAD batteries, each with one AN/TPY-2 radar, including units at Fort Bliss, Texas, in South Korea and on Guam, while forward-based radars have been stationed at sites including the Shariki area in Japan, Türkiye, Israel and Qatar. The radar is also sold abroad, and in 2020 the Missile Defense Agency awarded Raytheon a production contract worth up to $2.3 billion for seven AN/TPY-2 radars for Saudi Arabia, built with gallium nitride components that extend the radar’s range and sensitivity.
The radars have come under direct fire during the war with Iran this year, and satellite images analyzed by CNN showed that a THAAD radar at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan was apparently destroyed by an Iranian strike in early March, along with damage at radar sites near Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia and in the United Arab Emirates. Each AN/TPY-2 costs hundreds of millions of dollars and takes years to build, which makes keeping the existing fleet working a priority for the Missile Defense Agency while new radars are produced.
The original contract was awarded to Raytheon on a sole-source basis in 2018 as the radar’s designer and builder, and the extension was likewise issued without competition. The new ordering period gives the Missile Defense Agency two more years to keep the current support arrangement in place before it decides how to handle long-term sustainment of the AN/TPY-2 fleet beyond October 2028.

articles.title: One year of Ukrainian arms exports, and industry has questions: how much army gained, where Berlin office is, who joins joint ventures
articles.body:
Ukraine now builds far more weapons than it can afford to buy. A year ago, it promised to sell the surplus abroad and turn the proceeds back into its own army. However, 12 months later, that promise has barely materialized: a state fee of up to 30% is pricing Ukrainian arms out of foreign markets, and no one can say how much the army has actually gained, said Ihor Fedirko, executive director of the Ukrainian Council of Armorers.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the resumption of controlled weapons exports in October 2025, resting it on four promises: 1) sell what Ukraine makes beyond its own needs, 2) channel part of the proceeds into a special fund for the army, 3) open export offices in Europe and the US, and 4) establish joint ventures abroad.
The surplus is real: Ukraine's defense output is projected to reach $55 billion in 2026, far beyond what the state can finance. A year on, Fedirko checked each promise in turn.
1) Export of surpluses: rules that strangle businesses
On 1 July 2026, the government approved rules for controlled arms exports. They shortened the maximum application review period from 90 to 30 days, but also introduced an export fee: 20% for finished products and technologies, and 30% for components. For finished products exported under the special procedure, the contract value must be at least $334,000.
In September, the Ukrainian Council of Armorers, together with other associations, proposed a zero rate, no advance collection of the fee, refunds for deals that fall through, and simplified test shipments. The industry was promised that its amendments would be taken into account and that the resolution would be rewritten.
Even in early October, however, the rules still needed work. According to Fedirko, the new mechanism has effectively not started working. Whether it can bring in additional funds for defense depends on how acceptable the export terms are to manufacturers.
Fedirko says, though, that judging by current decisions, the state intends to keep the export fee.
“The industry is ready to discuss its contribution to defense financing. But the rate must be economically justified,” he says.
2) Procurement for the Ukrainian military: balance is only being established
He adds that the Ukrainian Council of Armorers intends to push for a rate significantly lower than 20%, one that would let companies fulfill contracts and invest in production.
With such high rates, Fedirko says, the competitiveness of Ukrainian weapons on foreign markets is in question, as is the ability to send even small test batches to potential buyers.
“The fundamental requirement is post-payment: after the contract has actually been fulfilled and the manufacturer has been paid. A company should not pay the state in advance a share of income it has not yet received,” he says.
Trending Now
He added that, given all this, the real export figures remain unclear, as does how much exports have actually brought the military.
“The military and manufacturers must feel the benefit of exports. I sincerely hope that next year will bring much better results,” he says.
In addition, on 12 October, the Ukrainian Parliament passed bill No. 15400 in the first reading. It provides for crediting the export fee to a special fund directed to the Ministry of Defense: 50% for the procurement, modernization, and repair of weapons and equipment, and 50% for the pay of Armed Forces personnel.
The bill has not yet been adopted, but Fedirko says he expects “final adoption and launch of the mechanism.”
3) Export offices: offices in Germany and Denmark
On 3 November, the Ukrainian government named the first cities for export offices: Berlin and Copenhagen. On 15 December, it again spoke of preparing an office in Berlin. In reality, Fedirko says he does not know the office’s status, and it likewise remains unclear how companies can apply to it and how many contracts it has helped close.
4) Joint ventures abroad: There are concrete results in this area
According to Fedirko, eight joint ventures have been created, five of which are already supplying products to Ukraine. He stresses that this is the result of work by Ukrainian companies, foreign partners and the state, and that it deserves recognition.
As early as February 2026, the authorities spoke of plans to create ten joint ventures in Europe within a year. At the same time, they announced Quantum Frontline Industries in Germany, with a planned annual capacity of 10,000 drones for Kyiv.
Beyond the number of ventures and deliveries, however, it is important to understand how other manufacturers can join the Build with Ukraine program.
“Who accepts applications, by what criteria are decisions made, and what support does a company receive?” Fedirko asks.
In other words, joint ventures are already delivering results, but the rules of participation and the state support mechanism must be clear to companies that want to develop production abroad.

articles.title: A communications edge helped Ukraine win Operation Vivaldi. US throttling of Starlink is now wearing it down
articles.body:
- Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi may have begun as early as March
- The counteroffensive seemingly inflicted more damage on a pair of Russian field armies than previously thought
- But the gains could be fleeting if a new speed cap on Ukraine's military Starlink terminals stays in place
The Ukrainian 3rd Army Corps' Operation Vivaldi—its secretive counteroffensive east of Sloviansk in northern Donetsk Oblast—started earlier than first reported, and by the time it ended on 14 October it had cost the Russians more than 8,000 troops, by the 3rd Army Corps' count.
It was a major Ukrainian victory in one of the most important sectors of Russia's 56-month wider war on Ukraine. But it could prove to be a temporary win, one the Russians may be able to partially reverse, if the administration of US President Donald Trump continues to throttle Starshield, the military version of Starlink that Ukraine's drones and commanders rely on.
The Ukrainians' former command and control advantage, largely attributable to once-reliable Starlink and Starshield access, was pivotal as Operation Vivaldi played out in the Donbas region in stages starting in March. That advantage shrank practically overnight on 14 October, when a new speed cap began cutting off Ukraine's Starshield terminals whenever they moved faster than about 160 km/h (100 mph).
The 3rd Army Corps attacked east of Sloviansk and north of Lyman as early as March, analyst and mapper Clément Molin concluded after scrutinizing official videos and interviews the Ukrainian defense ministry recently released. "The operation began much earlier than initially thought," Molin wrote.
The timing was probably no accident.
In early February, SpaceX, working from a Ukrainian defense ministry whitelist, switched off the thousands of stolen and smuggled Starlink terminals the Russians had been using.
That had the effect of grounding many Russian drones and blinding many Russian commanders. Taking advantage of the Russians' confusion, Ukrainian troops attacked in several key sectors: in Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk Oblasts in the southeast, and east of Sloviansk in northern Donetsk.
The Donetsk attack expanded into a full-blown counteroffensive under conditions of strict secrecy as the 3rd Army Corps probed for weaknesses along the flanks of the Russian 20th and 25th Combined Arms Armies, then overextended along the axis between the Zherebets River in the east and the outskirts of the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk urban conglomeration in the west.
The Russians had been threatening to lay siege to Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, the last two big free cities in Donetsk Oblast, from two directions: the north and the south. Operation Vivaldi eliminated the northern threat—and at great cost to the Russian 20th and 25th CAAs.
Drones lead
Aerial drones and unmanned ground vehicles led the attack, taking the Russians by surprise. "For an offensive operation, the Ukrainians sustained relatively few casualties compared to previous engagements," Molin explained. "Conversely, the defending Russian forces suffered significantly higher losses, largely due to the rapid encirclement of at least three regiments, not all of which managed to escape the area."
It's unclear how many casualties the Russians suffered, but they might number in the thousands. The 20th and 25th CAAs were particularly fragile because the 3rd Army Corps and supporting drone units had been bombarding their supply line with so-called "middle strike" drones.
Trending Now
But many middle strike drones rely on civilian-style Starlink satellite terminals or the more rugged, better-performing Starshield. Now that the 3rd Army Corps has wrecked Russia's 144th Motor Rifle Division, which the Institute for the Study of War assessed on 20 October has effectively ceased to exist as an organized fighting force, and pushed the Russian survivors back to the far bank of the Zherebets River, the Ukrainians are probably "consolidating their gains and adopting a defensive posture," according to Molin.
But that defensive posture, protecting Sloviansk from a northern attack, depends on reliable communications and responsive drones. On 14 October, a new speed cap hit Ukraine's Starshield terminals, cutting the link on any drone flying faster than about 160 km/h. Who ordered it is disputed. Sources told Reuters the order came from inside the White House, and that Pentagon leaders were told the service needed to be slowed.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk himself ordered the slowdown, and that he and Trump discussed it soon after it became public. While Trump has denied ordering the speed limit, it's worth noting that the American president has become more overtly friendly toward Russia as his Republican Party looks likely to lose control of the US Congress in the November mid-term elections.
The speed limit renders many of the faster middle-strike drones unflyable. As a result, "Ukrainian drone strikes have diminished significantly following yesterday's crippling of Ukraine's Starlink/Starshield connections, Russian sources report," the military history account ChrisO_wiki wrote on X on 15 October, the day after the speed limit took Ukrainian operators by surprise.
Russia is back at Dobropillia a year after it failed there. Now it’s the southern jaw of a pincer on Donbas’s last big free cities
A reduction in middle strikes on Russian supply lines could help Russian field armies recover from recent setbacks, including their retreat back across the Zherebets River. And if the communications confusion resulting from the partial loss of Starlink/Starshield connectivity persists, it could give the Russians the same kind of opportunity the Ukrainians had back in the spring.
An opportunity to go back on the attack—and an Azov communications engineer warned Euromaidan Press in February that the shoe might be on the other foot.
That's the worst-case scenario for the Ukrainians now that Operation Vivaldi has ended. The best case is that they get full Starlink and Starshield access back—or find command and control alternatives—and duplicate, in other sectors, the same success they enjoyed in northern Donetsk.
"Now that the northern flank of Donbas is secured, at least for some time, the focus will concentrate on the southern flank," Molin predicted.
Starlink crackdown cripples Russians—but American engineer warns Ukraine is just as vulnerable

articles.title: Trump Could Force Putin to Negotiate but Hasn’t, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has the leverage to bring Russian President Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table but has yet to use it, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
“Trump could very easily bring Putin to the negotiating table, because he has the means to do so. The way he speaks about me – President Trump should speak about Putin in the same way,” Zelensky said in an interview on The Diary of a CEO podcast.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Zelensky pointed to sanctions approved by the US Congress as one tool Trump could use to pressure the Kremlin.
“Sanctions are sitting on his desk. He didn’t vote for them – Congress voted for strong sanctions. He has the power to act,” Zelensky said.
Asked why Trump had not taken such action, Zelensky said he could only speculate about the reasons, including the relationship between Kremlin and US administration leaders and possible economic interests. He said:
“I don’t know why. Perhaps they have a special relationship. Perhaps it’s something else. I can’t say for sure; I don’t know everything. I can only speculate – perhaps there are some economic deals, or something of that nature.”
Zelensky disputes link between Russia and US fuel prices
The podcast host suggested that Trump might be more concerned about domestic energy prices ahead of the US midterm elections than about Ukraine.
Zelensky rejected the idea that American fuel prices depend on how much Russian energy is sold, arguing that the US exports its own energy resources. The president explained:
Russia’s New Filin Missile Uses US, Chinese Electronics
“I can tell you with 100% certainty that diesel prices do not depend on the volumes Russia sells. They don’t. The Americans export energy resources. There is no ban on American energy exports; it is American companies that are doing the exporting.”
Zelensky added that he saw little reason for Trump to restrict private companies’ energy exports when those businesses were making money from them.
“And why would he do that, when ‘it sells, and the money keeps coming in?’” Zelensky said.
He also expressed confidence that the truth about the war and the decisions surrounding it would eventually emerge. Zelensky said:
“All secrets, all mysteries eventually come to light. It just takes time. Time is definitely on the side of those who are open and ready for an honest dialogue and a struggle. This means that time will be on our side.”
Zelensky says Putin chose when to launch full-scale invasion
The host also asked Zelensky about Trump’s repeated claims that Russia would not have launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine had Trump been president at the time. Zelensky replied:
“To be honest, no one knows the answer. The fact remains: this happened during Biden’s presidency. That is a fact. It is also a fact that it did not happen under Trump. But it is equally a fact that it was Putin who chose the moment for a full-scale occupation.”
He acknowledged that Trump’s relationship with Putin might have influenced the Russian leader’s decision-making, but argued that personal ties between presidents would not resolve the underlying threat to Ukraine.
Zelensky said Putin would continue pursuing his goal of occupying Ukraine regardless of who held the US presidency:
“Neither I nor Trump will hold the presidency forever. Sooner or later, Trump’s presidency would have come to an end, and Putin still would not have abandoned his primary objective – the occupation of Ukraine.
“Therefore, frankly speaking, it does not matter who exactly is president, as long as Putin remains in power.”
Zelensky warns territorial concessions could expose more of Ukraine
Zelensky warned that surrendering Sloviansk and Kramatorsk in the Donetsk region could open the way for further Russian advances toward Dnipropetrovsk region, including Pavlohrad and Dnipro.
He described the area as a key industrial and machine-building hub that supports Ukraine’s economy and said its defenses had been heavily fortified. Zelensky said:
“If we surrender these cities of ours to them, the risk is enormous. If he decides to push further, he could capture a vast number of our cities. The risk is real. There are no guarantees.”
He also questioned what security guarantees could mean if Ukraine were required to withdraw from additional territory to meet Russia’s demands.
“While everyone is talking about security guarantees and we are open to such talks – the Russians, for their part, want us to withdraw even further,” he said. “If we withdraw, where are the security guarantees? Not to mention the fact that it would be unjust.”
Zelensky estimated that Russia currently controls approximately 18-19% of Ukrainian territory. He also said Moscow presents different maps to its domestic audience and continues to pursue territorial objectives beyond the areas it currently occupies.
According to Zelensky, Russia wants to capture the city of Zaporizhzhia but has been unable to do so. He added that Zaporizhzhia and Mykolaiv remain Russian targets, even if Moscow does not explicitly acknowledge those ambitions.
He also pointed to the situation in Kherson, where the Dnipro River divides the city, with Ukrainian-held territory on one bank and Russian forces on the other. The positions allow Russian troops to shell the city, he said.
Zelensky calls ceasefire Ukraine’s biggest compromise
Zelensky said Trump had repeatedly urged both sides to seek a compromise, but argued that Ukraine was already making a significant concession by agreeing to stop fighting along the current front line.
“The biggest compromise we are already making is a ceasefire. Let’s just stop this war,” he said.
Zelensky added that he had repeatedly urged Trump to understand the scale of the concession Ukraine was prepared to make by agreeing to halt the fighting without first resolving every territorial issue. Zelensky stated:
“I have tried to tell the US President many times: just understand us. It is a huge compromise – simply holding the lines where they are right now.”

articles.title: Khmara, Swedish defence minister discuss accelerating missile deliveries for IRIS-T, need for MANPADS, ammunition
articles.body:
Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara discussed with Swedish Defense Minister Pål Jonson the acceleration of missile deliveries for the IRIS-T air defense systems, as well as Ukraine's need for man-portable air-defense systems (MANPADS) and ammunition for them, the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense's press service has said on Thursday.
According to the ministry, during the conversation, Khmara briefed his Swedish counterpart on the consequences of the overnight Russian strike and Ukraine's critical needs for defending its airspace.
"It is now crucial to strengthen our response to ballistic threats as quickly as possible. This includes, in particular, interceptors for the Patriot system. Ukraine is ready to work with partners on various supply mechanisms. Every delivery of interceptors and every opportunity to protect people, civilian infrastructure, and critical infrastructure is important to us," the defense minister said.
He also said Ukraine has contracted quantities of missiles for the Patriot system but is asking partners to transfer interceptors from existing stockpiles in exchange for future deliveries intended for Ukraine.
Separately, the parties discussed the need for further deliveries of Swedish man-portable air-defense systems (MANPADS) and ammunition for them.
Another topic of discussion was the Gripen fighter jets. Ukraine and Sweden are proceeding according to the plan for crew training. According to Khmara, the delivery of these aircraft, along with their armaments, will strengthen the Ukrainian Air Force and its ability to counter Russian guided bombs targeting frontline cities.

articles.body:
Why Russia wants peace between Iran and the Gulf
On October 18, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov visited Manama, where he attended the ninth ministerial meeting of the Russia-Gulf Cooperation Council strategic dialogue and held separate talks with the foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia and Kuwait. The following day, he traveled to Tehran to meet with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and President Masoud Pezeshkian.
In Manama, discussions centered on de-escalation in the Persian Gulf, maritime security, and Russian proposals for a collective security framework, while bilateral meetings provided an opportunity to clarify individual countries’ positions. Lavrov and his Kuwaiti counterpart stressed the need to reduce tensions quickly and agreed that a political and diplomatic settlement is the only viable way forward. In Tehran, regional affairs featured alongside Russian-Iranian cooperation, with Moscow reaffirming its commitment to economic and investment agreements despite the deteriorating security environment.
Diplomacy between the Gulf’s two shores
The trip aimed to prevent a new divide between Iran and the Arab monarchies from becoming entrenched, as the consequences of the US-Israeli aggression against Iran are affecting the security of the entire region. Yet rebuilding trust also requires acknowledging that the Gulf states have their own grievances against Tehran over strikes on their territory and threats to maritime routes.
During the Manama talks, Arab representatives explicitly said they hope Moscow would use its relationship with Iran to convey their concerns. Discussions also covered Yemen, maintaining the ceasefire in Gaza, humanitarian access, and the resilience of energy and food supply chains – the various and interconnected sources of instability plaguing the Middle East.
In Tehran, Lavrov reaffirmed Moscow’s support for restoring security and shipping conditions to what they were before the US-Israeli military operation began. Iran, which sees the attack as the primary cause of the current crisis, likewise stated its commitment to resolving disputes through diplomacy. Agreement on broad principles, however, does not yet amount to agreement on the specific obligations that the parties must accept.
Russia could mediate efforts to de-escalate tensions and mitigate the deterioration in relations between Tehran and the Gulf monarchies, since it maintains close ties with Iran while developing political, economic, and energy cooperation with the Arab states. These relationships allow Moscow to relay messages, identify the scope for compromise, and facilitate direct dialogue, which can easily give way to competing ultimatums during a crisis.
However, this two-way access does not mean Moscow can dictate what its partners actually decide, and its closeness to Tehran may raise questions among Arab participants. The effectiveness of Russian mediation will ultimately depend on whether the parties themselves are willing to negotiate, acknowledge one another’s concerns, and take practical steps to address them.
Inclusive security as an alternative to permanent crisis
In Manama, Lavrov once again presented Russia’s updated concept of collective security in the Persian Gulf as a potential contribution to a lasting settlement. The proposal continues a longstanding initiative rather than a document developed solely for this visit. As early as June, he reported that updated proposals had been circulated to regional capitals and that Moscow was receiving initial responses.
The approach rests on the premise that the Arab monarchies and Iran must take part in a shared framework, because attempts to secure one group of states by isolating another reproduce the causes of confrontation. Confidence-building measures and regular contact are intended to reduce uncertainty gradually, while the Gulf countries and their immediate neighbors should have the decisive voice in shaping the regional order.
An earlier Russian concept circulated at the United Nations in 2019 already envisaged a gradual normalization of conditions, respect for sovereignty, the peaceful settlement of disputes, and the development of collective security mechanisms. The current proposals can be assumed to carry over the same spirit, even if specific provisions have changed or been updated.
Moscow has argued that the region needs an inclusive security system of its own, free from external military intervention and imposed political arrangements. This does not rule out international assistance, however, as Russian diplomacy allows for support from outside actors, including members of the UN Security Council, provided that it serves the interests of regional states.
The practical value of this model will depend on whether broad principles can be translated into agreed procedures for preventing incidents, protecting civilian infrastructure, and keeping maritime routes open. These arrangements could provide the first steps towards a more stable order, whereas an attempt to resolve every political disagreement at once could obstruct even limited measures to ease tensions.
Why expensive oil does not make war good for Russia
Western media and expert debates, including those focused on Middle Eastern politics, frequently portray Russia as a beneficiary of the war, arguing that disruptions to Gulf supplies drive up energy prices and create opportunities for Russian exporters.
A short-term price benefit is certainly possible, but to assume that war gives Russia a strategic advantage is analytically unsound, because the country’s national interests are not limited to a single source of export revenue. Additional income from commodity sales says little about the cost of damaged partnerships, postponed investment, and worsening conditions for long-term projects.
The Middle East matters to Russia as a political and economic partner, and stable relations depend on predictable institutions, transport routes, and financial transactions. A prolonged war raises shipping and insurance costs, complicates infrastructure agreements, and forces partners to divert resources from development toward immediate security needs.
This is evident in Russia’s cooperation with Iran, where its projects require a stable operating environment. In Tehran, Lavrov spoke of Russian specialists gradually returning to the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant, as well as prospects for cooperation in hydrocarbon production and transportation. A protracted war creates additional risks for these activities, and higher oil prices cannot remove them.
Moreover, a sustained energy shock can weaken the global economy, while the resulting decline in demand limits exporters’ initial gains. Even if some consequences of a Middle East war can benefit Russian suppliers in the short term, claims that Moscow wants endless war in the region are superficial at best. Russia’s strategic interest lies in the region’s long-term stability, which would allow it to preserve partnerships, markets, and opportunities for economic engagement.
Regional autonomy in a changing world order
The transformation of the world order and the erosion of Western hegemony give Middle Eastern states greater scope to pursue independent policies, but a redistribution of international influence does not in itself resolve regional disputes. If dependence on external guarantees is merely supplemented by new competing patrons, while mechanisms for direct dialogue remain weak, the Middle East will continue to serve as an arena where local conflicts intersect with rivalry among major powers.
Regional autonomy requires that neighboring states agree on rules for coexistence, even when their foreign policy priorities and perceptions of threats differ substantially. A durable system will require mutual respect for sovereignty, a rejection of imposed military solutions, and recognition that lasting security cannot be built on another state’s permanent vulnerability.
Russia can support this process by providing diplomatic channels and helping identify a workable sequence of agreements, but only the countries of the region can build a peaceful future. External mediation delivers results when it supports an existing willingness to compromise, while even substantive initiatives can remain on paper if that willingness is absent.
Lavrov’s visits to Manama and Tehran highlighted an opportunity to connect urgent de-escalation with discussions about a more durable regional order. Seizing this opportunity will take time and difficult political decisions, because the parties will need to constrain their own use of force, rebuild damaged trust, and accept reciprocal obligations. Moscow can mediate this process, but its outcome will depend on the desire and readiness of the Gulf states and Iran to reach an agreement.

articles.title: US midterms: Where key candidates stand on Israel, Gaza and Iran
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US midterms: Where do candidates in key Senate races stand on Israel, Gaza, and Iran?
Washington, DC - The midterm elections in the United States are in full swing, with early voting starting in most states.
The results will set the tone of US foreign and domestic policy for the rest of President Donald Trump's term. Control of both chambers of Congress - the Senate and the House of Representatives - is at stake.
If the Democrats flip one of the two chambers, which are currently under the control of Trump's Republican Party, they can thwart Trump's legislative agenda.
And if they can gain control of the Senate, they can block his judicial nominees. The upper chamber is also responsible for confirming cabinet appointees, ratifying treaties and holding impeachment trials.
There are 35 seats in the 100-member chamber up for grabs in this year's election, which will conclude on 3 November.
The current makeup of the Senate is now 53-47, so the Democrats need to flip four seats without losing any to reclaim the majority in the legislative body.
In most Senate races, the results are all but known before the votes are cast due to the political makeup of the states where the contests are playing out.
Barring a miracle, Republicans will win in Alabama, and Democrats will win in Massachusetts. That leaves a handful of competitive states that will determine the fate of the Senate.
The New Arab looks at the candidates in five key close races and where they stand on the issues.
Michigan (open seat): Abdul El-Sayed (Democrat) v Mike Rogers (Republican)
The Senate contest in Michigan is one of the most closely watched races in the election. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive public health advocate, is taking on Mike Rogers, a Trump-backed former Congress member.
In recent weeks, Rogers and his allies have tried to focus the race on El-Sayed's Muslim identity, smearing him with baseless accusations of ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, Hezbollah, Hamas, and Iran.
Trump has repeatedly mocked El-Sayed's name. "His name is actually Abduladadalalala. It's Adulbabababababa Mohammed Al-Sayed," the US president said at a rally last week.
El-Sayed has pushed to refocus the race on the issues - particularly the affordability crisis, tariffs and the rise in the price of gasoline linked to the Iran war and his support for universal healthcare.
The progressive Democrat opposes US aid to Israel and argues that Washington should focus on investing in communities at home.
He has accused Israel of carrying out a genocide in Gaza - an allegation backed by leading human rights groups and United Nations investigators.
"I oppose the illegal and unjustifiable war in Iran and demand an immediate end to the hostilities," El-Sayed says on his platform.
Rogers initially supported the war with Iran, calling the decision to launch the conflict the "right thing to do".
But the former Republican legislator curbed his enthusiasm for the conflict as it dragged on and proved unpopular with voters. "The war with Iran needs to end, and end quickly," he said in a campaign ad in September.
Rogers is a staunch supporter of Israel. "When I get to the United States Senate, I will continue to unconditionally support Israel's right to defend itself," he said earlier this year.
Texas (open seat): James Talarico (Democrat) v Ken Paxton (Republican)
In a sign that highlights the declining popularity of Republicans, Democrats are mounting a competitive Senate challenge in deep-red Texas, which has been a Republican stronghold for decades.
Public opinion polls have shown Democratic State Representative James Talarico neck-and-neck with Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Talarico has focused his campaign on fighting corruption, closing tax loopholes and lowering the cost of living. Paxton has presented himself as a defender of Trump's agenda, emphasising securing the southern border against irregular migration.
On foreign policy, Talarico calls for conditioning US aid to Israel. He broadly backs Israel's right to "defend itself", while focusing his criticism of Israeli atrocities in Gaza and the West Bank on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"As a former teacher, seeing the death and the destruction in Gaza, seeing what’s happening to children in particular, makes me sick to my stomach," he said at a CNN townhall last week.
Talarico has stopped short of calling the atrocities a genocide, saying that the issue is a legal determination that should be made by international courts.
He has pledged to work to "end the forever war in Iran that’s driving up the cost of gas and groceries".
In contrast, Paxton has backed Trump's military action in Iran, but in a recently leaked audio recording he bemoaned the war's impact on gasoline and diesel prices.
"It's the war, it's gas prices, it's diesel," he said when asked about the issues dragging his campaign, according to Axios, which first reported on the leaked remarks.
Paxton is a strong supporter of Israel. As attorney general, he has defended and enforced laws to penalise companies and individuals that boycott Israel.
Maine: Susan Collins (Republican incumbent) v Troy Jackson (Democrat)
Maine generally leans Democratic in presidential elections, but Republican Susan Collins has won five consecutive elections in the northeastern state, earning her a reputation as one of the most tenacious politicians in the country.
This time, Democrats are hoping to use the mounting anger against Trump to finally topple the 73-year-old senator.
But the Democratic push was off to a terrible start after the party's nominee, Graham Platner, stepped down due to allegations of sexual misconduct.
Platner was replaced by former state Senate President Troy Jackson.
Collins, who has shown willingness to break with Trump, has promoted herself as an experienced and hardworking "common sense" leader.
Jackson has focused on his deep roots in the state as a former logger and supporter of workers' rights.
The Democrat agrees that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza. "When I'm in the US Senate, I’ll never vote in favour of US taxpayer-funded military aid to Israel," he wrote in a social media post in July.
Collins is an unflinching advocate for Israel and has backed continuing military aid to the US ally, calling herself a "strong supporter" of the assistance, which totals at least $3.8 billion annually.
On Iran, the Maine senator has been a rare Republican dissenter against the conflict, voting repeatedly with Democrats to curb Trump's war powers.
Jackson, however, has argued that Collins' presence in the Senate tilts the balance in favour of Republicans and enables Trump's agenda, including the Iran war.
"Senator Susan Collins says that she voted against [the war] nine times, but she didn’t have the votes," Jackson said during a debate earlier this month.
"Well that sounds like then we probably ought to have Democrats in charge of the US Senate so that we have the votes."
Alaska: Dan Sullivan (Republican incumbent) v Mary Peltola (Democrat)
Alaska is another traditional Republican stronghold where Democrats are making gains and hoping to stage a big surprise.
The race pits Trump-backed two-term senator Dan Sullivan against former Democratic Congresswoman Mary Peltola. The Democratic candidate's campaign slogan is "fish, family, freedom", focusing on lowering costs in Alaska.
Sullivan is running on his record of helping push large tax cuts and "historic investments" in the US military. The senator has voted consistently against Democratic efforts to restrict Trump's ability to continue the war with Iran.
Last week, he appeared to blame the Democrats' energy regulations for the rising fuel prices in an effort to defend the war with Iran.
"Ladies and gentlemen, the conflict in the Middle East is temporary. The true forever war is the national Democrats’ war against Alaska oil and gas and our jobs. That’s the forever war," he said, according to Alaska Public Media.
Peltola has been overtly critical of the war and Sullivan's votes in support of Trump's military campaign in Iran.
"This war is driving up our energy bills and hurting Alaskans with no end in sight," she said earlier this month.
Both Peltola and Sullivan are staunch Israel supporters. Sullivan has voted repeatedly on pro-Israel measures in Congress, including sponsoring a measure to deepen military cooperation with the US ally.
When she served in the House of Representatives between 2023 and 2025, Peltola was one of the most uncompromising pro-Israel Democrats.
In 2024, she joined Republicans in voting to ban then-President Joe Biden from withholding weapons from Israel. She backed a bill to impose sanctions on the International Criminal Court in response to the arrest warrant against Netanyahu.
Ohio: Jon Husted (Republican incumbent) v Sherrod Brown (Democrat)
Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown is attempting to make a comeback in the Midwestern state that has been trending in Republicans' favour over the past decade.
He is taking on Jon Husted, who replaced Vice President JD Vance in the Senate after the Trump administration took office last year.
Beyond the single seat, the contest is of symbolic importance. It would restore the Democrats' competitive edge in the Midwestern state and serve as an early dig at Vance, who is expected to run for president in 2028.
Brown has made his opposition to the Iran war a key theme in his campaign.
"Jon Husted has voted 14 times to continue the reckless Iran war as gas and grocery prices continue to rise," he recently wrote in a social media post. "I’ll vote to end the war the first chance I get."
In March, Husted proclaimed that the war was going "much better than anyone thought it would".
But like other Republicans in competitive races, he has tempered his support for the conflict.
"The war needs to come to an end as quickly as possible so that we can lower gas prices," he told Politico earlier this month.
Husted and Brown are more closely aligned when it comes to Israel. Both are strong supporters of the US ally.
Ali Harb is a journalist based in Washington, DC. His work focuses on US foreign policy, elections, and Arab American communities
