articles.title: Denmark to acquire 2 types of long-range missiles to bolster deterrence
articles.body:
Necva Tastan Sevinc
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Denmark’s Defense Ministry said Thursday that it is acquiring two types of long-range precision missiles to strengthen its defenses and NATO’s collective deterrence.
The acquisitions include the Joint Strike Missile, manufactured by Norway’s Kongsberg for use on Danish F-35 fighter jets, and the land-launched Anthem cruise missile from the American company Covenant.
The ministry said the weapons use advanced navigation technology to strike targets precisely over long distances, enabling Denmark to deter attacks and, if necessary, retaliate deep inside enemy territory.
Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus said the acquisitions followed recommendations from the chief of defense.
“The acquisitions are a significant step towards making Denmark better able to defend itself, lifting our share of the burden in NATO, and at the same time we are sending a strong signal that we have the ability to strike back,” said Bruus.
The ministry described the missiles as capabilities sought by NATO that would contribute to Denmark’s security.
It did not disclose the value of the acquisitions, the number of missiles or a delivery timetable.

articles.title: IDF intelligence aids Saudi Arabia in military operations against Houthis through US mediation
articles.body:
IDF intelligence continues to provide Saudi Arabia with exceptional capabilities to assist its military operations against the Houthis through US mediation, a defense official confirmed on Thursday.
The assistance is being provided in accordance with Israel's national interests and directives from the political leadership, the official said, emphasizing that the Shi'ite-Sunni confrontation reflects developments taking place beneath the surface across the Middle East.
According to the official, Sunni countries are watching the escalation led by the Houthis against neighboring Saudi Arabia, with encouragement and support from Iran, and understand that they could be next.
Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, is concentrating its efforts on launching powerful attacks against an extensive range of targets in Houthi-controlled areas, seeking to degrade critical military capabilities, including infrastructure.
"Two main points need to be made about this. First, it serves Israel's interests quite well because it wears down the military strength of an Israeli enemy that is preparing and planning to harm us in the future. In addition, we are monitoring and observing methods of operation and tactics, and learning a great deal from what is happening there, including about weapons that are not necessarily manufactured by the Houthis," the official said.
IDF helps Saudi Arabia combat Houthis
The defense official added that the relentless attacks against the Houthis are eroding their capabilities and forcing them to expend considerable effort.
"The Houthis are accustomed to building up their forces, not employing them on this scale. They are a serious enemy, well structured for the long term, but this presents them with a significant challenge. It is no coincidence that they operate sequentially rather than simultaneously against their enemies."
The official further said that the pressure on Saudi Arabia is reshaping alliances and relationships across the Middle East, creating new opportunities.
"The question here is who will intervene on Saudi Arabia's behalf. There is apprehension among countries, but we assess that there will be intervention. Everything remains open, and it is not too late for that to happen."
Meanwhile, the IDF is completing preparations across the sea, air, land, and electromagnetic spectrum domains for a potential Houthi attack as part of a multi-front scenario involving Iran, Hezbollah, and Shi'ite militias operating from Iraq.
The preparations include not only the integration of new technologies and sensors, along with improved connectivity within the IDF and between organizations, but also coordination with the US military.
The US military has a clear interest in protecting Israel's home front because thousands of American troops, aircraft, and US military systems, including air defense systems, are stationed in Israel.

articles.title: Republicans’ negative reaction to the policy toward the Russian Federation promises Trump difficulties in Congress — media
articles.body:
Republicans’ negative reaction to the policy toward the Russian Federation promises Trump difficulties in Congress — media
Kyiv • UNN
Trump’s actions to ease sanctions against Russia and pressure Ukraine have met opposition from Democrats and Republicans in Congress. Lawmakers are threatening to review his policy after the elections.
The steps taken by U.S. President Donald Trump in recent weeks to ease economic pressure on Russia amid mounting criticism of Ukraine have faced opposition from both parties in Congress. This could complicate the implementation of his policy agenda after the midterm elections to be held next month, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
In an attempt to bring Russian dictator Vladimir Putin to negotiations on ending the war in Ukraine, Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel fuel exports and also suspended recently imposed sanctions against Russian officials, oligarchs, banks, and state-owned enterprises.
At the same time, he increased pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, calling for his replacement as the country's leader. As Reuters reported last week, the operation of the satellite system Ukraine uses for battlefield communications and drone control was restricted on orders from the White House.
In a letter dated October 15, 17 Democrats and five Republicans in the House of Representatives urged Trump to "fully and without delay impose the sanctions provided for under the Graham Act." The lawmakers added that Putin "has repeatedly demonstrated that he responds to pressure, not goodwill."
This refers to legislation promoted by the late South Carolina senator Lindsey Graham; Congress passed it by an overwhelming majority, and in mid-September Trump signed it into law.
Trump increases spending ahead of the midterm elections - media20.10.26, 21:20 • 7634 views
The Republicans who signed the letter included Representatives Brian Fitzpatrick (Pennsylvania), Joe Wilson (South Carolina), Michael McCaul (Texas), Don Bacon (Nebraska), and Dan Newhouse (Washington state).
Such a reaction could create new obstacles for Trump after the November 3 midterm elections, when Congress will consider legislation concerning defense and government spending. Lawmakers may use this opportunity to try to repeal or alter his policy toward Russia.
Fitzpatrick went even further. In a post on the social media platform X on Monday, he said that any attempts to restrict the use of intelligence from the "Starshield" system to warn Kyiv about Russian attacks would be subject to a "thorough investigation" by Congress, and that the agencies responsible or their leaders would face "severe cuts in budget funding."
In response to Reuters, the White House sent an email stating: "President Trump has made it clear that he wants to see an end to this brutal war," White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said. She added that Trump "retains the option to use these powers at any time if he concludes that doing so would advance the national interest."

articles.body:
Germany has arrested a Ukrainian man suspected of spying for Russia on military supplies and planning.
The man, identified as Vadym Y., was arrested in the German state of Brandenburg after starting to work with Russian intelligence via a middleman in July 2025, according to DW on Thursday.

The man allegedly gathered intelligence on “the production of armored vehicles, ammunition, and explosives, as well as information on personnel and military facilities at locations intended to secure NATO’s eastern flank,” according to the German Federal Prosecutor’s Office.
The suspect reportedly gathered intelligence via open-source channels and solicited help from “individuals from the European arms industry.”
“Some of the information was publicly available; for other information, the accused specifically recruited individuals from the European arms industry,” the office’s press release says.
The court is set to decide on the man’s pre-trial detention on Friday, it adds.

Berlin raised the sabotage level from Russia against its military to “significant” for the first time on Thursday.
The classification, reportedly triggered by a crashed drone carrying high explosives near the Wunstorf air base in mid-September, is the second-highest level on the internal threat scale of the German military.

In September, Berlin said Russia was responsible for the attempted drone attack at the Leipzig airport in August.
An explosives-laden drone was also discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft used for military supplies at the airport in eastern Germany, a key hub for NATO and Kyiv.
In September, Berlin said it has uncovered 165 suspected sabotage cases and 747 suspicious drone incidents nationwide during the first eight months of the year. In April, German authorities also arrested a Ukrainian and a Latvian national on suspicion of preparing sabotage activities.
European agencies have attributed the cases to heightened Russian sabotage attempts to disrupt Europe’s support for Ukraine.
Berlin also approved plans to close the Russian House, a prominent state-run cultural institution in Berlin, amid concerns that Moscow could use the facility to cover intelligence operations, though the closure would not occur until July 2027, when the contract expires.

articles.title: Race to rearm: Telford gun hall brings tank barrel production back to the UK
articles.body:
For the last 20 years, Britain was unable to put a barrel on its tanks without buying from abroad. Relying on foreign allies seemed like a reasonable choice during years of relative security (for wealthy countries at least) after the end of the cold war.
But Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has changed the calculation – and prompted a scramble to rearm among European countries, including the UK.
Evidence of that scramble was on display on Thursday in Shropshire, where the UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting, opened a factory hastily constructed by Germany’s Rheinmetall to make barrels for artillery and British tanks.
Such was the urgency that Rheinmetall’s chief executive, Armin Papperger, said the company had started investment “off the back of a handshake” before Christmas last year with Gen Sir Roly Walker, who leads the British army as chief of the general staff, without waiting for a formal contract.
Eight months later, production of the first barrels at the factory in Telford has started. Papperger said he was in talks to produce more ammunition in the UK as well, with a decision due in the next six to eight months.
Streeting said: “It is not enough to simply out-innovate those who would wish us harm – though we must. We must also out-produce them too. Because advantage increasingly belongs to those who can manufacture at scale and field the capability fastest.”
The factory takes a 3.2 tonne, 8-metre cylinder of specialised steel alloy and drills a hole through it to make the barrel shape. The surfaces are then honed to remove imperfections, before another turning tool adds spiral rifling to add to artillery accuracy. A specialised machine – one of only two in the world – increases the pressure inside the barrel to about 15,000 times the air at sea level to harden it for the explosive power needed to propel shells as far as 30km (18 miles).
The Ukraine war will go down in history as the moment when militaries woke up to the brutal new reality of drone warfare. But for all the focus on uncrewed weapons, Walker said they cannot rival more traditional armaments for sheer firepower.
“In Ukraine, we know that both sides fire tens of thousands of rounds of artillery ammunition every day, and that generates a weight of fire and levels of lethality across the battlefield that drones alone cannot replicate,” said Walker, in a speech at the factory opening.
He said it had been “sad” when the UK was unable to continue centuries of artillery manufacture that had lasted through the Napoleonic wars, two world wars and the cold war. Much of that work was carried out at the Royal Arsenal in Woolwich, which opened in the 17th century (and whose workers set up a football club that moved to north London in 1913). Yet production ceased in 1967, with the work scattered first around the country and then in some cases moving abroad.
The new Telford gun hall will bring that capability back to the UK, albeit starting with production for guns for German-made, self-propelled, remote-control howitzers that take Nato-standard 155mm ammunition. However, in the future it will also be able to make slightly smaller tank barrels that use 120mm rounds. These include the Challenger 3 tank, which is now going through final testing, and a British version of the remote-control howitzer planned for after May 2028.
The factory will be able to make 245 barrels a year, plus 50 breeches – the part at the base of the barrel – although Papperger said annual capacity could theoretically be expanded to as much as 1,000 within four or five years, but only if the orders came in. Exports may also be on the agenda.
Papperger added that Nato allies could manage with smaller output than Russia and its client states because of their higher quality. A Russian barrel will be able to fire about 500 times before breaking, while the products from Telford should survive as many as 4,000 shots, he said.
The Telford investment followed an agreement in 2024 between Keir Starmer, then prime minister, and his German counterpart, Olaf Scholz. It was part of a wide-ranging pact for the two largest military spenders in Europe to work together more closely.
Rheinmetall employs about 685 people in Telford, although only 35 will work in the gun hall, rising to 100 when it is at full capacity – hardly enough to kickstart the “reindustrialisation” of Britain desired by Andy Burnham. The bulk of the workers in Telford make the Challenger and Boxer armoured vehicles in a joint venture with Britain’s key arms maker, BAE Systems.
Rheinmetall has been among the biggest beneficiaries of the massive increase in European spending on defence and in supplying arms to Ukraine. US intelligence services in 2024 reportedly foiled a Russian plot to assassinate Papperger in apparent retaliation against the company’s production of weapons for Kyiv.
The German company’s market value has risen from about €4.2bn (£3.5bn) in the days before Russia’s invasion to €47bn on Wednesday, though it has dropped back from a peak of nearly double that last year. Rheinmetall and other European defence companies, including BAE Systems and the British jet engine maker Rolls-Royce, have benefited particularly from European governments eager to reduce reliance on the US arms industry at a time when the White House has shown itself willing to divert supplies to its own militaries ahead of allies.
Papperger said more governments were saying they wanted control over their weapons production. That could help to mollify Donald Trump, the US president, who has shown himself willing to undermine previously firm alliances.
“To be a strong partner, you need strong armies,” said Papperger. “But on the other side, you need a strong industry. And this is what we do at the moment. We build up the industry.”

Just hours after being bombed, we asked people in Kyiv about Witkoff's praise of Putin
Nataliia reacts as she looks at the damage inside her house following an aerial attack in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 22, 2026. (Diego Fedele / Getty Images)
On Oct. 21, U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff gushingly praised Russian President Vladimir Putin for being a "humanitarian."
Just a few hours later, Kyiv once again came under a fresh barrage of devastating Russian missiles, killing at least one person and injuring over 20.
"We thought this was a war and the destruction of Ukraine, but it turns out to be an act of humanity," Nataliia Stativko, a former journalist, told the Kyiv Independent on a street devastated by one of the missiles. .
"Now we will die and bury our children, knowing that this is an act of humanity."
The attack hit the city's central Pecherskyi District, which, throughout Russia's full-scale invasion, had been among the capital's least frequently targeted areas and was considered safe by many residents.
"Now there is no safe place in Kyiv — death is breathing down your neck everywhere," Dasha Bilous, 25, a local resident, told the Kyiv Independent.
"Now we will die and bury our children, knowing that this is an act of humanity."
Kniaziv Ostrozkykh Street is almost entirely covered in shattered glass, and barely a single window in the surrounding buildings remains intact. A crater over a meter in diameter marks the middle of the road, where a fragment of a Russian missile lay just hours ago.
Exhausted after a sleepless night, residents are gathering pieces of plywood and plastic sheeting to cover their broken windows and keep at least some warmth inside their homes, as rain falls outside and a piercing autumn wind cuts through the streets.
While Kyiv residents pick up the pieces and try to resume their lives, they are left grappling with Witkoff's words from his Oct. 21 meeting with Putin in Saint Petersburg, in which the two discussed a "peace settlement" to Russia's war against Ukraine.
During the meeting, Moscow announced the release of 74-year-old American citizen Stephen Hubbard. Russian forces detained Hubbard during the occupation of Ukraine's Kharkiv Oblast in the early months of the full-scale invasion in 2022. In 2024, a Russian court convicted him of serving as a mercenary in the Ukrainian military, an accusation his family and lawyer disputed.
Witkoff described Putin as a "humanitarian" while commenting on Hubbard's release.
The area where Stativko lives was likely targeted overnight not only with conventional cruise and ballistic missiles, but also with cluster munitions, which scatter smaller explosive charges upon detonation, causing more widespread damage across a larger area.
Andrii Saulevych, manager of the local coffee shop Khlibna Kraina, also felt the impact of Russia's missile attack firsthand. The cafe's windows were completely blown out, but by 8 a.m. local time, it was already serving coffee to customers again.
"We put a piece of ourselves into every coffee shop," he said. "It's deeply upsetting to see everything destroyed like this."
"Humanitarians don't act this way. This is something else. This is anti-humanitarian," Saulevych added.
Another resident of the district, teacher Yaroslav Bahai, spent the morning waiting in line for humanitarian aid instead of preparing his lessons. The windows in his apartment had been blown out, and shrapnel had pierced straight through his kitchen refrigerator. His family was fortunate to survive the attack unharmed: they had taken shelter in the hallway with their children when the missiles struck.
Bahai said the war has significantly changed the way he teaches. His school cannot accommodate all its students in the bomb shelter, while the constant air raid alerts that have plagued the capital in recent months have made learning increasingly difficult, even online.
"I used to give children an assignment asking who they see themselves becoming in five years. Now they say it's hard for them to even imagine what tomorrow will look like," he said.
Bahai and his family have no plans to leave Kyiv for now, despite the approaching winter, which could be one of Ukraine's most difficult since 2022 due to continued Russian attacks and damage to the country's energy infrastructure. Bilous, however, is considering leaving the capital. Although reluctant to abandon her home, she said she can no longer cope with the constant sense of danger, which only continues to grow.
A fragment of a Russian missile landed right next to her house, shattering all the windows.
"I thought I was going to die," Bilous said.
"Such a 'gift' arrived in Kyiv after the (Witkoff-Putin) meeting. Who was it from? Putin? Witkoff? Trump?"

articles.title: Ukraine and Norway Collaborate on Air Defense and Satellite Communications Projects
articles.body:
Ukraine and Norway are working on three joint defense projects.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced this during a press briefing with journalists, according to Ukrinform.
The first project aims to protect Ukrainian cities and infrastructure from Russian Geran-type strike drones.
According to the president, Ukraine expects to see concrete results in this area within the next six to eight weeks.
Zelensky decided not to disclose details of the second joint project until it has been fully implemented.
“Let everything arrive – everything we have been working on. The second project is FREYJA,” Volodymyr Zelensky noted.
The third joint defense project between the two countries is related to strengthening air defense and ensuring satellite communications.
As previously reported, Norwegian company Kongsberg has developed an anti-aircraft combat module for Ukrainian Inguar-3 armored vehicles.
The system is based on the CROWS platform, a mobile solution designed to detect and engage enemy drones, including Geran-type drones and, in some cases, cruise missiles.
According to sources familiar with the project, the platform is being developed specifically for Ukraine using donor funding. Once the first phase of testing is complete, it is expected to be handed over to the Ukrainian side.
The Norwegian government, together with Kongsberg and Ukraine, will also fund and develop missiles for the NASAMS surface-to-air missile system.
As part of the European FREYJA air and missile defense program, Norway could supply Kongsberg Fire Distribution Center (FDC) command posts featuring an open architecture, as well as Network Access Nodes.

‘Nothing personal between me and Trump’: Zelensky comments on tensions with U.S.
According to Ukrinform, he said this in an interview with CNN.
“My attitude to Putin is very clear. I think that if we lift sanctions, we will make him stronger. It’s not something personal between me and President Trump, and of course I’m against of any lifting of sanctions,” Zelensky said.
The Ukrainian President noted that although European allies have provided Ukraine with a certain number of air defense missiles, “it’s not enough to defend ourselves.”
Ukraine, Zelensky said, now mostly needs two things from its allies: “Not to lift sanctions from Putin … (and) to give us better missiles.”
The Ukrainian President described the meeting in Oslo as productive, saying he was not convinced that Putin was seeking peace.
“Putin is playing, you know, he is a player. It’s a pity because he plays with the lives of other people, and of course he doesn’t want (to stop the war). So what we want from our partners is not to give him a possibility to be stronger and break us,” Zelensky said.
The President hinted at the possibility of freezing the current front lines in order to “ceasefire, stop the killing, sit and speak.” However, he stressed that the idea of Ukraine handing over to Russia territories currently under its control is doomed to fail, and Kyiv will never recognize the occupied territories as part of Russia.
“Our land is very important because it’s about people. It’s not about kilometers. A lot of people died defending this land, defending our independence, our country. Nobody will recognize these territories, which are temporarily occupied, as Russian territories, and I think Russia understands it. It’s a pity if somebody doesn’t understand, but it’s up to them,” Zelensky said.

articles.title: Britain lacks what it needs in the High North, says report
articles.body:
Britain must address serious military capability gaps in the High North, and should consider whether the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force ought to focus more on threats in the region, particularly if it has to plan for uncertainty over American support for NATO, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, published its findings after an inquiry that took evidence between March and July this year and included visits to Norway, Denmark and Greenland.
Dhesi said: “The High North poses a major strategic challenge for the UK’s security. This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage.”
He said: “The UK needs to be willing to address a hard truth: it does not currently have all the capabilities to operate successfully in the High North. Russian submarine and sabotage forces in the High North pose direct risks to the North Atlantic and the UK, including the nuclear deterrent. Despite this, the Ministry of Defence has accepted a serious anti-submarine warfare gap. Publicly available evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines calls into question whether the UK can meet its commitments in the High North.”
He added: “And if the UK government means what it says – that Russia could attack NATO as soon as 2030 – then work to rectify these vulnerabilities cannot start soon enough.”
The report warns of serious consequences if the region is left inadequately defended. Failure to deter Russia there, particularly from underwater threats, would put subsea data cables and energy pipelines in and around British waters at particular risk during peacetime. In the event of hostilities, failure to counter Russia in the High North would threaten the British population, military and civilian critical national infrastructure including the nuclear deterrent, and Atlantic resupply routes from the United States.
On the capability gaps themselves, the committee sets out that the Royal Navy has a requirement for eight of its thirteen frigates to carry the Sonar 2087 towed array for anti-submarine work and currently holds five, all of them Type 23s. It records eleven frigates and destroyers in service against a requirement for nineteen, and calls for no further towed array-equipped Type 23 to leave service until replaced one-for-one by a Type 26.
It also finds that Britain has allowed its submarine under-ice capability to lapse just as the region has become strategically more important, leaving it less able to contest Russian freedom of action and at risk of being forced into a more defensive posture.
On the Joint Expeditionary Force, the ten-nation grouping Britain leads alongside the Netherlands and the Baltic and Nordic states, Dhesi said: “Our Defence in the High North inquiry found that the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force has not yet realised its full potential. Although it was originally conceived as capable of operating across the full spectrum of conflict, and of covering both the High North and Baltic regions, its role has become increasingly focused on countering sub-threshold and hybrid threats.”
He said: “Our report calls for the government to reassess the JEF’s role and consider whether it should focus more on countering threats in the High North, particularly if the UK has to plan for uncertainty over US support for NATO. The UK’s presence in the Baltics, particularly in Estonia, may need to be bolstered to offset the effects of any greater JEF focus on the High North.”
Building the British Army force in Estonia up to brigade strength would match what Germany is already undertaking in Lithuania. The committee also asks the government, within a year of assuming leadership of NATO’s Joint Force Command Norfolk, to reassess the added value the force brings to European security, and either strengthen it and align it more closely with NATO or focus its finite resources on NATO instead.
Sir Keir Starmer, then Prime Minister, said in June this year that it was the British intelligence assessment, and that of other NATO countries, that there could be an attack by Russia on NATO as soon as 2030. The Defence Investment Plan published the same month committed £298 billion over four years to 2029-30.
In evidence to the inquiry the Ministry of Defence described anti-submarine warfare as a core strength of Britain’s armed forces, and said capabilities are held at varying levels of readiness, with every platform going through a cycle of deployment, maintenance, training and preparation, and equipment held at different readiness depending on the capability it is required to meet for NATO.
The government is expected to respond to the report within two months.

articles.title: Swiss drone defence: ‘We’re flying partly blind’
articles.body:
Swiss drone defence: ‘We’re flying partly blind’
A drone suddenly appears over an airfield or nuclear power plant. Is it the mistake of a hobbyist or an act of espionage? According to security expert Ivo Capaul, Switzerland lacks a clear picture of the threat.
Swiss public broadcaster SRF: Is the danger posed by drones in Switzerland being underestimated?
Ivo Capaul: Generally speaking, yes. In Switzerland, we have lost some sense of the current threat situation. We certainly need to take this issue seriously and address it.
SRF: How serious is the problem? How often do potentially dangerous drones fly over critical infrastructure, for example?
I.C.: In a sense, we’re flying blind. There is no national, centralised record of drone sightings. Although the army records incidents, it is not always clear what is behind the figures.
More
What does the future hold for Swiss neutrality?
According to the army, around 80% of cases involve misidentifications or drones operated by harmless hobbyists. In 20% of cases, it could be a hybrid attack by a state.
Ivo Capaul is a researcher in the Defence Policy and Armaments Team at the Centre for Security Studies (CSS) at the federal technology institute ETH Zurich.
SRF: How difficult is it to distinguish between a harmless drone and a hostile one?
I.C.: It’s not that simple. These days a commercial drone effectively has a virtual number plate and is registered. A sensor can identify it. But a malicious actor can assemble a drone themselves using off-the-shelf parts or tamper with the control system. This makes identification difficult and requires sophisticated radar sensors.
More
Our newsletter on geopolitics
SRF: What would be the most important steps to take to get out of this “blind flight” situation?
I.C.: It is important to install sensors at critical infrastructure sites so that we can detect what is happening in the sky. Furthermore, there needs to be a reporting obligation for operators of critical infrastructure, similar to that for cyber-attacks.
They must report any drones they spot. This is the only way we can obtain a picture of the national situation on which we can take action.
SRF: What are the main aims of state actors that carry out drone flights over critical infrastructure?
I.C.: Often people think it’s all about sabotage: a drone loaded with explosives that flies into a target. But in the context of hybrid operations a drone can pursue a wide variety of objectives: espionage, testing a facility’s security measures, delegitimising the security authorities or sowing uncertainty among the public. The spectrum is very broad.
SRF: Who is operating these drones?
I.C.: Attribution is very difficult and time-consuming. The case at Leipzig Airport, where Germany clearly identified Russia as the perpetrator, is an exception. In most cases, it cannot be conclusively proven whether a state actor is behind it, or which one.
SRF: The war in Ukraine shows just how rapidly drone technology is developing. Is it possible to protect yourself effectively?
I.C.: There is no such thing as absolute security, nor will there ever be. It would be illusory to believe that every sensitive site in Switzerland could be protected by a defence system. That is why we must prioritise. Where is the threat greatest?
We must also strengthen our own defences, for example through structural measures. A protective net can shield critical infrastructure from espionage or sabotage. Resilience is also important, such as the ability to resume normal operations quickly following an attack.

articles.title: US Accuses Russia Of 'Deliberately Reckless' Move With Military Satellite Flyby
articles.body:
US officials publicly accused Russia of threatening a Finnish-operated commercial satellite that provides imagery and intelligence to Ukraine and other nations, calling the move “deliberately reckless.”
In response to the accusations, made during a United Nations debate on October 21, Russia broadly described US claims as "absurd" and accused Washington of its own “aggressive military space ambitions.”
The back-and-forth came days after a Russian military satellite known as Kosmos-2612 moved “dangerously” near to ICEYE-X36, a satellite registered in the United States and operated by a Finnish company called ICEYE.
The Russian satellite came “exceptionally close” -- within 200 meters, by some estimates -- something that space officials and amateur satellite watchers said was extremely unusual.
"This was not a routine conjunction or 'fly by,'" LeoLabs, an aerospace intelligence company, told RFE/RL. "The behavior is consistent with sophisticated rendezvous and proximity operations."
ICEYE-X36 carries a radar technology that can gather detailed terrestrial images, even through cloud cover. The Finnish company in January signed a contract with the Ukrainian Defense Ministry to provide intelligence.
Kosmos-2612 “exhibited threatening behavior by intentionally maneuvering dangerously close to a commercial satellite,” Brian Hardesty, an adviser to the US Delegation to the Conference on Disarmament, said during a meeting in New York of the UN First Committee, a body that debates arms control and disarmament issues. “These behaviors appear consistent with an on-orbit weapons operation."
“The decision to conduct these activities was deliberately reckless,” he said.
Russia’s representative who could not be immediately identified, did not directly address the assertion.
"We call on member states to give the proper response to the aggressive military space ambitions of the United States," he said.
He also referenced comments made last month by the secretary of the US Air Force, the top civilian official for that military branch.
Speaking to a conference outside of Washington, Troy Meink’s comments that Washington has in fact deployed actual weapons in space -- “on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action” -- caused a jolt among policy experts.
Other longtime space watchers, however, said, the announcement merely stated publicly what had already been obvious for some time.
“The United States did not suddenly weaponize space by acknowledging that it possesses these capabilities,” wrote Mallory Stewart, a former top arms control secretary at the US State Department. “An arms race in space has been under way for years.”

articles.title: Macron targets Trump over French riots
articles.body:
Macron targets Trump over French riots
French President Emmanuel Macron has slammed as “stupid” and “unacceptable” remarks by foreign leaders about the unrest gripping France, in an apparent swipe at US President Donald Trump, who blamed the violence on Paris’ lax border policies.
France has been rocked by some of its worst riots in years, sparked last month by teacher shortages and crumbling schools before escalating into nationwide protests over inequality, soaring living costs and public service cuts.
Hundreds of thousands took to the streets over the weekend as demonstrations descended into clashes with police, arson and looting. Nearly 2,400 people were arrested, around 1,000 officers injured, hundreds of businesses looted and buildings torched, with damage estimated at “hundreds of millions of euros.”
Trump pours fuel on the fire
Trump claimed that “migrants, jihadists, and communists” had “conquered, looted, and burned” France, accusing Macron of failing to secure its borders. He urged European leaders to “close their borders,” before seizing on the unrest to rally Republicans ahead of the November 3 midterms, warning that scenes of “burning steeples and raging fires” were “what the Radical Dumocrats want to do to AMERICA” with their own migration agenda.
Macron isn’t amused
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Macron accused outside actors of manipulating information about the events to their gain.
“There was foreign manipulation of information, which gave rise to unacceptable and stupid comments from many people, including foreign leaders,” he said. “We have had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false… These people annoy me.”
Asked whether he was referring to Trump, Macron replied: “Among others.”
President Emmanuel Macron said Wednesday that foreign leaders — including those “on the other side of the Atlantic” — were seeking to exploit France’s tense social climate for political gain following a weekend of street violence and looting.
Protests over soaring living costs… pic.twitter.com/XlitrzVoK6
— The Associated Press (@AP) October 21, 2026
While there is no clear evidence that migrants have played a disproportionate role in the unrest, multiple videos posted online have shown protesters waving Palestinian flags alongside French ones.
They said the riots and destruction in France were about the cost of living and schools.
Then explain the Palestinian flags and keffiyehs.
Allowing mass third-world migration is why France is done. pic.twitter.com/jDr733vcOx
— TaraBull (@TaraBull) October 19, 2026
French authorities have largely blamed the violence on radical far-left groups and opportunistic criminals, without linking its organization to immigrants. Meanwhile, politicians across France’s political spectrum blamed Macron and his government for the unrest, accusing the administration of undermining public services and failing to maintain order.
Macron leaves the building
Macron made his remarks during a Middle East trip that he refused to postpone despite the turmoil at home, leaving his government to deal with the fallout. He tried to defend his decision, insisting that changing his plans would have signaled “nervousness” and that he had given his government a “sufficient roadmap.” Yet with just six months until France’s presidential election and his approval rating at a record-low 15%, the trip has only fueled perceptions of a lame-duck presidency as Macron quite literally left the scene as Paris and other cities burned.
His absence drew criticism of an “absent president” and left rivals Marine Le Pen, who leads first-round polling for April 2027 with 32-36% support, and Jean-Luc Melenchon, to dominate the debate at home.
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has ordered curfews ahead of fresh protests, with gatherings banned near Paris landmarks including the Louvre and Champs-Elysees for three days. France also plans to deploy 1,000 counterterrorism troops to reinforce police on Saturday, October 24. Lecornu is due to meet mayors of riot-hit cities on Thursday to coordinate efforts to prevent further violence.
Russia, the usual suspect
In his remarks, Macron also dismissed suggestions of foreign interference in the unrest itself, citing a lack of evidence. His remarks followed a flurry of Western media speculation seeking to blame the riots, which spread from France to Belgium, Italy, Portugal and Albania, on outside meddling – with Russia once again cast as the usual suspect.
Outlets such as The Financial Times and the Telegraph, citing “anonymous” sources, reported that several EU governments had asked intelligence agencies to investigate possible Russian involvement. The FT expanded the suspect list to Iran and Algeria, claiming some officials had even demanded a formal EU probe.
European officials also joined the finger-pointing. Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto suggested the riots were part of a “hybrid war” waged through social media by an unidentified actor. Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama went further, accusing Russian and Iranian intelligence services outright.
Yet the allegations have apparently failed to convince even Brussels. According to Euronews, the European Commission has declined to launch an investigation, citing insufficient evidence.
The speculation follows a familiar pattern of EU officials invoking “hybrid warfare” and the alleged “Russian threat” amid domestic turmoil. Just this week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen accused Moscow and Minsk of “weaponizing migration,” linking them to the summer crisis in Spain’s Ceuta, where an estimated 70,000 migrants crossed from Morocco, sparking a border emergency and political fallout over EU migration policies. However, yet again, she presented no evidence connecting either country to the crisis.
Moscow says look closer to home
Moscow routinely dismisses allegations of interference and claims of a Russian threat as “absurd” fabrications, accusing EU leaders of using the narrative to deflect blame for their own policy failures and distract from mounting domestic crises.
Responding to Rama’s accusations, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told him to look closer to home.
“These are citizens of your own country who took to the streets to protest. Don’t shift your responsibility onto others. Deal with your own domestic problems,” she said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, meanwhile, described the unrest sweeping the EU as evidence of “a major crisis… bordering on chaos.”

articles.title: Ukraine Receives Finnish Variant of Crotale Air Defense System to Counter Russian Drones and Missiles
articles.body:
Ukraine’s 1039th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment, named after General Mykola Kapustianskyi, has received Finnish ItO 90M air defense systems.
The delivery was revealed in a video showing the systems in operation, published on the regiment’s Facebook account.
The ItO 90M is Finland’s version of the French Crotale NG short-range air defense system, developed by Thales.
The main difference in the Finnish version is its use of the Sisu XA-181 6×6 armored personnel carrier chassis instead of a French-made vehicle.
The story of this deal began in 1988, when Finland signed an agreement with France to purchase 21 Crotale NG air defense systems for its armed forces.
The Finnish systems underwent a major upgrade in the 2000s, receiving modern thermal imaging systems, upgraded daylight cameras, and improved fire-control systems. These upgrades are reflected in the designation ‘M,’ which stands for Modernisoitu (modernized).
The history of the Crotale NG system dates back to the late 1980s, when French developers created a new air defense system designed to engage cruise missiles, unmanned aerial vehicles, and low-flying aircraft.
The standard Crotale NG system integrates a radar detection system, electro-optical tracking equipment, and an eight-missile launcher on a single turret.
In terms of its technical specifications, the ItO 90M can detect aerial targets at ranges of up to 20 km.
Its primary interceptor is the high-speed VT-1 missile, which reaches speeds of up to Mach 3.5 (approximately 1,200 m/s) and has an engagement range of up to 11 km and an engagement altitude of up to 6 km.
The system has a reaction time of just five seconds from target detection to missile launch, enabling it to effectively intercept high-speed aerial targets.
As previously reported, Ukrainian air defense forces used a combination of a Kub surface-to-air missile system launcher and a Buk self-propelled firing unit to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones.

articles.title: Poland detains second suspect in murder of Russian artist and Putin critic Semyon Skrepetsky
articles.body:
Poland detains second suspect in murder of Russian artist and Putin critic Semyon Skrepetsky
Officers from Poland’s Internal Security Agency have detained a 22-year-old Georgian citizen in connection with the murder of Russian performance artist Semyon Skrepetsky, said Tomasz Siemoniak, the coordinator of Poland’s intelligence services.
RMF24 identified the man as Makhmud A. The outlet reported that he helped the suspected killer, who had been detained earlier, by keeping Skrepetsky’s home under surveillance and gathering information about his habits.
Makhmud A. arrived in Poland the day before he was detained and was traveling with two other Georgian citizens. The other two were expelled from the country, RMF24 reported.
Makhmud A. was charged with aiding and abetting murder and illegally possessing weapons and ammunition. He denied the charges.
Russian performance artist Semyon Skrepetsky was killed on June 15 in the Polish city of Biała Podlaska. The first suspect in his murder was detained near Warsaw on June 18. Police said he “was using a passport issued in the name of a 36-year-old Georgian citizen.”
Skrepetsky was known for his caricatures of figures including Vladimir Putin and Ramzan Kadyrov. He moved to Poland in 2021, fearing persecution. On June 12 — three days before his murder — he staged a protest outside the Russian Embassy in Berlin. He brought a painting depicting Putin in Stalin’s arms to the embassy. After the protest, Skrepetsky received threats, which he wrote about on his Telegram channel on the day he was killed.

articles.title: NSDC Secretary Klymenko meets NATO delegation to discuss Patriot missiles and PURL prospects
articles.body:
NSDC Secretary Klymenko meets NATO delegation to discuss Patriot missiles and PURL prospects
According to Ukrinform, Klymenko said this in a Telegram post.
The NATO delegation was led by the Alliance’s Assistant Secretaries General Christian Buck and Douglas Jones.
During the meeting, Klymenko stressed that Ukraine needs timely and sufficient deliveries of interceptors for Patriot systems and air-to-air missiles to protect people, the economy and critical infrastructure from Russian attacks.
They also discussed the prospects of the PURL program.
“This is one of the key mechanisms for obtaining critically needed weapons, so it is important to increase funding for the program and ensure its stable operation. At the same time, we need to pool our efforts in the technology sector, develop joint production and strengthen the resilience of Ukraine and its allies,” Klymenko said.
The NSDC Secretary expressed gratitude to the Alliance and all NATO member states for their support for Ukraine since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion. He separately thanked Buck and Jones for the substantive discussion.
Among other things, he emphasized the importance of partners understanding that supporting Ukraine is the best response to the threat posed by the Russian Federation.
“The NSDC is ready for further cooperation, information sharing and the exchange of practical experience,” Klymenko said.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that, according to intelligence agencies, Russia had already identified its priorities for terrorizing Ukrainians over the coming weeks. He said it was clear that the aggressor state was taking advantage of delays in air defense deliveries from partners.

articles.title: Yemeni army says 512 Houthi fighters neutralized in 24 hours
articles.body:
Yemen’s government forces carried out 780 strikes against Houthi positions over the past 24 hours, neutralizing approximately 512 fighters and destroying or damaging more than 330 military vehicles, a military spokesman said Thursday, Anadolu reports.
Majed Abdullah al-Nuzayli, spokesman for the Yemeni Armed Forces, said in a statement that the operations were conducted as part of the ongoing “Operation Dawn of Yemen.”
He said the strikes targeted Houthi field commanders, troop concentrations, reinforcements, heavy weapons positions, fortified sites and military vehicles across the northern fronts as well as Al-Jawf, western Marib, and Al-Bayda provinces.
According to al-Nuzayli, the operations also destroyed heavy weapons and reinforcements heading toward front lines in Taiz province.
He said the strikes had disrupted Houthi military operations and prevented reinforcements from reaching forward positions, allowing government forces to maintain their offensive.
READ: More than 250,000 displaced in Yemen since August as fighting escalates: UNHCR
The spokesman vowed to continue targeting Houthi military positions and reinforcements while taking precautions to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure in accordance with international humanitarian law.
The military’s casualty and damage figures could not be independently verified, and there was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
The announcement comes amid intensified fighting between government forces, backed by a Saudi-led coalition, and the Houthis across several Yemeni provinces.
Earlier Thursday, Yemeni state television reported airstrikes targeting Houthi missile launchers, radar systems, military communications equipment and weapons depots in Taiz.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention in March 2015 to support the country’s internationally recognized government.

articles.title: Ukrainian national detained in Germany on suspicion of spying for Russia
articles.body:
Ukrainian national detained in Germany on suspicion of spying for Russia
Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office detained a Ukrainian national, Vadym Y., on 22 October on suspicion of gathering information about NATO military facilities for Russian intelligence.
Source: a statement by the German Federal Public Prosecutor General's Office, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The Ukrainian national was detained in the Oder-Spree district of Brandenburg under a warrant issued on 15 October.
Vadym Y. is suspected of acting on behalf of a foreign intelligence service.
According to law enforcement authorities, he had been in contact with Russian intelligence through an intermediary since at least July 2025.
He also collected military-related information in Germany, including details about the production of armoured vehicles, ammunition and explosives, as well as personnel and military facilities in areas responsible for protecting NATO's eastern flank.
Some of the information was publicly available, while the suspect deliberately obtained other details from individuals connected to the European defence industry.
Der Spiegel reports that the man had shown an interest in the Bundeswehr's 45th Armoured Brigade, which is due to be fully deployed in Lithuania next year and ready for combat.
The prosecutor's office said the suspect will be brought before an investigating judge at the Federal Court of Justice on 23 October. The judge will formally notify him of the arrest warrant and decide whether to remand him in custody.
Background:
- Poland's Military Gendarmerie detained a participant in a reservist training course at the Military Medical Academy in Łódź. Media reports said he is suspected of espionage and holds Polish-Ukrainian citizenship.
- In September, prosecutors in Düsseldorf, Germany, brought charges against a Ukrainian national suspected of spying for Russia.

Russia and Ukraine trade major attacks as Trump touts progress
Zelensky said the strikes, which came hours after US envoy Witkoff met Putin, showed ‘no change’ in Moscow’s position
Moscow firing ballistic missiles at Ukraine shortly after talks between US envoy Steve Witkoff and Russia’s Vladimir Putin showed the Kremlin’s position on the war had not changed, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday.
The Kremlin had said it was willing to restart trilateral talks with Kyiv and Washington next month, though dismissed new ideas brought by Witkoff – developed with European countries and Ukraine – as lacking substance.
Russia hit a dozen Ukrainian regions overnight, including Kyiv, killing at least two people and wounding 34, Zelensky said, adding that children were among those hurt.

articles.title: Romania to speed up development of Black Sea capabilities after cargo ship attacks
articles.body:
Romania to speed up development of Black Sea capabilities after cargo ship attacks
BUCHAREST, Oct 22 - Romania will accelerate its development of surveillance capabilities and equipment to counter mines and drones in the Black Sea after a series of drone attacks on commercial ships off its coast, its top defence council said on Thursday.
At least seven cargo ships have been hit near the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria in the past two weeks, with some 30 sailors reported dead or missing. Romanian F-16 fighter jet pilots shot down two of the latest generation of Russian drones over Romanian territorial waters on Saturday.
NATO said on Tuesday it will send more maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and drones to the Black Sea.
• Romania's top defence council said latest ship attacks are direct consequences of Russia's aggression beyond Ukraine's borders.
• Threats to freedom of navigation and critical energy projects in the Black Sea pose a security crisis for Romania.
• The current risks require concrete measures to protect human lives, maintain free access to national ports, and ensure the security of energy facilities in the Exclusive Economic Zone.
• The top defence council said it will accelerate the development of capabilities for maritime surveillance, countering naval mines and intervening against drones illegally breaching national airspace and waters.
• Authorities will practice to improve the efficiency of their operational response.
• Romania will seek to improve cooperation with fellow NATO members Bulgaria and Turkey with whom it shares the Black Sea.
• "The Council members also analyzed ways to intensify coordination within NATO. This includes strengthening the deterrence and defense posture on the Eastern Flank and identifying new measures to respond to threats in the Black Sea region." REUTERS

articles.title: Palantir’s Thiel laments Iran war – Politico
articles.body:
Palantir’s Thiel laments Iran war – Politico
Billionaire tech investor and Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel has expressed regret over the US war against Iran, warning that it could ultimately lead to International Criminal Court warrants for the Trump administration and have broader implications for the US, Politico reported on Thursday.
The outlet cited a transcript of a lecture given by Thiel earlier this month, part of the series of private events held in Nashville.
Thiel, a staunch backer of US President Donald Trump, has expressed doubts over the Iran war, which was launched by the US and Israel earlier this year, suggesting that it has exposed America’s weaknesses.
“I’m skeptical of [the war], I think we should not have done it. There were a lot of mistakes that were made,” Thiel said, as quoted by Politico.
Maybe we don’t have the hard power. Maybe we’re going to lose the soft power war.
While reiterating his support for Trump, he warned that the war could backfire for the administration and lead to legal troubles with the International Criminal Court (ICC). 
The Trump administration has had a hostile relationship with the ICC, particularly over the decision to issue arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes in Gaza.
The US, which does not recognize the ICC’s jurisdiction, has enacted sanctions against the court’s top officials, describing it as a “corrupt and fatally politicized supranational court that has maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate.”
“I have come to suspect that the threat of an ICC arrest warrant is the sword of Damocles hanging over the Trump administration as it tries to persecute this war in Iran,” Thiel said.
He also claimed that George W. Bush-era neocon figures such as Donald Rumsfeld and Dick Cheney have been colluding with the ICC against Trump. “I read the Cheney family’s Trump derangement syndrome as an attempt to buy favor with the [ICC] and avoid prosecution. Probably too late,” he said.
Palantir has been heavily involved in the hostilities, as its products have been used by the US military. The use of AI products was reportedly linked to one of the worst mass-casualty events of the war – the strike on a school in Minab on the first day of the conflict, which killed at least 156 civilians, predominantly schoolchildren. According to media reports, the facility was targeted based on outdated data used by Palantir’s analysis and surveillance software.

articles.title: Iran sets 7 conditions for reopening Strait of Hormuz, resuming talks: Official

He said Iran’s preference was “de-escalation,” but “the longer the US prolonged the war, the stronger Iran would become, although this was not what Tehran wanted.”

The US and Israel launched the war against Iran on Feb. 28, prompting Tehran to respond with missile and drone attacks in the region and effectively close the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.

articles.title: Tsahkna: the stronger Ukraine is, the less leverage Russia has to dictate the terms of peace
articles.body:
“Russia has not abandoned its objectives and continues to attack Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure as the country faces another difficult winter. Ukraine must be able to defend itself so that it can enter any potential peace negotiations from the strongest possible position. The stronger Ukraine is, the less leverage Russia has to dictate the terms of peace,” Foreign Minister Tsahkna said.
“Military support for Ukraine and pressure on Russia must continue hand in hand. Our goal is a just and lasting peace, not a situation in which Russia demands at the negotiating table what it has failed to achieve on the battlefield. This is important for the future and security of both Ukraine and Europe as a whole,” Tsahkna stressed.
Before today’s decision, Estonia had provided €21 million in support for Ukraine through PURL.
PURL, or the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List, is a NATO-coordinated initiative through which European Allies and Canada fund the procurement of weapons for Ukraine from the United States. It is one of the most effective ways for Allies to channel financial support towards purchasing weapons Ukraine needs urgently, particularly air defence systems and ammunition. NATO coordinates the delivery of this assistance to Ukraine.

articles.title: Why is Libya-Turkey maritime deal causing a regional dispute?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Why is the Libya-Turkey maritime deal causing a regional dispute?
Libya's parliament has unanimously approved a controversial maritime agreement with Turkey, reversing years of opposition and reigniting a regional dispute over territorial waters, energy resources and political influence in the eastern Mediterranean.
The vote on Tuesday by Libya's eastern-based House of Representatives marked a significant shift in the country's divided political landscape, bringing rival authorities in Tripoli and Benghazi into agreement on a deal first signed in 2019.
But the decision has drawn strong objections from Egypt, Greece, Cyprus, the European Union and Israel, which have challenged the agreement's legitimacy and its implications for maritime sovereignty.
Turkey has rejected the criticism, insisting that the agreement is lawful and protects the rights of both countries.
The dispute goes beyond maritime boundaries, touching on competition for offshore gas, Turkey's growing influence in Libya and the shifting alliances of regional powers.
So what does the agreement involve, why has it caused such controversy, and what happens next?
What is the Libya-Turkey maritime agreement?
The agreement was signed on 27 November 2019 by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Fayez al-Sarraj, then head of Libya's internationally recognised Government of National Accord (GNA).
It establishes maritime jurisdiction zones between Libya and Turkey across the eastern Mediterranean, giving both countries a basis to claim rights over areas believed to contain potentially valuable oil and gas resources.
The deal was signed during Libya's civil war, when Turkey was providing military support to the Tripoli-based government against an offensive by forces loyal to eastern commander Khalifa Haftar.
Turkey subsequently deployed drones and military advisers to help repel Haftar's assault on the capital.
At the time, Libya's eastern-based House of Representatives, which supported Haftar, rejected the agreement.
However, on Tuesday, the parliament unanimously voted to ratify the deal, reversing its previous position.
The decision was welcomed by Libya's Government of National Unity, Presidential Council and High Council of State, as well as Ankara.
Why are Egypt, Greece and the EU opposed?
The agreement has faced longstanding opposition from several eastern Mediterranean countries that argue it infringes on their maritime rights.
Greece maintains that Turkey and Libya do not have opposite or adjacent coastlines that would justify the maritime boundary established under the deal.
Athens argues that the agreement disregards the maritime rights of Greek islands, including Crete, Rhodes and Karpathos.
The Greek foreign ministry has warned that it will take appropriate measures to defend the country's sovereign rights and has raised the issue with the UN Security Council.
Egypt has also rejected the ratification, arguing that the agreement encroaches on its exclusive economic zone and continental shelf.
Cairo's foreign ministry said the deal "constitutes a clear infringement upon Egypt's sovereign rights within its exclusive economic zone and continental shelf", insisting that Libya's parliamentary approval has no legal consequences for Egypt.
The European Union has similarly reaffirmed its opposition.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa said in a joint statement that the agreement infringes on the sovereign rights of third countries and is incompatible with the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).
The bloc reiterated its support for Greece and Cyprus, both EU member states.
Turkey, which is not a party to UNCLOS, rejects these objections.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan described the agreement as "entirely legitimate", while Omer Celik, spokesperson for the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP), argued that it rested on strong legal foundations.
The dispute also has implications for the planned Great Sea Interconnector, a subsea electricity cable intended to connect Greece and Cyprus, and eventually Israel.
The project, estimated to cost approximately $2.1 billion, has already encountered delays linked to maritime disagreements between Greece and Turkey.
Why is the agreement important for oil and gas?
The eastern Mediterranean has become an increasingly important region for energy exploration, with competing maritime claims affecting access to potential offshore oil and gas reserves.
The Libya-Turkey agreement defines maritime economic zones and creates a framework for exploring natural resources, including hydrocarbons.
Neither country has announced proven reserves in the maritime areas covered by the deal.
However, a 2021 assessment by the US Geological Survey estimated that the wider eastern Mediterranean region contained an average of 286.2 trillion cubic feet of undiscovered, technically recoverable conventional natural gas resources.
Energy cooperation between Ankara and Tripoli has continued despite the political dispute.
In October 2022, Turkey and Libya's Government of National Unity signed a separate hydrocarbons cooperation agreement covering scientific, technical, legal and commercial collaboration.
In June 2025, Libya's National Oil Corporation and Turkish Petroleum signed a memorandum of understanding to conduct geological and geophysical studies in four offshore areas.
The arrangement included discussions over a two-dimensional seismic survey covering 10,000 kilometres.
For Libya, offshore exploration could attract investment and diversify energy revenues beyond its existing production of approximately 1.4 million barrels of oil per day and 72 million cubic metres of natural gas daily.
For Turkey, the deal could strengthen its position in the eastern Mediterranean energy sector and support efforts to reduce its dependence on imported energy.
However, the existence of a maritime agreement does not guarantee commercially viable discoveries or immediate production.
Why has eastern Libya changed its position?
The parliamentary reversal reflects significant changes in Libya's internal politics and Turkey's relations with the country's eastern leadership.
When the agreement was first signed, Ankara was supporting the Tripoli government against Haftar's forces.
Since then, Turkey has worked to improve relations with the eastern authorities, including Haftar and his son Saddam, the deputy commander of the Libyan National Army.
In July, Ankara and the eastern military leadership reportedly reached agreements involving military facilities, surveillance systems and training programmes.
The parliamentary vote also followed a change in leadership.
On 6 October, Al-Salhin Abdelnabi al-Obeidi replaced Aguila Saleh as speaker of the House of Representatives after more than 12 years.
Saleh, who was considered close to Cairo, had long resisted ratifying the agreement.
His successor, who previously chaired the Libyan-Turkish parliamentary friendship committee, oversaw its approval as one of his first major decisions.
Youssef Essaied, an academic and researcher specialising in oil and energy economics, told The New Arab that the timing of the vote was linked to broader political developments, including US-backed efforts to unify Libya's rival authorities.
He pointed to the role of Massad Boulos, US President Donald Trump's adviser, in attempting to bring together the rival administrations in Tripoli and Benghazi.
The shift suggests that Ankara's influence now extends beyond its traditional allies in western Libya.
Does this mean Libya's rival authorities are uniting?
Not necessarily. The approval is significant because both Libya's rival centres of power now support the maritime agreement. However, the country's deeper political divisions remain unresolved.
Libya continues to have competing authorities, while disputes over control of the national budget, armed forces and electoral institutions remain central obstacles to political reunification.
The agreement therefore represents a notable area of cooperation between rival political camps rather than evidence of a comprehensive political settlement.
What happens next?
Despite parliamentary ratification, implementing the agreement could take years and face substantial legal, political and economic obstacles.
Essaied told The New Arab that the agreement was not an operational contract and that commercial energy production would require extensive geological surveys, exploration, financial assessments and negotiations.
He warned that Libya's political instability and unresolved maritime disputes could discourage international investment.
Companies may be reluctant to invest in offshore projects exposed to legal challenges from Greece or Egypt, particularly where competing sovereignty claims remain unresolved.
Essaied also highlighted concerns about corruption, weak oversight and the need for transparent management of Libya's energy resources.
Beyond the economic challenges, there is a risk that exploration activities in contested waters could provoke further tensions.
In August 2020, Turkey deployed the seismic survey vessel Oruç Reis to waters claimed by Greece, bringing the two NATO members close to military confrontation.
For now, the ratification represents a diplomatic gain for Ankara and a significant change in eastern Libya's position.

articles.title: Europe cannot count on American rescue, inquiry told
articles.body:
Europe cannot count on the United States returning to the European Arctic as the security partner and ally that Britain and Europe previously relied on, and NATO’s Article 5 is functionally moribund in the American sense, according to evidence published by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, examined the implications of American policy for High North security as part of its inquiry.
Dhesi said: “Our report calls for the government to reassess the JEF’s role and consider whether it should focus more on countering threats in the High North, particularly if the UK has to plan for uncertainty over US support for NATO. The UK’s presence in the Baltics, particularly in Estonia, may need to be bolstered to offset the effects of any greater JEF focus on the High North.”
Professor David Blagden of the University of Exeter told the committee: “[w]e can talk about the formal aspects of withdrawal or not but, functionally, you would probably say Article 5 in the American sense is pretty much moribund at the moment now anyway. No one really believes that the Americans are riding to the rescue if there were some situation in the Baltic states.”
The report sets out that the American 2026 National Defense Strategy outlined four lines of effort to achieve its America First strategic approach, covering defence of the United States homeland, deterring China in the Indo-Pacific through strength, increasing burden-sharing with allies and partners, and supercharging the American defence industrial base. The committee states that none of these suggest a return to greater engagement in Europe’s defence over the medium term, including the High North, and that where the Arctic is mentioned in the strategy it is in relation to American homeland defence.
The committee was told that “[e]ven if the next US President was a dyed in the wool Atlanticist—Eisenhower 2.0 or something—the US would not have the capacity to pivot back to playing the role it did in Europe and the High North”, largely because the United States perceives the maximum likelihood of conflict in East Asia as between 2027 and 2035.
On troop numbers, the report records a reported plan to cut between 25,000 and 40,000 American troops from the roughly 80,000 currently stationed in Europe, despite congressional provisions in the FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act restricting reductions below 76,000 personnel, and notes that significant future reductions in fighter jets, strategic bombers, destroyers, submarines, tanker aircraft and armed drones could also follow.
The Kiel Institute calculated that replacing American military capabilities with European weapons would cost an extra €50 billion each year over the next decade.
Professor Blagden also told the committee: “[t]he caveat, though, to all that glass-half-full stuff is that the UK, for years and years, has been generating SDSR-type documents in which we talk about how far we lean on allies. It has ultimately reached the point where the greatest of those allies has suddenly become unreliable… [w]e cannot just say, ‘We lean on an ally for this. We lean on an ally for that.’ When it comes to the High North, the UK is the major power now. The American cavalry is not about to ride over the horizon and save our fecklessness.”
Ministry of Defence witnesses drew a distinction between American capabilities and American commitments. On capabilities, the department said the United States is making it known to the rest of NATO that “[h]ere are the capabilities we [America] intend not to offer in the future. That is what we think a more European NATO looks like…” On commitments, Brigadier Jeremy Lamb, Head of Euro-Atlantic Security at the department, told the committee that “[w]hat they are talking about, is basing; it is not necessarily what they will make available to the SACEUR (Supreme Allied Commander Europe) in a crisis.”

articles.title: Downing Street rejects Witkoff’s description of Putin as a ‘humanitarian’
articles.body:
Downing Street has rejected the description of Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian” made by Donald Trump’s chief negotiator on the Ukraine war.
Steve Witkoff met the Russian president in St Petersburg on Wednesday as he sought to make a new push to end the invasion of Ukraine, with the US putting pressure on Kyiv to agree to a settlement.
In a Russian state media video clip posted on X, Witkoff told Putin: “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also sir, and I salute that. I commend you.”
When asked about Witkoff’s description of Putin, a Downing Street spokesperson said: “We certainly do not recognise that characterisation, and President Putin has killed thousands of people, both innocent Ukrainians and his own Russian people, who he has sent to their deaths on the frontline.
“He is starving children and the elderly of the heat and warmth, and systematically targeting critical national infrastructure. Ukraine’s foreign minister summed it up well this morning when he said: ‘This night, the residents of Kyiv heard what Russian humanitarianism really sounds like.’”
Asked if the government would make this argument directly to the US administration, the spokesperson said: “We engage regularly at a range of levels with a range of partners on Ukraine, and I’m sure we will continue to do so.”
Downing Street’s remarks came after the Scottish secretary, Douglas Alexander, told LBC that Britain viewed Putin as “somebody who illegally invaded Ukraine at the start of this conflict, who has been responsible for conduct by his government that included attempted assassinations on UK soil”.
Alexander added: “We simply do not recognise the description of Vladimir Putin as a humanitarian.”
After Witkoff met Putin, Russia agreed to resume peace talks with Ukraine and the US in principle. Trump has suggested Russia and Ukraine are “maybe now the closest we’ve been” to ending the war.
Despite this, Russia has continued to launch missile attacks at Ukraine, including a drone strike on Kharkiv as Putin and Witkoff spoke.
Last week, Andy Burnham welcomed Volodymyr Zelenskyy to Downing Street and backed the Ukrainian president amid Trump’s attacks.
Trump had suggested Zelenskyy should be replaced and declined to say whether Russia was responsible for the war.

articles.title: Pentagon and Lockheed have agreed to produce 850 F-35 fighter jets
articles.body:
Pentagon and Lockheed have agreed to produce 850 F-35 fighter jets
Kyiv • UNN
Lockheed Martin has reached a preliminary agreement with the Pentagon to produce and support 850 F-35s over 10 years. The company will invest at least $7 billion.
Lockheed Martin has reached a preliminary agreement with the U.S. Department of Defense to produce and support at least 850 F-35 Lightning II fighter jets over the next 10 years, they said on October 22. UNN reports this, citing Reuters.
Details
The Pentagon said the defense contractor would independently finance at least $7 billion in initiatives supporting the F-35 program.
The F-35, built using stealth technology that allows it to avoid detection by the enemy, is considered the most advanced fighter jet in the world and is the backbone of Lockheed’s aeronautics division, which accounts for about 40% of its quarterly revenue.
Under the agreement with the Pentagon, Lockheed aims to maintain annual production at 156 aircraft.
The agreement is not an order but is considered a preliminarily agreed long-term contract.
"If multiyear authorization is provided in the coming months, the F-35 Joint Program Office and Lockheed Martin will work toward finalizing the contract terms, pricing, and schedule through the formal award of a contract," the company said.
The agreement also covers international orders for the F-35, as well as initial spare parts and modification kits, according to a statement from Lockheed, based in Arlington, U.S.
"We have fundamentally changed our approach to stabilizing the American defense industrial base to ensure rapid and large-scale production," said U.S. Deputy Secretary of Defense Michael Duffy.
"This agreement with Lockheed Martin proves it. By aligning financial incentives with actual performance, we ensure that our military is equipped with the lethal capabilities necessary to fight and win," he said.
Lockheed and its colleagues across the United States have benefited from increased global defense spending amid ongoing geopolitical conflicts, the publication notes.
According to Lockheed’s estimates, the agreement will support 317,000 jobs in the United States and generate nearly $79 billion in annual economic activity over the next decade. It also expects the arrangement to reduce production costs and ease supply-chain constraints, from raw materials to finished parts.

Kuzovkov was shot five times near his home in the eastern Polish town of Biała Podlaska on 15 June. He was an artist whose work, published under the name Skrepetsky, focused on creating satirical cartoons mocking Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
He had fled Russia in 2021 due to fear of political prosecution. Before his death, Kuzovkov had reported on social media that he had received death threats from supporters of Chechen leader and Putin ally Ramzan Kadyrov, who had also been the subject of the artist’s satirical cartoons.
After the shooting, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that “everything points to this being a political assassination”. He also revealed that Kuzavkov had previously been offered protection by the Polish authorities, but “for reasons unknown” had refused.
On 18 June, the Polish authorities announced they had captured Elnur A. in a hostel near Warsaw. The following day, he was charged with the murder of Kuzovkov. He has remained in custody since then.
Police have detained a man suspected of carrying out the murder of Russian dissident Semyon Skrepetsky, who was shot dead near his home in Poland this week.
