On Thursday, Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office revealed that Makhmud A. had been detained on 19 October by the Internal Security Agency (ABW) in a car park along the A2 motorway.
The ABW itself confirmed that it detained the suspect after he flew to Poland from Georgia on 18 October. He had been travelling with two other Georgians, who will now be expelled from Poland and handed a 10-year re-entry ban.
Makhmud A. was subsequently charged with aiding and abetting the killing of Kuzovkov by “undertaking a number of actions in the period from 1 to 11 June 2026 that made it easier for Elnur A. to commit the murder”. He is additionally charged with illegal possession of firearms and ammunition.
Makhmud A. is accused of providing the perpetrator with a weapon, means of transportation and a mobile phone with an application enabling monitoring of the victim’s vehicle, a spokeswoman for the district court in Lublin told broadcaster TVN.
The court has approved a period of three months’ detention for Makhmud A., with prosecutors saying that they fear he could otherwise “flee, go into hiding, or unlawfully obstruct proceedings”.
Under Polish law, someone found guilty of aiding and abetting a crime can face the same punishment as the person who committed the crime itself, meaning that both suspects face potential prison sentences of between 10 years and life if found guilty. They have pleaded not guilty.
A Russian man has been shot dead in Poland, with reports indicating that he was an artist whose work ridiculed Putin and that his killing appeared to be an “execution”.

The Polish authorities have not yet revealed who they believe was ultimately behind the murder of Kuzovkov. However, in June, Tusk said that, if Russia’s involvement was confirmed, it would be a case of “state terrorism”.
In recent years, Poland has become a primary target for Russia’s campaign of so-called “hybrid warfare”, which has involved acts of sabotage, disinformation, cyberattacks, and airspace violations.
Most known on-the-ground activity has been carried out not by Russian operatives themselves, but by so-called “disposable agents” hired through messaging service Telegram and paid in cryptocurrency. In some cases, Russia has used existing criminal networks to carry out such tasks.

articles.title: Canada opens free trade talks with Turkey
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Canada opens free trade talks with Turkey
Canada, which is in the midst of a trade war with the United States, opened talks with Turkey Thursday on a free trade agreement during a landmark visit by Prime Minister Mark Carney.
Carney, a former central banker, has made reducing dependence on Washington and diversifying Canada's partnerships one of the cornerstones of his term, which began in March 2025.
"We decided to begin negotiations for a free trade agreement, which includes increasing trade and investment, before the end of the year," Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said in a joint address to reporters.
Carney is the first Canadian prime minister to pay an official visit to Turkey.
"We hope to increase our trade volume, which is currently around $3 billion, to $5 billion and then $10 billion. We will approximately double direct flights between our countries," Erdogan said.
Carney said Canadian negotiators would come to Ankara next month for the first round of free trade talks.
"Our goal is not self-sufficiency, it is collective resilience," said Carney.
"And that's why Canada is building deeper partnerships with reliable partners that create new opportunities for us both. And in Turkey, we have an exceptional partner."
Carney is due to meet on Friday with Turkish business leaders in Istanbul, in strategic sectors such as energy, aerospace and critical minerals.
Canada and Turkey have also identified potential for cooperation in nuclear energy.
They also announced a partnership agreement in the defence industry.
"Today's new Agreement on Defence Industry Partnership will connect Canadian and Turkish companies to work together, creating good jobs at home, export opportunities abroad, greater security for our citizens, and contributing to a stronger NATO alliance," Carney said.
Carney has multiplied overseas trips, renewing ties with nations such as Saudi Arabia, India and China with which relations had been strained or even broken under his predecessor Justin Trudeau.
Carney has also drawn closer to Europe.

articles.title: Britain still plans new nuclear sub every eighteen months
articles.body:
Ministers have confirmed that the intention remains to procure up to twelve SSN-AUKUS submarines, and that the investments needed to establish industrial capacity for a submarine every eighteen months from the mid-2030s have been made, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Andrew Rosindell, the Reform UK member for Romford, asked the Secretary of State for Defence whether he would make it his department’s policy to increase total hull numbers in the submarine service.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “As set out in the Defence Investment Plan (DIP), the Ministry of Defence intends to procure up to 12 SSN AUKUS submarines.
“The programme is currently midway through the Detailed Design and Long Lead (D2L2) phase and we anticipate that the number of submarines will be confirmed before the end of this phase in 2028.
“Through the DIP, the Government has made the investments necessary to establish the industrial capacity required to ultimately deliver a submarine every 18 months from the mid-2030s to ensure we can deliver an expanded SSN force.”
Britain currently operates seven Astute class attack submarines, and this publication reported the government’s commitment to build twelve new nuclear attack submarines when the plan appeared. A drumbeat of one boat every eighteen months would be the fastest sustained British submarine production rate since the Cold War, and the figure follows from the capacity being built at Barrow.
Barrow has been expanding through the Barrow Infrastructure Programme, with new build halls, a reconfigured yard and a recruitment effort that has taken the BAE Systems workforce there past twelve thousand. Rolls-Royce Submarines in Derby has doubled its site to produce reactors for both Dreadnought and SSN-AUKUS, and the Sheffield Forgemasters work on large forgings feeds the same chain.
Confirmation of the final number before the end of the detailed design phase in 2028 ties the fleet size to what the yard can actually sustain. Senior officials told the Commons Defence Committee earlier this year that submarine fleet size was conditional on Barrow output, and a decision due in 2028 falls inside this Parliament.
Australia will build its own SSN-AUKUS boats at Osborne in South Australia to a common design, and the two production lines are intended to share a supply chain, which is part of the case for the industrial investment on the British side. Dreadnought holds priority at Barrow through the late 2020s, so attack submarine production builds up behind the ballistic missile boats.
Pollard confirmed in a separate answer the same day that steel will be cut on the first British SSN-AUKUS next year, and that the Preliminary Design Review for the class concluded on the first of July. Twelve boats remains an upper bound until the design phase closes.

articles.title: Driver at Russian-held Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant killed in drone attacks, managers say
articles.body:
Driver at Russian-held Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant killed in drone attacks, managers say
Oct 21 - Management at the Russian-held Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in southeastern Ukraine said a driver at the station had been killed on Wednesday after two days of Ukrainian drone attacks.
Russian forces seized the station, Europe's largest with six reactors, in the first weeks of the February 2022 invasion. Each side has since repeatedly accused the other of military activity liable to jeopardise nuclear safety.
The plant's managers in a post on Telegram said buses carrying staff to and from the plant had come under attack for two days in a row.
"The second straight day of attacks on the station's transport shows that these strikes are deliberate," the statement said.
It said the attacks "pose a direct threat" to staff who ensured operations at the plant.
Russia has in recent months accused Ukraine of attacking sites and services associated with the plant, including transport.
Rosatom, Russia's state nuclear corporation, said a Ukrainian drone attack on a service car in July killed the plant's chief engineer and the vehicle's driver.
The city of Enerhodar, where most of the nuclear station's staff live, has also been a frequent target.
Rosatom last week said a truce agreement, mediated by the UN's nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency, was in place to allow repairs at a thermal power station supplying power to the nuclear plant. REUTERS

By expanding its Unmanned Systems Forces, which numbered 87,000 personnel at the end of 2025 and are expected to grow to 165,000 by the end of 2026, Russia is facing a shortage of military personnel.
In addition, the Rubicon Center is competing with the 50th Varyag Brigade for specialists.
Due to the overall personnel shortage in the Russian army, the center continues to recruit specialists from frontline brigades.

articles.title: Denmark to Provide €100.5 Million Loan Guarantee for Fire Point Subsidiary
articles.body:
Denmark is providing a state-backed loan guarantee of DKK 750 million (approximately €100.5million) to a subsidiary of Fire Point Rocket Technologies.
According to a press release published by ViaRitzau, the guarantee is intended to help the company secure a loan from a Danish bank.
Because of the war in Ukraine, the company has been unable to obtain financing under normal commercial terms.
Under the guarantee, the Danish state will not provide the loan directly. Instead, it will cover the bank’s losses if the company fails to repay the loan, subject to the guarantee’s terms.
The financing is being arranged through the Export and Investment Fund of Denmark (EIFO), which is currently involved in nearly 40 projects supporting Ukraine and its reconstruction.
Danish Minister for Business and Competitiveness Martin Lidegaard noted that establishing Ukrainian defence production in Denmark promotes knowledge sharing, strengthens Danish industry, and makes Europe more independent.
Meanwhile, Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus stressed that locating production facilities outside Ukraine protects them from Russian strikes and helps ensure reliable supply chains.
In addition, the cooperation gives the Danish armed forces and businesses access to unique technologies and combat experience gained by Ukrainian specialists during the war.
As a reminder, Denmark became the first country to allow a Ukrainian defence company to establish production facilities on its territory, allocating a site in Southern Jutland.
The facility is designed to produce solid rocket propellant.
The project is being carried out by the Danish subsidiary of Fire Point Rocket Technologies, which operates under its parent company in Ukraine.
Construction was initially estimated to cost €50 million. The total project cost has since increased to more than €150 million. The company has already obtained all the necessary permits to begin operations.

articles.title: Russia returns bodies of 252 Ukrainian soldiers
articles.body:
Russia returns bodies of 252 Ukrainian soldiers
Russia has handed over the remains of 252 Ukrainian soldiers killed in the conflict and received the bodies of 25 Russian troops in return, according to multiple reports.
The transfer reportedly took place on Thursday in Belarus near the Novaya Guta border crossing with Ukraine. Officials and media outlets in all three countries confirmed the details of the repatriations.
Footage from the scene shows monitors from the International Committee of the Red Cross overseeing the transfer.
The disparity in the number of bodies returned is typical, unlike prisoner-of-war swaps, which are generally conducted on an equal basis.
Pro-Kiev commentators have long argued that the imbalance does not reflect the actual ratio of battlefield casualties, as advancing Russian forces are better positioned to recover the bodies of fallen Ukrainian soldiers. However, the latest round, which followed Kiev’s claims of a major offensive near the city of Liman, showed no significant change in the proportion.
Neither Russia nor Ukraine officially publishes comprehensive figures for its military casualties. Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky has cited death tolls that even pro-Kiev commentators consider implausibly low. In July, he claimed that “about 50,000” Ukrainian troops had been killed, down from the 55,000 deaths he reported in February.
Many Ukrainian battlefield casualties are classified as missing in action, which allows the cash-strapped government to defer compensation to the families of the fallen soldiers.
In summer 2025, Russian officials accused their Ukrainian counterparts of refusing to take hundreds of remains. The Ukrainians rejected the allegations, which the Russians said could be explained by a shortage of bodies in Kiev’s reserves and its concerns over the bad optics of a one-sided repatriation.
On three separate days in mid-June 2025, Russia unilaterally returned 1,200 bodies to Ukraine.
